islands.title: The library

territories.title: 1 · Project libraries
territories.description: Each project gets its own library, a separate database on one Postgres server, created the first time the project is opened, with its tables set up automatically, and brought up to date by the next open after storytree adds to them. Opening a project whose tables are already current touches no table, so an account let only read, or write a few kinds of record, can open it too. Storytree can list the projects on the server, and nothing written in one project can ever show up in another.

territories.title: 2 · Library transactions
territories.description: The only data actions the library allows are: save a record, fetch it, list records of one type, change only named fields, or retire a record with a reason. Every change is all-or-nothing, and is written first to a permanent, append-only history, so nothing is ever truly erased.

territories.title: 3 · Data schema
territories.description: Every record has a declared type with a fixed set of fields, and a badly filled-in record is refused with a message naming the problem field. Every record is stamped with the schema version it was written on, so a later change to a type is handled deliberately rather than silently misread: an older record is upgraded automatically, step by step, and stored upgraded the next time it is written, because every user's library is their own database and nobody else can repair it.

territories.title: 4 · Work model
territories.description: The library holds each project's plan of work: arcs (initiatives), stories (what a user can do), capabilities (the parts that make a story work) and contracts (single testable promises). Capabilities and contracts point at their parent. Stories belong to the project directly, and an arc *may* list the stories it grows, though a research arc may list none. The library refuses broken structure. A capability carries a proposed flag, on from its birth until the agent says it is built (`setProposed`, ADR-0744 D2); switching it says nothing about health, and a capability written before the flag reads proposed. A story is made mapped (ADR-0993 D2) only by mapStories, which an import calls: one mapped story per package of the import, keyed by the package, with no capabilities; a mapped field given to addStory or editStory is refused.

territories.title: 6 · Knowledge artifacts
territories.description:
Alongside the plan, the library keeps what the project has learned: decisions and definitions of terms, and principles, guardrails, patterns, processes, agent roles, friction, re-steers and tech stack, each with 0.2's fields. Each can link to the other artifacts it relates to, and you can find them again by searching their words; an edit keeps the old wording in history. An artifact never links straight to the work: capability 9 is how the work reaches its knowledge.

Planned, not yet built (ADR-0956 D3, contract 6.12): a ninth kind, the quality control check, one yes-or-no question about a finished change, linked to the principle or guardrail note it enforces.

territories.title: 5 · Health record
territories.description: Every story, capability and contract has a health record with two separate columns: what the agent **reported**, and what storytree **verified** by seeing it for itself. Each column is one of three states: `passing`, `failing` or `not-checked`. A missing entry always reads as `not-checked`, never as `passing`. A capability also has a word, as its card says it (ADR-0744 D1, D3): `proposed` while its flag is on; once the agent switches it off, `healthy` when every contract is verified passing, `unhealthy` when any is verified failing, and `untested` otherwise. Only the verified column counts: the agent's report never makes a capability healthy.

territories.title: 7 · Library API
territories.description: One small, fixed list of functions is the only way anything outside the library reads or writes it. The agent link, arc surface, forest and desktop app all call these, and `changesSince` lets them see what just changed without re-reading everything.

territories.title: 8 · Cloud connection (GCP)
territories.description: Instead of the local Postgres, a user can point storytree at a Postgres database in Google Cloud (Cloud SQL) and sign in with their Google account rather than a stored password. Everything above works the same, and each project still gets its own database, now on the cloud server.

territories.title: 9 · Knowledge entrances
territories.description: Every story and capability has its own shelf of front-cover decisions, and a decision can be a front cover of one of them at most. Artifacts link only to other artifacts, so the only way from the work into the knowledge is through a front cover.

territories.title: 10 · Work in flight
territories.description: Each arc is whole: its intent, its end state and its increments. An increment moves from proposal to active to closed (ADR-0909 D4 retired the ready step; one stored as ready reads as a proposal). An arc reads closed when its last increment closes, and reopens when new work is parked on it, unless the owner has parked the arc. A closed increment stays, as the arc's log entry: its date, pull request, note, and whether it landed, failed or was withdrawn.

territories.title: 11 · Waits
territories.description: An arc waits on an arc, and an increment on an increment on any arc, each with a reason. A loop across both kinds is refused when it is written. The library alone answers whether a wait holds (`waitHolds`), naming its blockers and saying when one can never release.

territories.title: 12 · Owner questions
territories.description: A question is raised on an arc, with its stakes, statement, context and options, and settled with the owner's answer, which stays on the arc. An increment held on an open question reads as waiting on him (`heldOnQuestion`), and the library alone answers that.

territories.title: 13 · Decision log
territories.description: Decision numbers do not collide, even across concurrent writers, and history reserves every number a decision has held. Other projects start at 1. In the project named exactly `storytree`, automatic numbers exceed the persisted floor and every number any non-health record has ever held; automatic numbering is refused if that setting is absent. An explicit free number remains accepted. The N1 move is complete: the 29 Full record decisions retain their 0.2 numbers, the floor is 662, and the 53 founding books are ADR-0663..0715. Ordinary edits cannot change or remove a decision's number. A decision's status is proposed or accepted, and it can be superseded: the superseded decision is kept, and reads as superseded. A decision carries the load-bearing mark, who decided it, in their own words, and one composed statement. Health events never reserve decision numbers, including in repair previews and writes; legacy non-health reservations remain.

territories.title: 14 · Ranked search
territories.description:
A library search ranks the live artifacts by how close their meaning is to the question, using an embedding model (bge-small) run on this computer, with no LLM, paid API or extra service, as the owner directed (0.2's ADR-0664). An artifact written or edited is embedded again before the next search ranks it, and with no model to hand the search falls back to word matches and says why.

As built: Windows delivery stages the locked Transformers Node distribution, ONNX Runtime CPU binding and DLL, and the Sharp runtime dependency beside the CLI and MCP entrypoints for x64 and arm64. No model weights ship. The existing lazy loader downloads bge-small on first use into <storytree home>/models. The installed-layout check imports Transformers and runs a weight-free ONNX Identity graph on the native CPU backend without a source checkout. Windows x64 execution is checked by installer CI; ARM64 PE headers are inspected, with ARM64 execution awaiting a native Windows acceptance run.

territories.title: 15 · Connection by address
territories.description: Instead of the local app's Postgres or Cloud SQL with Google sign-in, storytree reaches any Postgres by its address (Neon, Supabase, RDS, self-hosted, Cloud SQL with an ordinary user), its password resolved as a key.

islands.title: Session management

territories.title: 1 · Project routing
territories.description: The first time an agent session starts in a folder that isn't a storytree project, storytree asks the user (through the agent) whether to set one up; if they say yes, this leaves a small marker in the folder naming the project, and from then on it routes everything an agent does anywhere in that folder to that project, whichever project the user happens to be looking at in the app. It never picks a project by itself: a folder the user hasn't said yes to is ignored, and when storytree isn't running it says so at once, so everything built on it quietly does nothing.

territories.title: 2 · Agent activity log
territories.description: Session management's own logbook of what agents do, one per project and kept beside the library rather than inside it, with one line for each thing that happens: a session starts or ends, a file is edited, a command runs, an artifact is read, work is claimed, released or landed. Lines are only ever added, never changed, and can be read back in order as "everything since line N", including lines that other processes wrote.

territories.title: 3 · Hooks
territories.description: Small commands that Claude Code and Codex run by themselves when a session starts, after every file edit, before and after every shell command, at the end of each turn, and when it ends, each adding one line about that session to the agent activity log, so an agent that never calls storytree still shows up. At each prompt, one more adds the project's definitions for the terms the prompt names, for the agent to read: every matching term not yet given this session, longest first, with no cap (3.7). The cap of five that 0.2's ADR-0201 set, never measured and never chosen by the owner, is removed by the owner's named choice ("turn the cap off.", 2026-09-28; ADR-0739 D3, ADR-0633); the once-per-session and harness-notice rules, which 0.2 did measure, stay. The same prompt hook carries capability 9's fresh-session nudge to a Claude Code session past its context guidance (9.9). At a session's start in a folder that isn't a storytree project yet, the harness waits for one more (Codex's own start hook, a second one for Claude Code), which has the agent ask the user whether to set storytree up there before the task it was given, and sets nothing up itself (8.12). Every hook also records the transcript path the harness named for its session, so capability 9 can work out any session's tokens used when asked, never from a transcript found by folder (ADR-0725, ADR-0728). They run in the background and always exit cleanly, so they can never slow down or break the agent, and when storytree isn't running they do nothing.

territories.title: 4 · Sessions
territories.description: Reads the agent activity log as a list of agent sessions, one per Claude Code or Codex window, each showing which of the two it is, which folder it works in, when it started and when it was last seen. A session is working from a prompt until its turn ends, or while a command it started runs, and waiting otherwise (ADR-0754 D5); ended once its end line arrives. A session whose hooks report no turns (no prompt line: hooks not running, or installed before D5) is working while its lines keep arriving and waiting after the quiet time, the user's `idle-after` setting (capability 10, 10.10; ADR-0739 D2), 30 minutes when unset. So it never reads as working just because nobody said otherwise.

territories.title: 5 · Claims
territories.description: Before building a capability, the agent claims it with a one-line reason, so the user and the other agents can see who is on what, and every edit its session makes while holding the claim counts toward that capability. Only one live session can hold a capability: a second agent is refused with the holder's name and picks other work instead of queueing, and a claim ends when the agent lands or releases it, when its session ends, or when another agent takes it over after the holder has gone idle.

territories.title: 9 · Context readings
territories.description:
How many tokens a session's own context window holds, worked out when it is asked for from what the hooks recorded (ADR-0725, ADR-0728; 0.2's `storytree context`, ADR-0716 O2). The hooks record each session's transcript path (capability 3). A reading is computed at ask time from that transcript as it stands, so it is fresh mid-turn, and in a `claude -p` run whose turn has not ended. On the session's own machine (the status line, `storytree context`) that means the transcript file itself. The app reads no transcript file: its readings and windows are parsed from the transcript records the hooks stream into the shared log (3.13; ADR-0749 D3), so an app on any machine reads every machine's sessions. Those records have obvious secrets scrubbed on the way in (9.12) and are kept 180 days, after which what was worked out from them is kept instead (9.13; ADR-0749 D4). A reading is a plain record: the session, its harness, tokens used, when it was read, and its source (the transcript it was read from). It carries no window size and no fraction (ADR-0728 D1). The guidance a session judges against is a token figure the user sets on the agent link settings surface (capability 10, `context-guidance`; ADR-0728 D2, D3). A reading states that guidance and whether tokens used are past it or under it (9.7); it is a soft line, never enforced. The same figure is the line past which a Claude Code session is nudged, through the prompt hook (capability 3), to hand off and start fresh (9.9; ADR-0739 D1): one setting, no second figure, and 0.2's separate 850,000 hard mark is not brought across. The nudge is advice; nothing stops the session. Codex sessions get no nudge until Codex matures (ADR-0739 D5). This capability owns the nudge because whether a session is past its guidance is this capability's reading (9.7); the prompt hook only carries the words. Built with advice once per session; later prompts in the same session do not repeat it.

For Claude Code, tokens used are the latest request of the session's own conversation: `input_tokens` + `cache_read_input_tokens` + `cache_creation_input_tokens`, counted once per `requestId`, with subagent (`isSidechain`) and `<synthetic>` lines left out. A transcript with nothing to count is an absence with its reason, never 0. For Codex, tokens used are the rollout's last token count. Any live session's reading can be worked out this way without that session asking, so the board can later show one per session; that display is not built here. It reads and never enforces: the session still decides whether to take on more work.

The transcript is always the one the hooks recorded as named by the harness (`transcript_path`, on every Claude Code and Codex hook input). Nothing ever looks for a session's transcript by folder. That is what fixes 0.2's two blind spots. 0.2 worked out who was asking from the `.claude/worktrees/<name>` folder the command ran in, then matched transcripts whose recorded `cwd` sat inside it. A batch (`claude -p`) session run from a main checkout or from outside that folder was refused or matched nothing (0.2 friction `storytree-context-cannot-read-a-batch-sessions-own-window`). A session that moved into a fresh worktree kept writing its transcript under the project directory of the folder it started in, so the new folder matched nothing. And because worktree folders are reused, the fallback could read another session's window (0.2 friction `context-verb-blinded-by-the-fresh-worktree-its-own-rule-mandates`: no reading from the new worktree, 506,097 tokens from the old one in the same minute).

As built (guidance-reading): `contextReading` and `readContext` add `guidance` without changing the existing session, harness, tokens, composition, at or transcript-source fields. Guidance is `{ value, source: "default" | "set", position: "under" | "at" | "past" }`, read afresh through capability 10's `readSettings`; its default is 600,000 tokens (ADR-0739 D1). An unusable settings file gives `{ absent: <the reader's reason> }` while retaining an available token count. No transcript remains an absence with no token count. `storytree context` and `read_context` state the guidance in their text and include it in their data; a count under, at or past guidance is never refused. Contract 9.7 is pinned in `packages/agent-link/src/context/context.test.ts`, and the existing 6.22 MCP test checks guidance output.

Remaining integration for 9.7: the current library-location routing reads the same settings file before it can open the activity log (ADR-0735). If that file is already unusable when `storytree context` or `read_context` starts routing, the call cannot reach the transcript record; the reader's token-preserving guidance error is therefore not reachable through those entry points in that case. This lane does not guess a local library or bypass the settings reader. Resolving that routing dependency is outside its context/tools-output file fence. Contract 9.7 must not be marked fully proved until that end-to-end case is resolved. `packages/agent-link/evidence/guidance-reading/captures.txt` records both the successful reader case and the route refusal.

As built (fresh-nudge): the Claude Code prompt hook calls the existing `readContext` for the session named by the recorded hook input. It adds advice to hand off and start a fresh session at the next safe boundary only when that reading is past its current guidance, naming both tokens used and the guidance. Definitions and context advice use separate per-session ledgers through the definitions hook's extracted `notYetGivenIds` helper; each nudge is given once per session across separate hook processes. Under or at guidance, absent readings, unreadable settings, and Codex inputs add no nudge. No threshold or switch is added: the existing reading supplies the sole setting, including the default change owned by capability 10. The built-hook contract 9.9 test covers boundaries, changed settings, repetition, definitions alongside advice, Codex, and absence/recovery; every prompt exits 0 with no blocking decision. The existing 9.7 routing qualification above remains.

territories.title: 10 · Settings
territories.description: The user's own settings for Session management: read and written by this package, set from the command line and from the app's settings panel (ADR-0728 D2, D3; ADR-0729; ADR-0739; ADR-0649). Per user only: one file, `settings.json`, in the storytree home (`STORYTREE_HOME`, else `[home], capability 1) beside `project-choice.json`. Each setting has a name, a type, a default and a plain-language meaning. An unset setting reads as its default, marked as the default. A value of the wrong type, or a name that is not a setting, is refused with its reason and nothing is written. A settings file that cannot be read or is not valid is reported, naming the file and the problem; it is never silently replaced, and a set refuses to overwrite it.

territories.title: 11 · Machines
territories.description: The computers that work on a project, each with a short name its owner gives it, its hostname and its id, read from what the trunks and machine.json already hold; a way to give this computer its name and to ask which one it is; and the sessions list showing each session's machine by that name.

islands.title: The app

territories.title: 1 · Lifecycle
territories.description: When the app opens it starts the database that holds every project's library, and it keeps it running until the app is quit: closing the window leaves both running in the background, with a tray icon whose Quit stops them, so agents' work is still recorded. The app can also be controlled from outside (ADR-0656 D0): asking it to quit from the command line stops it as the tray's Quit does. There is one owner at a time: opening the app again brings its window forward, another program holding the database is named, and while it runs the app leaves records saying where the database is and how to open the app, which is how an agent's session finds it or opens it.

territories.title: 2 · Storytree projects
territories.description: The app lists the storytree projects in its database and shows one at a time. Its always-visible, full-width top app bar holds only a gear at the right. The gear opens a large centred overlay with Projects, Settings, Updates and Help sections. Projects moves the whole app to another project in place; Settings mounts the agent link's per-user panel, Updates mounts the app's existing update status, and Help mounts app-setup's existing help surface. The separate arcs-only bar sits below the app bar and the forest starts below both. This capability also decides which project is on show when the app opens.

territories.title: 3 · Surfaces
territories.description: The app's window hosts the surfaces for the project on show: the forest, which the app opens on (until it lands, today's plain list), with the arc surface as an overlay that the forest hosts. The page cannot reach the database, so the app carries everything a surface reads to it, and tells the surfaces when the project changes.

territories.title: 4 · Updates
territories.description:
The app keeps itself up to date by itself: on the owner's machine it runs from its own copy of merged main, notices new merges within a few minutes, and rebuilds and restarts itself in the background, so it never runs unmerged work and nobody rebuilds it by hand. Check for updates in the top-right gear asks that same merged-main updater to check now and shows the running build and its progress or failure. A ready build waits with the window open until no seed or start-up or daily snapshot is being written. A checkout explains that it does not update itself. Installed apps select releases from their own channel: development follows each merged release; stable follows only the owner-pinned existing build (ADR-0871). As built (increment_aca4e6853237): an installed app's downloaded release waits for a quiet moment (packages/app whenToInstall: ten minutes after launch, ten minutes without window input or agent activity from a session that has not ended), because a first install was replaced 17 seconds after setup said the app was open (packages/app-setup/evidence/acceptance, F1). The gear answers from the release updater in an installed app, marks itself with a dot while an update is pending, and its Restart to update installs at once. A seed or snapshot still holds any restart, including one requested from the gear. The owner accepted contracts 4.4 and 4.7's wording for this on 2026-09-29 (a question).

As built (increment_c3e1441890f9, contract 4.12): installed release updates read named, independent run holds under the app home/update-holds before each automatic installation. packages/app/src/updates/hold-run.mjs wraps a foreground command, publishes its hold before launch, removes it on return and preserves its exit code. Holds expire after the requested positive duration, at most six hours; overlapping runs do not release one another. Downloads continue, the pending status names the run, and the user's Restart to update still overrides holds while respecting seed writes and snapshots. The standalone wrapper and usage/proof are in packages/app/evidence/update-hold. No laptop acceptance run is part of this implementation.


As built (increment_402e76453e34, contract 4.17): the follow-main updater start-checks each new build before it may restart into it (apps/desktop/src/main/start-check.ts, wrapping follow-main's build through mainUpdates' update option). The build is started with --start-check, which goes only as far as registering the main process's handlers and exits 0: no library, no network, so a library on Cloud SQL or a local Postgres the running app holds never holds back a good build. A check that does not exit 0 within 60 s fails the build as 4.2 does, and that commit is remembered and not rebuilt. Lifecycle 1.13: run()'s rejection now ends the app (exit 1) instead of leaving it half-started holding the single-instance lock.

islands.title: The forest

territories.title: 1 · Story nodes
territories.description: The forest keeps one story node for every story in the project: where the story sits in the forest, with its title and its overall health. Nodes follow the library, so a new story appears as a new node and a retired story's node goes, with nothing arranged by hand.

territories.title: 2 · Capability tree
territories.description: Each story node carries its capability tree: the story's capabilities, which ones build on which, and where each one stands, from planned through built to landed, and it grows as they land. Where a capability stands comes from two records kept side by side: the arc surface's rule for planned, in progress or landed, and the health the agent reports for its tests, always labelled as the agent's own.

territories.title: 3 · Story node render
territories.description: The page opens in Forest mode, drawing every story node on the globe as a flat island cut into its capabilities' territories (ADR-0804 D1, D2) with the library core beneath them. Forest / Library switches this one globe (ADR-0660 D4): Library hides the story nodes and shows the knowledge points alone. You can turn and zoom in either mode, hover a visible artifact dot to see its title, and click a dot to read its summary in the right-hand story-panel slot (ADR-0661 D1/D2). Forest also lets you open a story by clicking its island. An artifact card and a story panel replace one another; Close and Escape dismiss the card. Switching modes preserves the scene, camera, rotation and zoom. Each launch defaults to Forest, with no saved mode. The flat forest and separate Look-inside view remain unavailable (ADR-0655).

territories.title: 4 · Drill-down
territories.description: Clicking a story node opens a panel that explains the story in plain words: its sentences, and its capability tree, each capability pointing at the ones it builds on, including any in other stories, named with their story. The tree has a space of its own inside the panel, where the user drags it around and zooms it; it opens zoomed out to fit the whole tree, as far as the least zoom allows, and an icon in that space's corner opens the same tree in a larger window over the forest, which opens fitted too. Each capability's card says proposed, healthy, unhealthy or untested on a strip coloured as 0.2 coloured those words, with the agent's report and storytree's as labelled marks (ADR-0743, ADR-0744). Clicking one of the story's own capabilities, in the panel's tree or in the larger window, shows it below the panel's tree: its sentences, its health as the agent reports it, and its contracts on request (ADR-0659).

territories.title: 5 · Agent capability claims
territories.description: Shows on the world what each running session holds. Each capability claimed by a session that has a row in the running-sessions list (capability 7) carries one flag in that session's colour, standing inside the capability's territory (ADR-0968, which replaced the inset border band of ADR-0923 D1 and the outline of ADR-0825 D3). Each session has its own stable colour, the same on its flags and on its row, never the proven green or the needs-you amber. The flag keeps its size on screen and becomes a dot on an island too small to carry a pennant; it drops in with one ring at its foot when the claim arrives, stands still while held, furls and greys when its holder goes quiet, and lifts away when the claim is released or lands, with no movement under reduced motion. On an island with no surveyed code the claimed capability's equal share is marked as a staked lot, a dashed white line inside its border; a capability with no code on an island that has code draws nothing. No band, outline, fill or coast tint is drawn for a claim, so a territory's fill stays health's. A flag carries no visible agent name, reason text or hooks warning. It follows the agent link's claims and sessions, so a holder whose hooks have reported goes quiet after the quiet time; a holder whose hooks have never reported is never quiet as idle. Subagents and supervised lanes folded under a parent flag in the parent's colour, a session with no row flags nothing, and an increment claim draws nothing on the world (ADR-0923 D2). A growth replay flags the capabilities its recorded sessions held as it reaches them (contract 5.7). Missing hooks are reported by the agent link's setup check (capability 8, contract 8.5). *History: the wisps of ADR-0736 were removed by ADR-0804 D9; ADR-0825 D3 outlined a claimed territory and tinted the coast; ADR-0923 dropped the coast tint; ADR-0968 (2026-10-10) made the mark a flag and added lots.*

territories.title: 7 · Running sessions
territories.description: A see-through strip along the forest pane's bottom, spanning its width and collapsible by its header (contract 7.17) lists one plain row per session that has not ended, claimed or not (ADR-0749 D1; ADR-0737 D1's removal of off-plan rows and their evidence stands, and capability 6 stays retired), showing facts as labels and no prose on the owner's behalf: anything that needs the owner is an open question on the arc surface (ADR-0824). An unclaimed row is named from its harness and what it works in; a session working in several worktrees says so (D2). Each row shows what it is doing, its context bar and its available context total. Explicitly related subagents and supervised lanes fold beneath their parent behind “+N”. Each row has one expander (the same control as “+N”), closed at first; expanded, it lists each worktree the session works in (full path on hover) labelled unmerged or merged, the commands it started and has not seen finish, and the files in its window, read from the agent link's window reading (9.10) only when expanded, then its children. No row uses a state colour; each root row wears its session’s own colour, the colour of its wisps on the forest (capability 5, ADR-0736), and a hovered wisp highlights its row. Hovering or focusing a row lights its claimed islands and dims the others. Waiting rows stay plain, working and waiting read from each session's turns (ADR-0754 D5); rows neither working nor waiting are idle by their state alone, and are listed first under the strip's History tab rather than on Live, which a search box narrows (ADR-1002 D4); ended sessions are hidden. Parent relationships and totals are read only when recorded or supplied by the agent link; missing values are not guessed. *Narrowed in place, 2026-10-05 (ADR-0804 D9, decision_5aadb523c1cb; ADR-0923 D2, decision_027f3b08bb8b): no wisps are drawn, so a row's colour is the colour of its traversal and of its claimed territories' outlines, and the hovered-wisp clause no longer applies. Hovering or focusing a row lights only the islands holding capabilities it, or a subagent folded under it, claimed; an increment it holds lights none, whatever its touches name (contract 7.4).*

islands.title: The arc surface

territories.title: 1 · Work states
territories.description: Every part, increment and arc shows exactly one state, worked out by one rule from the records, so no two views, and no two lines of one view, can disagree. A part is planned, in progress or landed; an increment, once closed, is landed or not completed (failed, withdrawn, or closed with nothing recorded), and before that is waiting on you, queued, held by an agent or open; an arc is waiting, blocked, claimed, idle, quiet, parked or closed.

territories.title: 2 · Agents on the board
territories.description: Every increment and part an agent holds shows which agent: Claude Code or Codex, when its window opened, the reason it gave when it claimed, and whether it is live or idle, and for how long. It reads the agent link's own claim reading, so the overlay and the claim tool always agree, and an idle holder still holds its work.

territories.title: 3 · Arc surface
territories.description: A full-width arcs-only bar sits below the app story's separate gear-only app bar and opens one read-only drawer over the forest. The bar carries no project name. Both bars reserve their space above the forest so its controls remain reachable, and the drawer opens below them. The drawer, half the window's height, leaves the forest usable below; it can be expanded to fill the window below the bars and restored (3.10). It lists root arcs as dense two-line lanes (state chip, title and small counted wait marks, then the bars alone, wrapping), with a bar for each increment, finished work first, each bar coloured by its work state, a count of what landed and what is open spoken on the bars' label but not shown (ADR-0980), and a chip with the lane's state and who is on it; Active, Parked and Closed each show their own arcs. It stays current while it is open: about every two seconds it asks for what changed in the library and the agent log, which the app carries to it, and it re-checks the clock once a minute, so an agent that goes quiet turns idle without any new record.

territories.title: 4 · Waits
territories.description: Every arc or increment that waits on other work says so and names what it waits for: an arc queued behind another arc folds away under that arc’s lane, behind a ▸/▾ caret in a fixed gutter; expansion shows chips, and an increment waiting on another increment, on any arc, draws yellow and names its blocker and why. A blocker shows what it holds up, a wait that will never release by itself says so, and an arc with something waiting on you is never hidden under its blocker.

territories.title: 5 · Briefing
territories.description: Picking a lane, or a queued arc, opens its briefing: rows you scan, each a door into its prose, and no prose until something is opened (ADR-0980 D5). The arc's intent is one folded line. Its questions are one table, open first, each row a title and a status (open or settled); opening a row replaces the table with the full reading, the answer on top when settled, and “← back to questions” restores it. The reading is statement first, with its stakes, diagram, options as for and against, a recommendation marked not binding, and the longer parts folded with their word counts. After the questions, every increment on the arc is a row: its colour, its title and one short cell of chips for what it is doing, landed ones folded behind one row; opening a row shows its objective, its waits by name, the questions it waits behind, what it holds up, who holds it and how it closed.

islands.title: The command line

territories.title: 1 · Front door
territories.description: `storytree <family> <verb>` works out which project the folder you are in belongs to, opens that project's library, and hands the command to the owning story's function, keeping no rule of its own. Every answer is a short plain sentence or listing; where it names records it may offer, under `next:`, the commands that open them, and nothing else (ADR-0786). A failure exits non-zero and says what to do; a command it does not have answers with the real one for that job.

territories.title: 2 · Who wrote it
territories.description: Every write made through the command line is recorded as the person who ran it (their computer user name), so the library's history can tell a person's change from an agent's. When an agent runs the command from its own shell, the write is recorded as that agent's session instead (A1).

territories.title: 3 · Library
territories.description: Read any record whole, list a kind (optionally filtered by a field), search the artifacts, see what links to an artifact, and see a record's history of changes, all through the library's own reads. Write a new record of any kind, or edit named fields of one, with long text taken from a file, and a bad record is refused with the library's own message. Retire a record with a reason and its writer through the library's existing retire, preserving its refusals.

territories.title: 4 · Arcs and increments
territories.description: See the arcs, and one arc whole: its intent, end state, increments and their states, the questions waiting on you, and what each waiting item waits for. Create, edit, park or unpark an arc; park an increment, record a landing that was never parked, close one with its outcome, and make an arc or increment wait on another with a reason, or clear the wait.

territories.title: 5 · Questions
territories.description: Raise a question for the owner on an arc (stakes, question, context, options, plus the analogy, diagram and recommendation 0.2 expected), optionally holding increments on it. Settle it with his answer in his words and the decision that carried it, retire one that was wrong, or list the open ones.

territories.title: 6 · Decisions
territories.description: List decisions (current, by status, load-bearing) and record a new one with an explicit `--number <n>` or the next number, its status, who decided it in their own words, and what it supersedes. In storytree, automatic numbers exceed the persisted floor and every number any record has ever held; omitting a number is refused if the floor is absent. Other projects start at 1. All numbering rules belong to the library; the CLI parses and reports them. Pull a decision out as a markdown file, edit it, push it back, and write its composed statement (the owner's C2). The one-time number, renumber (both modes), and set-floor commands have been retired after the completed N1 move.

territories.title: 10 · Plan view
territories.description:
`storytree tree` prints the plan as an indented tree: stories, capabilities and contracts, each with the health its agent reported (labelled as the agent's) and any claim on it. Name a story to see only that story.
`storytree capability built <capability>` says a capability is built, so it is no longer proposed, and `storytree capability proposed <capability>` says it is proposed again (ADR-0744 D2); both call the library's `setProposed`.

territories.title: 7 · Board, read only
territories.description: Show who is on what right now: each claim on an increment or a capability, with its agent's harness, window and reason, and whether it is live or idle; or who holds one piece of work. Claiming and releasing stay with the agents' tools.

territories.title: 8 · Doctor
territories.description: Run storytree's setup check from a terminal, the same one every agent session start runs: is storytree running, are the hooks registered and last seen firing, is this folder a project, is `storytree` on the path, is `gh` signed in, is Claude Code or Codex installed and signed in, and are git and a Node of at least 24 there. It fixes what the check fixes by itself and names the fix for the rest, and it sets a folder up as a project only when you tell it to.

territories.title: 9 · Friction and re-steers
territories.description: File friction with concrete evidence, or a re-steer with your own quoted words, through the agent link's own capture functions, so vague evidence is refused from a person exactly as from an agent. Add a recurrence to a friction item when it happens again. List the friction due for a landing's pass and route it, through the librarian's own drain and route.

territories.title: 11 · Workspace
territories.description: `storytree workspace <increment> --reason <text>` makes a claimed Claude Code workspace, or prepares a Codex workspace by checking availability and fetching main. For Codex it prints the exact ref and name for the agent to pass to the app's `create_worktree`; the agent then runs `storytree workspace attach <increment> --folder <returned-directory> --ref <commit> --name <name> --reason <text>`. Storytree verifies the worktree and claims its branch; only the app creates the Codex folder. Both steps refuse held or waiting work, and only a running agent session may claim.

territories.title: 12 · Check
territories.description: `storytree check`: a terminal front door onto the Guardrails story's check, so a user's CI and a person at a terminal run the package and allocation rules over their checkout.

islands.title: The librarian

territories.title: 1 · Links
territories.description: The librarian links one artifact to another only where the first really rests on the second. It finds neighbours no edge reaches with related-but-unlinked search, alongside plain search (ADR-0654). This is how the whole-project decisions come to sit behind the covers that rest on them.

territories.title: 2 · Decision log
territories.description: Every accepted decision stays true in full. When a later landing overtakes something a decision says, the librarian corrects it in place if the decision did not change, and records a new decision that supersedes it if it did; finished business is retired or consolidated.

territories.title: 3 · Catalogue
territories.description: Every artifact that lands is either genuinely new or an edit to the artifact that already covers it, and never a near-copy. Guidance any capable agent would work out for itself is pruned.

territories.title: 4 · Graduation
territories.description: ADR-0650 keeps the built graduation functions, but graduation is not needed for the MVP. Harness memories remain outside the library; promotion writes a proper artifact kind.

territories.title: 5 · Queues
territories.description: Open questions whose review lease has lapsed and unrouted friction reports are looked at on the librarian's pass, and nothing is closed without a reason. The library owns the review date and lease; the librarian uses its lapsed-question drain (ADR-0654).

territories.title: 6 · Rounds
territories.description: When the librarian runs, and how an agent is told to put on its hat. At a landing where the session wrote to a curated kind of artifact, storytree asks for the librarian's pass before the landing is reported.

islands.title: The knowledge core

territories.title: 2 · Earlier decisions beside their replacements
territories.description: A replaced decision appears as a see-through ghost beside the decision that replaced it, and lights when its recorded reader reaches it. Its card tells an explicit supersession from an earlier cover found in write history. Proposed decisions stay out of this first slice.

territories.title: 1 · Knowledge under its shelves
territories.description: The project's artifacts hang below the stories' and capabilities' front covers, with depth counting the longest chain of references from any shelf. A shared artifact appears once, a loop is drawn as a labelled error, and an artifact no shelf reaches has "no depth". On the globe, shelf-placed knowledge is drawn beneath its islands. Story-text definitions are excluded from the drawing; the remaining no-shelf artifacts fill a ball within 0.55 globe radii, separated from one another and shelf points by at least 0.035 radii (ADR-0661 D3). Forest shows the core beneath the story nodes; Library shows it alone on the same globe (ADR-0660 D4). The separate Look-inside view stays unmounted.

territories.title: 3 · Reads by session and agent
territories.description: Choose one recorded session and see which artifacts its orchestrator and named agents reached, each in its own colour, with visits counted across the project's captured sessions. A peek only lights its artifact, full reads advance as jumps, and an unknown agent stays pale with no path.

territories.title: 4 · Look inside and inspect an artifact
territories.description: On the globe in Forest or Library mode, clicking an artifact dot pins it and opens its summary card in the right-hand slot used by the story panel (ADR-0661 D2). The card shows the artifact's kind, title and description or another summary field; when there is no summary it shows the whole text. It has no links list, read counts, depth figures or entrances. Close and Escape dismiss it. Opening a story replaces the card, and opening a card replaces the story panel. The separate look-inside view, with its replay and size controls, was removed after staying unmounted (increment_64a16707ff78); the notes are drawn under the islands, each dot sized by how many distinct sessions read its note in the last 90 days (ADR-0926), and lit only by a selected session's reads and traversal (ADR-0921), which never changes a dot's size.

islands.title: The app setup

territories.title: 8 · Setup check
territories.description:
The only thing the user installs is the storytree tool server, once, with the one-line command Claude Code or Codex already uses for any MCP server, and after that every session start checks storytree's setup and fixes whatever is missing on the spot. It opens storytree if it is closed, registers the hooks if they are missing (walking Codex users through Codex's one-time approval), and in a folder that isn't a storytree project yet it asks the user, through the agent, whether to set one up. It also says whether Claude Code or Codex is signed in and whether git and a usable Node are there, naming the fix for each that is missing, and never waits on a tool that does not answer (ADR-0716). It registers hooks for each harness home it finds except a harness the user disconnected from storytree (the app setup's contract 2.5), which gets its hooks back only when it is connected again. It also puts the `storytree` command on the user's path (contract 8.9): a shell script, or on Windows a small program of its own that hands each word on as the caller's command line spelled it (ADR-0854).

As built (increment_e0065ed16d5a, PR #452, contract 8.20): check_setup asks the agent to write .storytree-check with its own file-editing tool. Once this session's edit hook has arrived, each check file it names is deleted at the recorded path, resolving relative paths against that hook line's folder, including a worktree different from the tool server's folder, even while other hooks are missing. A file the operating system refuses to remove stays for the agent. The repository deliberately does not ignore .storytree-check: a leftover remains visible as evidence that the edit never arrived or cleanup failed.

territories.title: 1 · Get storytree
territories.description:
One command gets the Windows app and the tools its agent needs onto the computer, ready to run without a storytree checkout. Running it again reuses a working installation or explains what failed and how to retry.

As built: the release publishes install-storytree.ps1, its PowerShell one-liner and a version-matched SHA-256 manifest alongside the existing combined Windows x64/arm64 NSIS installer. Desktop packaging ships a native pinned Node 24 runtime, the complete agent-link buildBins output including imported chunks, a delivery helper and Node's license in resources/agent-tools. Delivery verifies and reuses a working installation before contacting the feed, explicitly launches its executable to show a hidden window or establish the first app launch, and waits for the app-owned database. It records stable installed tool paths in the 0.3 home's delivery.json and puts its CLI wrapper on the per-user Windows PATH; unrelated storytree commands are preserved and named. Failed steps include a retry action, incomplete existing apps are retained with repair/update instructions, and delivery does not create projects, change harness settings, install a developer toolchain, or touch 0.2. Ordinary updates remain the app's existing NSIS update route and replace the tool payload at the same paths. setup install retains its existing hook/command meaning; capability 2 owns connection.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/deliver/README.md. Linux tests use temporary homes, fake app launch/readiness and real PowerShell orchestration with injected effects; the actual built CLI, hook, setup, delivery helper and MCP server run outside a checkout. Both Windows runtime downloads match pinned SHA-256 values and their PE architectures. Windows CI additionally checks the installed x64 tool payload from a path with spaces. These proofs do not attest real first-ever/hidden-window startup, fresh-terminal registry propagation, interrupted NSIS installation, native arm64 execution, a live release update with active agent processes, or the agent-link 8.6 two-harness walkthrough; those remain the laptop acceptance lane.

As built: after delivery is ready, the one-liner prompts for Claude Code, Codex, both, or skip and calls the delivered Node/CLI directly with setup connect and the selected switches. This connects capability 1's installed paths to capability 2's existing registration functions through delivery.json. A connection failure does not reinstall the app or discard a successful connection; the command reports per-agent recovery. Tools registration is never presented as hooks verified. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/join/README.md.

As built (ADR-0854): on Windows the installed command is `storytree.exe`, a 5 KB program of its own built with LLVM from the agent link's launcher source and shipped in the payload as `storytree-launcher.exe`, so no shell reads its words: from Git Bash, Windows PowerShell or a program that starts it, each word reaches the CLI as the caller's command line spelled it (contract 1.9). The batch file it was before, `storytree.cmd`, is replaced by it in its folder. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/native-launcher/README.md.

As built (groundwork for the macOS arc, arc_5b467265f126, contract 1.11): the delivery API also stages Apple Silicon's runtime. `macRuntime("arm64")` pins Node 24.21.0's darwin-arm64 archive and its bin/node hash, and `stageRuntime` extracts that executable with mode 755, refusing any checksum mismatch and keeping the previous runtime. `writePayloadManifest` takes the platform: a Mac payload needs `node` and no Windows launcher. `toolPaths`/`verifyPayload` read a .app bundle's Contents/Resources/agent-tools and Contents/MacOS/storytree-0.3. macOS packaging, the shell install and notarisation are the arc's later increments. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/deliver/README.md.

territories.title: 2 · Connect an agent
territories.description:
The user chooses Claude Code, Codex or both, and storytree connects its installed tools to those agents. The next session uses the existing setup check to ask about the project and show whether the connection actually works.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/connect exports connectAgents and disconnectAgents for the chosen harnesses, with installedToolServerCommand(bundledNodePath, installedMcpScriptPath) as the delivery seam. Registration is per user, keeps unrelated settings and old entries, uses the existing storytree MCP name, and reports incompatible entries without overwriting. It captures no project or working directory. Repeating it leaves the compatible entry untouched. Missing harnesses, invalid settings, missing installed tools and failed writes produce separate recovery results for each harness.

As built: disconnect removes the selected registration and only hooks matching this installation, preserving other commands in mixed groups and any other installation's hooks. It keeps the shared command until no connection remains and removes only the matching launcher. A disconnected harness stays disconnected: disconnect records it in the storytree home (disconnected-harnesses.json), and the setup check, run from the other harness's sessions, registers no hooks for it until Connect connects it again. Installation results distinguish tools registration from hooks not verified; the existing setup check owns project consent and received-event verification. Connect also registers the chosen harness's hooks (and Claude Code's status line), never the unchosen one's, so the first session after installing already runs the start hook that asks the setup question; before this, hooks arrived only when that first session's tool server ran the setup check, too late for its own start. Registering is still not verifying: results keep saying "hooks not verified" until the setup check has received each event.

territories.title: 3 · First-run guide
territories.description:
A short in-app guide tells the user what to do next, what storytree will ask, and what a working first project looks like. They can reopen it when adding another project or recovering from a connection problem.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/view mounts one Help entry outside the project surface, available with no project, either forest or a library error. First launch offers the guide; dismissal is remembered locally and Help reopens it. The guide covers the chosen agent, explicit project consent, harness approval, received-hook verification, first visible work, a second project, the unsigned Windows installer and feedback. Check a folder calls the agent link’s public runSetupCheck and displays its diagnostic lines and fixes. The adjacent copy action prepares a check_setup request for the agent; this folder check does not install hooks or the command and cannot verify hook receipt. The app’s existing projectSelection/followProjects refresh remains responsible for the project list.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Headless Chromium exercises the actual renderer and isolated library, including two setup fixtures and both selectable forests. Contract 3.3’s real two-empty-folder/two-yes harness walkthrough and the final installer handoff remain Windows acceptance work.

territories.title: 4 · Read the license
territories.description:
The license travels with the installed product and is available without visiting the source repository. The user can open it from the same help surface they use after installation.

As built: the desktop build copies the repository LICENSE and both Windows distribution paths carry it at resources/LICENSE. Help → License reads that resource and displays it inside the app without network access or a source checkout. Each open reads the current installation’s file; a failed read offers retry. The Windows installer check compares the NSIS-installed and arm64 unpacked resources with the repository license.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Unit tests and headless Chromium cover offline reading, a replaced resource and retry; a real installed-release update and arm64 installation remain Windows acceptance work.

territories.title: 5 · Send feedback
territories.description:
A button in the app lets the user describe a problem or suggestion and opens it as a draft GitHub issue on storytree's repository. They see what they are sending and submit it themselves.

As built: Help → Send feedback provides editable title and message fields and an explicit Open GitHub draft action. The package constructs https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/issues/new with only those two user-authored fields; the desktop carries the OS external-browser action. It attaches no project contents, paths, transcripts or logs. A failed handoff preserves the message and offers retry or copy, with an explicit copy failure and selectable original text. Success says “Opened a draft”, leaving GitHub submission to the user. Closing help sends nothing.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Fake-opener tests and the actual desktop renderer cover no-project and both-forest access, cancellation, editing, retry, copy, exact payloads and honest success status. No issue was submitted by the checks.

2026-10-06 foundation: the view additionally accepts an optional feedbackIdentity bridge. Only entering Send feedback queries its status. Sign-in remains optional, and a separate Add account to message action inserts the verified email and portable Storytree ID into the editable message, which the user may remove before copy or browser handoff. No bridge is wired into the shipped desktop yet; that integration is parked on the identity arc. Local contract 5.5 and Chromium fixture captures: packages/app-setup/evidence/identity/README.md. These are not live provider or deployed desktop acceptance.

territories.title: 11 · Pipeline wiring
territories.description: At setup, or when a project adopts a pipeline, the agent wires the project's tests and storytree check into the user's CI through `wire_pipeline`, and proposes branch protection for the user to approve.

territories.title: 6 · Make a folder a project
territories.description: After the user says yes, a folder becomes a storytree project: the one check that refuses a folder already part of a project or a second trunk, the project opened (and its library seeded with the starter pack the first time), the folder recorded and approved as this machine's trunk, the marker left, and the app's choice recorded. Joining an existing project from another machine's checkout is the same step on purpose. Reading which project a folder belongs to stays with the hooks, in project routing.

territories.title: 12 · Import an existing project
territories.description: A storytree project imports an existing JavaScript or TypeScript project's folder (ADR-0993 D1, D2, D6): the folder is recorded on the project beside its trunk, with its repository and commit when it is a git checkout with a remote, and each package the folder declares (pnpm-workspace.yaml, else package.json workspaces, else the folder itself) becomes a mapped story through the library's mapStories, the only way a story is made mapped. Importing again maps the folder afresh, keeping what stands. The founding choice: the import reads the folder and writes nothing into it; the deliberate act of importing is its approval (ADR-0942). Front doors: storytree import <folder> and the import_project tool.

islands.title: Process ledger

territories.title: 1 · Record who started each run
territories.description:
Every tracked run names the session that started it and the computer where it runs. Background shells and detached servers keep that owner after the request or launcher that started them has gone away.

As built (foundation): @storytree/processes supplies one launchOwned boundary for resolved Claude Code/Codex callers and explicitly session-bound manual callers, with ownerFromCall accepting the agent link's public caller and agent context. Each launch durably records its owner, machine, optional project, executable/arguments, folder, launch time, PID and native lifetime observation before reporting tracked. Explicit parentRun/parentSession/subagent links survive the launcher; no PID adoption or folder/time/command inference assigns ownership. Failed launches or registration return a named gap, including a surviving PID when known. Installed CLI/MCP inventory, stop and clear doors are wired through the own package. Existing command hooks alone still do not register runs; this landing does not add launch coverage.

territories.title: 2 · Keep sight of unfinished runs
territories.description:
A request ending or timing out does not mean its work has stopped. Each run stays visible until the computer confirms it has ended, with anything it cannot establish shown as uncertain.

As built (foundation): readLedger and observeRuns retain records independently of requests, turns, sessions, claims and age, without a library connection. Request outcomes stay unknown unless the caller records evidence; explicit timeout evidence never implies process death. Native probes distinguish live/gone/unknown and compare Linux boot/start ticks, macOS boot/native microsecond start time or Windows exact creation FILETIME before attributing the current PID to a recorded lifetime. Failed or partial reads stay visible alongside readable records. Only registered runs and explicit child links are covered; unregistered launch paths and descendants remain untracked. Stopping and closing consume these observations in later capabilities and must revalidate identity before any signal.

territories.title: 3 · See what remains
territories.description:
The session can list its remaining work or inspect all recorded sessions' work on this computer with an owner beside each run. The answer identifies what is running, what ended without reporting back, and what the inventory could not observe.

As built (listing API): @storytree/processes/listing exports listRuns and renderInventory over the foundation's observeRuns. The self view requires an explicit resolved owner and includes explicitly delegated descendants; the all-session view needs no owner and grants no cross-session stop authority. Rows keep command/arguments, folder, age, owner, machine, run/PID/lifetime identity and independent process/request findings. Only the inspector's exact lifetime is excluded. Read gaps, uncertain readings, foreign-machine records and coverage remain visible offline. Optional shared lifecycle readings have no stop action. The API offers an action only when a surface supplies an installed stop entry point and the row has an owned local live identity; otherwise it explains the absence.

As built (scope alignment): inventory uses the same ownership and conflicting-registration checks as stopOwned. An explicitly unknown calling agent refuses self inventory with a pointer to all-session inspection rather than reporting an empty scope. A named subagent sees only its own runs in self scope; its siblings and parent have no stop offer. Session callers retain explicitly delegated descendants, including established multi-hop parentSession links. An unchanged ledger no longer offers an action that stopping refuses for scope or conflicting ownership. Stopping still revalidates at invocation, so changed ownership or lifetime can alter the outcome.

As built (installed doors): storytree processes / own --all and MCP list_own_runs / list_all_runs call the listing API outside a project and with the app/database absent. Each self view offers only its installed stop entry point (CLI command or MCP tool), retaining the API's scope checks and explicit coverage. Both doors include the public app/database lifecycle reading as shared work with unknown native identity and no stop action, pointing to storytree app status / storytree app quit. An unknown shared lifetime keeps the overall reading incomplete.

As built (caller identity, supervisor-directed): with the app/database down, a CLI caller's self is the harness session named by CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID or CODEX_THREAD_ID, using the workspace command's environment seam. Missing or competing harness signals refuse self inventory, stop and clear and point to read-only own --all. MCP uses Codex's per-call session/thread metadata offline. When the library is reachable, exact call-id hook records supply the corrected session and named subagent, limiting it to its own runs. Claude MCP's shared server environment cannot identify an offline calling agent, so unresolved self operations refuse and point to list_all_runs / own --all. No authority is inferred from folder, timing, commands or a synthetic MCP session.

As built (delivery): the shared agent-link builder bundles both installed doors and stages Koffi's physical loader plus the host native module in its supported build/koffi/<ABI> prebuild layout, accepted by the unchanged installer payload verifier; the standalone CLI uses the same staging function. Desktop packaging replaces the host native package with the exact win32-x64 or win32-arm64 target before hashing each payload. The desktop manifest explicitly copies the native dependency directory as an extra resource, because electron-builder excludes a root node_modules directory from its general resource copy. Missing native targets fail the build. The habits card teaches all four own tools. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/doors2/. Built CLI and stdio MCP tests execute native inventory/stop/clear on each CI host; Linux additionally assembled both Windows payloads and checked target PE architecture and manifest hashes. Real installed Windows x64/arm64 harness acceptance remains with the laptop supervisor.

territories.title: 4 · Stop the work I own
territories.description:
The session can stop the runs it names without stopping another session's work. It checks the run and its covered children after each attempt, and reports failure whenever their disappearance cannot be confirmed.

As built: `@storytree/processes/stopping` exports `stopOwned({ owner, targets, home?, graceMs?, forceMs? })`. Targets are registered run UUIDs. Parent sessions cover explicitly delegated sessions and registered `parentRun` descendants; a named subagent cannot stop its parent or siblings. Malformed/unregistered, foreign-machine and conflicting-owner targets are refused; uncertain or replaced lifetimes never authorize signalling.

Each result states its computer, registered membership, exclusions, gaps, attempts and final process readings. Ownership is reread before each delivery. Polite and forced phases each check the root and every covered child; survivors, unknown readings, ownership changes, late registrations and unreadable inventory make the result unsuccessful. All records remain for capability 5.

Coverage is explicitly `registered-runs-and-linked-descendants`, with `nativeTree: unconfirmed` and the foundation launch-coverage warning. A successful scoped stop is not proof that unregistered OS descendants or the whole computer are clear. Linux uses identity-checked pidfds; macOS uses combined birth/PID-version evidence and audit-token signals; Windows uses a FILETIME-checked handle, targeted WM_CLOSE when available, then bounded force. No process-group or PID-only fallback is used.

As built (installed stop doors): storytree processes stop <run…> and MCP stop_own_run call stopOwned directly. They preserve every per-target stopped, already-gone, refused or incomplete outcome, native-tree limits, exclusions and gaps; unsuccessful results exit nonzero / set MCP isError. Unknown callers receive no authority. CLI, bundled CLI, source MCP and bundled stdio MCP tests stop a real owned child while refusing another session or sibling. Online Claude hook attribution also retains the named subagent boundary after a session reset. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/stopping/ and packages/processes/evidence/doors2/.

territories.title: 5 · Finish with an honest inventory
territories.description:
The session can clear records of work confirmed gone without hiding work that may still be running. Its closing check distinguishes an empty observed inventory from an incomplete observation, so a tidy record cannot become a false claim that the computer is idle.

As built: `@storytree/processes/closing` and `@storytree/processes` export `clearOwned({ owner, home?, knownGaps? })`, `readClosing({ home?, owner?, knownGaps?, shared? })` and `renderClosing(reading)`. Clear removes only the caller session/harness's records, with named subagents limited to their own records; delegated sessions' records are untouched. Original lifetimes and all registered descendants must be confirmed gone. Live, unknown and foreign records remain; unreadable records and known gaps prevent unproved child clearance. Removal failures are reported separately from successful removals.

Clear rereads records and child membership after probing and before unlinking. Changed, disappearing, reparented or newly registered children retain the affected parent; only this call's confirmed removals may shrink its previously observed membership. It preserves request evidence and gap records, never signals processes, and changes neither claims, sessions nor increments.

The closing reading reuses the listing API in all-session scope, irrespective of the caller, session end or released claims. Its status is `empty`, `remaining` or `incomplete`. Live/unknown rows stay visible; persisted read/registration gaps and caller-carried gaps whose persistence failed make it incomplete and name missing evidence separately. An empty verdict says “no tracked session work remains on this machine”, with the launch coverage and an explicit remote-machine limit. Shared work remains separately visible and is never stopped automatically.

These are point-in-time observations, without a launch interlock. Only explicitly registered descendants are covered; neither whole-machine idleness nor remote clearance is claimed. Evidence: `packages/processes/evidence/closing/README.md`, `red.txt`, `red-membership.txt`, `green.txt`, `gate.txt`, and the PR's three native CI checks. As built (installed clear doors): storytree processes clear and MCP clear_own_runs call clearOwned without signalling, preserve removed, retained, failed and gaps as separate fields, then return an all-session readClosing. Read gaps from clear are carried as knownGaps into that closing reading. Failed removals or clear gaps exit nonzero / set MCP isError while retaining the full result. Remaining live work and unknown shared app identity remain visible in the closing verdict; clear success does not claim closure or whole-computer idleness. The current doors perform no launches and have no additional unpersisted launch-gap source. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/doors2/.

islands.title: The website

territories.title: 1 · Home page
territories.description: A visitor opens on chapter 1: one Run tap plays the agent swarm, with a silent default, exits to the globe, remembered return visits and static fallbacks. The static home page also explains storytree and provides its waitlist entry point, repository, license and LinkedIn contact without JavaScript, including a LinkedIn alternative for joining. It builds with esbuild into dist and leaves the globe to the forest capability; all website code stays in packages/website.

territories.title: 3 · Saved snapshot
territories.description: A session refreshes a committed public snapshot of storytree 0.3 with one command. The website and CI read that file without connecting to the library; only the fields required to draw and explain the public plan are exported.

territories.title: 2 · The forest on the site
territories.description: A visitor sees storytree 0.3 as a live 3D project map drawn by the same forest-world engine as the desktop app, from the committed snapshot. The scene loads after the page text and shows a still of that same scene when WebGL is unavailable.

territories.title: 4 · Publish on merge
territories.description: A merged website change republishes its static output at crisp-globe-bf6v.here.now using the repository HERENOW_TOKEN secret. An absent token produces an explicit skipped-publish log; publishing never needs a live library connection.

territories.title: 5 · Waitlist
territories.description: A visitor joins the invitation waitlist from the public website using an email and optional computer and coding-agent answers. The form, its entry point and here.now Site Data manifest live in packages/website; the host accepts visitor inserts while the owner alone may read, update or delete entries.

islands.title: The world

territories.title: 1 · Scene layout
territories.description: Turns a project's stories and capabilities into a forest scene: islands and parcels on a hex lattice, trails between them and the props they carry, then maps that scene to 3D descriptors (src/core, src/scene.ts, src/world-to-3d.ts). *Noted in place, 2026-10-05 (ADR-0804 D1): the globe keeps only the scene's ground cells (each island's coast, parcels and reach); the trees, flora and props it still computes are drawn by nothing on a product surface.*

territories.title: 2 · Island ground
territories.description: Builds each island's ground for the globe: its relaxed parcel cells and the coast rims clipped from them, drawn in exact colour. *Noted in place, 2026-10-06: the stepped cliff edge and the banded ground shader with its grass, sand, wheat, rock, wear and shadow layers left with the flat canvas (ADR-0920); the shore band and the land's fall to its waterline left with the last road that stood on them (increment_1c39930c645a). Only the waterline's dip (SHORE_DIP) and the relief's height bound (landHeightRange) remain, sizing the plates' clearance above the shell.*

territories.title: 5 · The canvas
territories.description: The React-Three-Fiber canvas that hosts the globe: it says when it is ready, frames the camera, reuses prepared ground when the scene has not changed, and draws on demand, including under a camera another canvas drives. PlanetWorldCanvas is the live canvas; the flat ForestWorldCanvas and its evidence page were deleted under ADR-0920.

territories.title: 6 · The planet
territories.description: Draws the world on a globe: each island a flat plate standing on the sphere at its spot, a glass globe whose far side is hidden, and trail ribbons running between the plates (src/planet).

territories.title: 7 · Growth
territories.description: The globe replays a recorded sequence of plan states as growth: islands rise, roads draw on with the dependency-lane motion, and parts and files fill in, at a chosen speed.

islands.title: The local database

territories.title: 1 · Postgres binaries
territories.description: Finds initdb, pg_ctl and postgres for this machine: from the @embedded-postgres package built for it (the x64 one on Windows arm64, run under emulation), or from the directory a packaged app ships them in.

territories.title: 2 · A server on a data directory
territories.description: Makes a cluster in a data directory the first time, asking every connection for the installation's password (SCRAM; a legacy trust cluster is converted at start), starts a server on it listening on 127.0.0.1 only, makes sure clients' ordinary role (storytree: may create databases, owns every database, no superuser) exists and owns what the superuser made before, hands back its url signing in as that role, and publishes the private connection handoff (ADR-0941) while it runs; stops it; while it runs, an owner record beside the directory (`<dataDir>.owner.json`) names the process that holds it, which is how others learn whether storytree is running and where.
