islands.title: The dev loop

territories.title: 1 · Test scoping
territories.description: Decides from a branch's changes which packages `pnpm test` runs, the same way locally and in CI, and says so on its first line (`scope: ...`); flags force everything, name units, or rerun what failed (test-scope.mjs).

territories.title: 2 · Worktree setup
territories.description: Installs a fresh or stale worktree when a session starts, so a session can build at once, and keeps the owner's local app following merged main (provision-worktree.mjs, follow-main.mjs).

territories.title: 3 · Package boundaries
territories.description: Holds this repository to the package rule by running Guardrails' package rule (packages/guardrails, ADR-0911 D2) with storytree's own declarations: its stories, the frame (packages/app, apps/desktop), the front door (packages/cli) and the owner's sanctioned edges in package-edges.json. It also checks, for storytree alone, that a capability depending on another story's matches the code's package direction (plan edges, ADR-0840 D2); test-ratio.mjs reports test lines per implementation line alongside, and never fails.

territories.title: 4 · Agent guidance
territories.description: Builds CLAUDE.md's generated region, AGENTS.md and the role files from the agent roles in the library, and a SKILL.md for Claude Code and Codex from each process note marked as a skill (ADR-0837), and checks the checked-in copies for drift and size (build-guidance.mjs, guidance.mjs).

territories.title: 5 · Library tools
territories.description: Reaches storytree's own library from the command line to export its stories and decisions as read-only files, restore a snapshot, and record each contract's verified health from a test run (library-server.mjs, export-library.mjs, library-export.mjs, restore-library.mjs, own-health.mjs, check-own-health.mjs).

territories.title: 6 · Running the tests
territories.description: `pnpm test` runs the scoped units against a throwaway local Postgres, each unit under a deadline, reporting which test is still running, and ends in a PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN table; a second heavy run on the machine queues behind the first, and a Node.js known to crash is refused at the start (test.mjs, unit-run.mjs, test-running-reporter.mjs, heavy-lock.mjs, node-runtime.mjs).

territories.title: 7 · The gate
territories.description: `pnpm gate` runs the typecheck, the scoped tests and, when generated guidance may have changed, the guidance check, in one foreground run ending in a PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN table with a reason for every NOT RUN (gate.mjs).

territories.title: 8 · Lag instruments
territories.description: The kept instruments that measure the app's lag (ADR-0836, ADR-1001), so every lane and re-measure compares before and after with the same instrument and the same seed: `pnpm lag:reads` times the page's reads over a throwaway Postgres with added latency per query, and `pnpm lag:desktop` performs the catalogue of named actions (opening the smallest, largest and a named story's island, closing the panel, Library and back, opening a Library note and a session's row, a hover sweep, idle) through real input on an instrumented copy of the desktop app, or the desktop page in headless Chromium over the stand-in bridge (`--chromium`, as on the Mint box), and prints each action's response, longest frame, settled time and IPC count against its budget, saying NOT RUN for any it could not perform. With `--against <ref | built app dir>` it measures this checkout's build and the other in alternating rounds on the same seed and says, per action, slower, the same or faster, with any read whose count differs as its own finding. The whole run queues behind the heavy-run lock. On the Mint box, `pnpm lag:box` runs it after merges rather than by hand (ADR-1001 D3): a systemd user timer every 15 minutes measures the newest main against each action's baseline, one bounded run at a time with the merges between skipped; a slowdown counts when a second run agrees, holds the baseline back, and is halved down to the pull request that caused it; the history sits in the storytree-lag database beside the library, which `pnpm lag:box` prints from any machine, and `pnpm lag:box rebaseline` accepts a cost with its reason. Never a gate: nothing of it runs in CI or a pull request's checks.

territories.title: 9 · Code allocation guardrail
territories.description: Every pnpm test run, and so CI, refuses a checkout that leaves any source file of a story package reached by no numbered test (ADR-0838 D5), by running Guardrails' allocation rule (packages/guardrails, ADR-0911 D2) over this repository.

territories.title: 10 · A Mint lane runs on the engine its allowance allows
territories.description: Codex below 95%, Claude at the limit, one handover and a queue-preserving fast-fail exit. Founded on decision_2122230a3140 (ADR-0929).

territories.title: 11 · The Mint pool keeps its lanes fed
territories.description: One survey of the library names every active arc's ready increments, oldest first and an arc no live session is on before a busy one, under the manager's skip rules (another machine, waits and held-on questions; the website arc is no longer skipped whole, increment_84b94c1f40b8); claims are the only conflict guard, and a refused increment is retried only once the refusing claim clears (ADR-0955 D2). Work this dispatcher ran whose session ended and which is back in the pool (it bounced on a capability claim, say) is offered again after a back-off, without a restart (increment_ac90da057d6c). Overtakes the night tracks' fenced feed (ADR-0931 D1), retired by increment_2c26fdf14cb0.

territories.title: 12 · The Mint pool's dispatcher runs its lanes under the box's cap
territories.description: The box's dispatcher runs through packages/dev-loop/src/lanes/launch.mjs pool (ADR-0955 D2, D4): one dispatcher at a time, filling free slots (the cap in night-max-lanes less the engines running) from the pool, each lane waiting for a slot and bringing the checkout to origin/main, pushing over SSH, under the shared lock, then running its composed brief through the lane runner; the stop file ends it after its running lanes. Founded on decision_2122230a3140 (ADR-0929 D3); the night tracks and the mintlib queue it once ran retired with increment_2c26fdf14cb0.

territories.title: 13 · A watcher lands a handed-over pull request
territories.description: A session on any machine ends once its pull request is open and its gate is green, and hands the PR to a watcher with no model (packages/dev-loop/src/lanes/watch.mjs): `watch.mjs handover <pr> <increment>` runs `hand` on the box directly, or over `ssh mint` from another machine with the session's own id, refusing with the reason when the box is out of reach (ADR-0974). `hand` records the hand-off in [home], sets an event wait on the increment so no other session takes it while it lands, and starts the watcher if none runs. The watcher polls GitHub: on MERGED it clears the wait, closes the increment landed with the PR and releases the session's remaining claims; on a red (a failed check, a conflict with main, or an ejection from the merge queue) it clears the wait and starts one fix session for that PR, which fixes, pushes and hands back; after its fix limit it writes an owner wait with the PR and the logs. The watcher (`run`) is a keeper over its look loop (`watch`), which exits with the restart code once the dev loop's code in the shared checkout changes, so the keeper starts it again on the new code. It is not an engine, so it counts against no engine slot; its fix sessions are. Founded on decision_e101df427118 (ADR-0955 D3).

islands.title: Keys

territories.title: 1 · Key store and resolver
territories.description: Keeps the keys storytree must hold in one auth.json in storytree's home, only the user can read and write it, and many processes can write it at once safely. It resolves a named key the same way in every process: an explicit value, then the file entry (a literal, or a `!<command>` run once per process), then the environment variable. `storytree auth set|list|remove` is its command-line front door: the cli family parses, calls this package and prints.

islands.title: The map

territories.title: 8 · Code survey
territories.description: Surveys story source packages and app frame paths (apps/desktop/src) for file ownership, source line counts and imports. Retains tests with numbered N.M titles and import edges, separately tagged as tests and excluded from source line counts. Ownership follows existing nearest numbered-test reach, execution coverage and type-import rules (8.1, 8.6, 8.7); unmatched files remain unclaimed. Lives in packages/map under ADR-0864; the forest consumes this survey for drawing. Callers may survey the current checkout explicitly. The main default reads immutable Git blobs from fetched origin/main, with shared bounded asynchronous fetches, keeping the last fetched main offline and reporting failure when none exists. No checkout is changed. Without origin, the primary folder is surveyed; non-Git folders are read directly. Unchanged blob identities retain file and story surveys. The forest owns request pacing; each later request checks for the next landing, so no cooldown can swallow its only refresh.

territories.description: Read-only graph of plan, code and tests, owned by packages/map. Demonstrate Projects 2.5 reached from the desktop view file using a fixture plan.

territories.title: 2 · Focus selection
territories.description: Select any file, capability, promise or story by upstream and downstream dependency depth and node kind.

territories.title: 3 · Counts before detail
territories.description: Return complete counts and estimated token cost before detail; show every selected row or refuse above the ceiling, never truncate.

territories.title: 4 · Diff impact
territories.description: Focus a git diff on changed files, their promises and dependents, including the tests that name those promises.

islands.title: Identity

territories.title: 1 · Portable user identity
territories.description: A trusted sign-in resolves to a durable Storytree user id. The identity-owned Cloud SQL users store retains linked provider+subject identities, the verified email and a replaceable WorkOS user pointer. Proof uses real PostgreSQL persistence to resolve first, repeat, linked and conflicting sign-ins without using email equality as identity.

territories.title: 2 · Social sign-in and session
territories.description: The desktop and storytree sign-in use the system browser to authenticate through WorkOS with Google, GitHub or Microsoft only. The identity package owns PKCE/device-flow orchestration, trusted session verification, session persistence, status and sign-out; clients contain no WorkOS API key. Proof covers successful and refused exchanges plus a real authorized staging journey; production activation remains an explicit owner prerequisite.

islands.title: Guardrails

territories.title: 1 · The package rule
territories.description: Refuses a checkout that breaks the package rule: a story with no package or a package that is no story's, a story's code in a declared frame or front door, a reach into another story's files, workspace packages depending on each other in a cycle, and a story depending on a declared frame or front door unless the owner sanctioned that edge; a sanctioned edge no package.json uses is reported.

territories.title: 2 · The allocation rule
territories.description: Fails a checkout that leaves a story package's source file reached by no numbered test, naming each such file with its lines and the three ways out (number a test, plan a contract, delete the code).

territories.title: 3 · The check command
territories.description: `storytree check`, run in a checkout, runs the package rule and the allocation rule over it and reports every failure plainly, exiting non-zero, or says it passes and exits zero. It reads the checkout alone.

territories.title: 4 · Graduated checks
territories.description: Deterministic checks on a change, run from a checkout far more often than CI runs. Each is all of a quality control check, or the part of one that is a fixed pattern, graduated from the Quality assurance story's reviewer (ADR-0956 D5). Run on the files a branch changes against origin/main, it reports every place a graduated check trips, by the check's name, the file and the line. It reads the checkout alone and records nothing: Guardrails does not reach the library, so Quality assurance runs it and records its hits in the QA ledger. If this capability grows too big it becomes its own story (ADR-0956 D5).

islands.title: Quality assurance

territories.title: 1 · Quality control checks
territories.description: A quality control check is one question a reviewer can answer yes or no about a finished change (for example: is any expected value computed the way the code computes it?). Each is its own artifact in the library, of the kind the library declares for it (the library story, Knowledge artifacts), linked to the principle or guardrail note it enforces; the notes stay, carrying the reason for the rule (ADR-0956 D3). This capability gives the checks as one reading, for the change-reviewer and for people, the same from both front doors.

territories.title: 2 · Change review
territories.description: The review of one change (one increment's branch) by the `change-reviewer` role, run as an ordinary subagent with a fresh context once the change is green and before the gate (ADR-0956 D1). This capability makes what the reviewer reads, the review brief: the branch's diff against origin/main, the contracts of the capabilities the increment names, and the live checks, with nothing of the implementer's reasoning. And it takes what the reviewer returns: for every check, whether the change trips it and where; for every contract, whether the change does what it says. The role's own text is an agent role in the library, a note, and is not contracted here.

territories.title: 3 · QA ledger
territories.description:
The record of what quality control finds, kept in the library's Postgres (ADR-0956 D4). Every review records, for each check it ran, whether it hit, and for each hit the implementer's answer: fixed, or rejected with a reason. Rows are scoped by check, project and package from the first row, because products differ in shape and a global count hides where a check matters. Its reading gives the counts per check per package, the same from both front doors. It only records: nothing here samples, reduces or retires a check (ADR-0956 D6).

Not settled by this plan (2026-10-10, raised with the dispatching session): where the rows sit inside the library's Postgres, as a record type the library declares, or as this story's own tables reached through the library's connection, as the agent link's activity log is. The contracts hold either way.

territories.title: 5 · Graduation
territories.description: Graduating a check moves all of it, or the part of it that is a fixed pattern, from the reviewer to a deterministic check in Guardrails (ADR-0956 D5). The check's record says which part graduated and where it is now enforced; the part that still needs judgement stays with the reviewer. Guardrails does not reach the library, so this story runs Guardrails' graduated checks on the change under review and records what they find in the QA ledger, under the check each graduated from.

islands.title: The MCP server

territories.title: 6 · Agent tools (the MCP server)
territories.description:
The toolbox the agent calls, served as an MCP server: plan work (arc, story, capability, contract), see the plan and who is on what, claim or release a capability, report a contract red or green, report a capability landed, say a capability is built so it is no longer proposed (`mark_built`, ADR-0744 D2), and search, read and write artifacts (plus list and add a node's front covers, once the library has them). Each tool is a thin wrapper over the library API and the claims above that answers in a short plain sentence the agent can act on, and every artifact read is logged in the agent activity log (ADR-0624); a new artifact with no place named goes onto the claimed capability's shelf of front covers (ADR-0627 D4, which redirected ADR-0624's default link).

As built: the 6.21 MCP cancellation checks cover claim, make_workspace and attach_workspace before and after library admission. They wait for their blocking and observing database connections to disconnect before removing the throwaway project. An admitted claim still finishes normally; this corrects the test teardown, not the cancellation contract.

territories.title: 7 · Instructions (the habits card)
territories.description: One short text, a screen or less, that teaches the agent storytree's habits: plan the story first, claim a capability and open the knowledge it needs before touching it, write the failing test and report red, make it pass and report green, report it landed, and record an artifact for anything worth remembering. The tool server hands this text to the agent at the start of every session, as its instructions; Claude Code reads it from there. Codex (0.158 on) does not: it shows the model neither a tool server's instructions nor its tools until the agent searches for them, so connecting Codex also writes one short marked section into the AGENTS.md in Codex's home that sends the agent to check_setup before its first change in a storytree project and keeps it silent elsewhere (7.4; measured 0 of 3 without, 3 of 3 with, packages/app-setup/evidence/codex-first-session).

stories.title: The library
stories.description: The library is where one project's records live: the plan of work, how healthy each piece is, and what the project has learned. Every later storytree 0.3 story reads and writes the library, and only through its API. People never browse it directly; they see it through the forest and the arc surface, while agents reach it through the MCP server.

capabilities.title: 1 · Project libraries
capabilities.description: Each project gets its own library, a separate database on one Postgres server, created the first time the project is opened, with its tables set up automatically, and brought up to date by the next open after storytree adds to them. Opening a project whose tables are already current touches no table, so an account let only read, or write a few kinds of record, can open it too. Storytree can list the projects on the server, and nothing written in one project can ever show up in another.

contracts.title: 1.1 · `openProject("site")` on a server with no storytree databases creates the project's database and its tables.
1.2 · Opening the same project again succeeds and changes nothing (no error, no second database, its records are untouched).
1.3 · After opening "site" and "app", `listProjects()` returns exactly `["app", "site"]`. Databases on the server that are not storytree projects are never listed.
1.4 · A record saved in "site" cannot be read from "app".

1.5 · A project name that is not lower-case letters, digits and single hyphens (1–40 characters, starting with a letter or digit) is refused before anything touches the server, and the error names the rule.
1.6 · `snapshot("site")` returns every record of the project and its whole history, as they stood at one moment, while writes go on.

1.7 · `restore("copy", snapshot)` into a project with no records and no history gives back the same records and the same history, sequence numbers, actors and times included, and the next write continues after them.
1.8 · Restoring into a project that holds any record or any history is refused, naming the project, and writes nothing.

1.9 · A local database that accepts TCP but never completes a fresh handshake is refused at a 3-second connection deadline by default, for both the server and project pools, with an actionable "storytree isn't reachable" answer. This includes library opens made by the CLI. A later call recovers once the database answers.

1.10 · Opening a project whose tables are current runs no table setup and writes nothing, so an account that may only read its tables (not their owner, no right to create in its schema) opens it and reads its records.

1.11 · Opening a project whose tables are not current, as an account that may not set them up, is refused with a ConnectionError (`project-owner`) naming the project and the account and saying that only the role owning its database may set them up; its owner's next open sets them up as before.

1.12 · `dropProject(name)` deletes the project's database, with every record and all its history, for every machine using the server; it is listed no more, other projects are untouched, and an unknown project is refused. An open that only reaches an existing project (`openProject(name, { create: false })`, how a folder that names a project opens it) refuses a deleted one as gone and never makes it again.
contracts.description: The library call under deleting a project (ADR-0831). Irreversible: a snapshot taken first is the only way back. Others' connections to the database are ended (DROP DATABASE … WITH (FORCE)).

contracts.title: 1.13 · Closing a server connection waits for project and own-database openings already in flight, releases every pool they create, and refuses new openings once closing starts.
contracts.description: Concurrent callers of close wait for the same cleanup. An opening stalled on real Postgres when shutdown starts cannot return a live pool after shutdown; later reads or opens cannot revive the closed server. Pin with throwaway Postgres connection counts and a held schema-read lock.

reported.note: Both 1.13 regressions now pass against throwaway Postgres; all 42 focused tests pass, including existing Cloud SQL path cap/retry and own-database coverage. Full gate follows.

contracts.title: 1.14 · Loopback database connections refuse cleartext and MD5 password requests before sending credential material, for both admin and project pools; SCRAM and passwordless test connections still work.

capabilities.title: 2 · Library transactions
capabilities.description: The only data actions the library allows are: save a record, fetch it, list records of one type, change only named fields, or retire a record with a reason. Every change is all-or-nothing, and is written first to a permanent, append-only history, so nothing is ever truly erased.

contracts.title: 2.1 · `save` creates a record. Saving the same id again replaces it, and each save appends one history entry.
2.2 · `edit` changes only the fields it names; every other field keeps its stored value.
2.3 · `edit` merges onto what is stored NOW, not onto a copy the caller read earlier. If two edits of different fields race, both survive.
2.4 · `edit` of a missing record returns `null` and creates nothing.
2.5 · `get` of a missing record returns `null` and never throws.
2.6 · `list(type)` returns only that type's current records (none retired), and `[]` when there are none.
2.7 · `retire(id, reason)` removes the record from `get`/`list`, keeps the reason in the history, and retiring an already-retired or missing record is a harmless no-op.

2.8 · `history()` returns every change in the order it happened, with strictly increasing sequence numbers. `history({ id })` filters to one record, and `history({ since })` returns only entries after that sequence number.
2.9 · A `validate` check passed to `save`/`edit` sees the merged result. If it throws, nothing is written (no record change and no history entry).

2.10 · A write naming an `actor` keeps it in history. A write without one is accepted and its history entry has no actor; an edit or retirement never inherits an earlier write's actor. Refused writes and harmless no-ops add no history entry.

2.11 · Save, edit and retire accept an optional abort signal. If aborted before write admission, including while waiting for the project write lock, they reject without changing records or history. After admission, cancellation does not interrupt the write or undo its history. The in-memory twin applies the same boundary at write entry.

2.12 · `history` also narrows on the server: `from` (a time) keeps the changes made at or after it, to the millisecond, however the time is written; `types` keeps only changes to records of those types (none for an empty list); `oldest: n` or `newest: n` keeps only the first or last n of what matches, still in order. Filters combine with each other and with `id` and `since`; a malformed one (a limit that is not a whole number above 0, both limits, or a time that is not one) is refused with a RangeError before anything is read.
contracts.description: So a reader that needs one change, or the changes of a few types or since a time, takes only those from the store, not the whole history (arc_0ab31fd59c88, decision_54c045d61591's rule applied to the library's history).

reported.note: memory and postgres behaviour suites pass 2.12

contracts.title: 2.13 · Lists narrow on the server by ids and stored field values, take an ordered limit, and project only requested fields on the named schema version; memory and Postgres agree.
contracts.description: Predicates compare stored JSON scalars before schema upgrades. Projection applies only to its named schema version; other versions arrive whole so SchemaRecords can upgrade without losing source fields or refuse a future version. All SQL paths, values, ids and projection names are parameters.

reported.note: The same transaction behaviour suite passes 22 tests across memory and Postgres, including filtering, ordered limits, nested scalar predicates and version-safe projection.

capabilities.title: 3 · Data schema
capabilities.description: Every record has a declared type with a fixed set of fields, and a badly filled-in record is refused with a message naming the problem field. Every record is stamped with the schema version it was written on, so a later change to a type is handled deliberately rather than silently misread: an older record is upgraded automatically, step by step, and stored upgraded the next time it is written, because every user's library is their own database and nobody else can repair it.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Saving a `story` with no `title` is refused, the error names `title`, and nothing is written.
3.2 · An unknown field (for example `titel`) is refused and named.
3.3 · An unknown type is refused.
3.4 · Every stored record carries its schema version (1 today).

3.5 · Reading a record stamped with a version newer than this code knows is refused, never guessed at. The error names the record and both schema versions, gives the update and agent-link restart steps, and reports the running code commit distance behind locally fetched origin/main when known; unavailable Git information never masks the refusal or invents a distance.

reported.note: The source-URL guard makes all three code-distance tests pass, including loading the real CommonJS bundle and preserving recovery text with unknown distance.

contracts.title: 3.6 · An `edit` that would leave the record invalid (for example blanking a required field) is refused, and nothing is written.
3.7 · A record written on an OLDER version of its type is read (`get`, `list`) upgraded to the current version, its upgrade steps applied in order. Reading it writes nothing.

3.8 · An `edit` of such a record merges onto its upgraded fields and stores it on the current version, in place, in the same all-or-nothing write. If the upgraded result does not fit, nothing is written.
3.9 · An older record that no upgrade step brings to the next version is refused by `get`, `list` and `edit`, with an error naming the missing step. It is never guessed at.

capabilities.title: 4 · Work model
capabilities.description: The library holds each project's plan of work: arcs (initiatives), stories (what a user can do), capabilities (the parts that make a story work) and contracts (single testable promises). Capabilities and contracts point at their parent. Stories belong to the project directly, and an arc *may* list the stories it grows, though a research arc may list none. The library refuses broken structure. A capability carries a proposed flag, on from its birth until the agent says it is built (`setProposed`, ADR-0744 D2); switching it says nothing about health, and a capability written before the flag reads proposed. A story is made mapped (ADR-0993 D2) only by mapStories, which an import calls: one mapped story per package of the import, keyed by the package, with no capabilities; a mapped field given to addStory or editStory is refused.

contracts.title: 4.1 · Add a story, a capability under it and a contract under that, and `projectTree()` returns them nested: story › capability › contract.
4.2 · An arc listing that story is returned by `arcsFor(storyId)`. An arc listing no stories is accepted.
4.3 · A capability naming a missing (or retired) story is refused, as is a contract naming a missing capability and an arc listing a missing story.
4.4 · A capability depending on another capability that does not exist is refused.
4.5 · A dependency loop between capabilities (A → B → A, or longer) is refused, and nothing is written.

4.6 · A capability is born proposed. The agent switches the flag off, and back on, and history names the writer; only a live capability has the flag, and a capability written before the flag reads proposed.

4.7 · A contract planned without a number is given its capability's next free one (after the highest its live contracts carry); a title whose number another live contract of the capability carries is refused, on planning and on correcting, and nothing is written. A capability with no number numbers nothing.

4.8 · A capability planned without a number is given its story's next free one (after the highest its live capabilities carry), so the contracts planned on it are numbered from the start; a number given is kept.
contracts.description: Regression for a contract planned moments after its capability that stayed unnumbered (2026-10-01): contract numbering keys off the capability's stored number.

contracts.title: 4.9 · Retiring a capability with live dependents is refused, naming every dependent and dependsOn, with nothing written; after those links are removed or the dependents retired, retirement succeeds with its reason and writer kept in history.
4.10 · A contract planned without a number skips the numbers the capability's tests already carry, past the highest; a number given is kept
4.11 · a contract planned without a number never takes the number of a numbered test no live contract carries: it gets the next free number past it, and only a number given binds it to that test
4.12 · A story is made mapped only by mapStories: a mapped field given to addStory or editStory is refused, and nothing is written

4.13 · mapStories(from, packages) adds a mapped story, with no capabilities, for each package no live story of that import maps, retires that import's stories whose package is gone, and leaves every other story as it stands
4.14 · The plan's tree carries a mapped story's import, package and folders as mapStories recorded them; a story storytree built carries none
4.15 · A number given in a contract's title is written in the numbered form, number then " · ", so every reader of contract numbers finds it
contracts.description: addContract and editContract take a title that starts with a contract number followed by its text, with or without the separator ("5.38 Text" or "5.38 · Text"), and store it as "5.38 · Text"; a title that is the number alone, or already carries the separator, is stored as given. CI's health reader and the worklist recognise a contract's number only in that form, so a title stored as "5.38 Text" read "no test names it" though its tests ran (contracts 5.38, 5.39 and 11.18 on 2026-10-11).

capabilities.title: 6 · Knowledge artifacts
capabilities.description:
Alongside the plan, the library keeps what the project has learned: decisions and definitions of terms, and principles, guardrails, patterns, processes, agent roles, friction, re-steers and tech stack, each with 0.2's fields. Each can link to the other artifacts it relates to, and you can find them again by searching their words; an edit keeps the old wording in history. An artifact never links straight to the work: capability 9 is how the work reaches its knowledge.

Planned, not yet built (ADR-0956 D3, contract 6.12): a ninth kind, the quality control check, one yes-or-no question about a finished change, linked to the principle or guardrail note it enforces.

contracts.title: 6.3 · Editing a decision keeps its old wording in history.
6.4 · A link to a record that does not exist is refused.
6.1 · An artifact is found by `search` on any word it contains (case-insensitive).
6.2 · `relatedNotes(noteId)` returns every artifact that links to that artifact.

6.5 · `definitions()` returns every live definition, and nothing else, in creation order. Added for the agent link's definition lookups at each prompt (ADR-0636 D1, b2), which adds `definitions` to 7's list of functions.

6.7 · Friction with no evidence is refused, and so is a re-steer marked a defect with no failure mode. Friction stores the optional dischargedBy reference to the remedy that landed, alongside its route and reason; editing other fields preserves the reference.
6.6 · Each of the eight kinds is saved with its required fields, and refused, naming the field, without one.
6.9 · Opening an older project converts an explicitly classified memory once, keeping its id, links and history, and reports an unclassified memory while preserving its original record.
6.8 · Saving a `memory` is refused with the reason that memories belong to the harness, and nothing is written.

6.10 · `related(noteId)` ranks the other live artifacts by likeness to one, saying of each whether a link joins them in either direction; with `unlinked`, only those no link reaches. An artifact sharing no word with it is never listed.

6.11 · `searchEach(queries)` and `relatedEach(ids, options)` answer as search() and related() would for each, in order, from one reading of the artifacts; an id that is not a live artifact is left out of relatedEach's answer.
contracts.description: So a reader asking many questions of the artifacts (the librarian's catalogue and related lists) pays one read of the library, not one per question.

contracts.title: 6.12 · A quality control check is a ninth kind (ADR-0956 D3): saved with its title, one-line description, its question and at least one link to a live principle or guardrail, and refused, naming the field, without its question or without such a link; it may carry what has graduated, each part with where it is now enforced.

capabilities.title: 5 · Health record
capabilities.description: Every story, capability and contract has a health record with two separate columns: what the agent **reported**, and what storytree **verified** by seeing it for itself. Each column is one of three states: `passing`, `failing` or `not-checked`. A missing entry always reads as `not-checked`, never as `passing`. A capability also has a word, as its card says it (ADR-0744 D1, D3): `proposed` while its flag is on; once the agent switches it off, `healthy` when every contract is verified passing, `unhealthy` when any is verified failing, and `untested` otherwise. Only the verified column counts: the agent's report never makes a capability healthy.

contracts.title: 5.1 · A node with no health entries reads `reported: not-checked, verified: not-checked`.
5.2 · After an agent reports a contract `passing`, it reads `reported: passing, verified: not-checked`.
5.3 · After storytree records the same contract verified `failing`, both columns are kept and shown side by side (`reported: passing, verified: failing`).

5.4 · A capability or story's health is rolled up from its contracts, column by column: `failing` if any contract is failing; `passing` only if it has at least one contract and every one is passing; otherwise `not-checked`. A single never-checked contract keeps its story `not-checked`.
5.5 · Every health entry is kept in history with who wrote it and when. A health entry for a node that does not exist is refused.

5.6 · A capability's word is proposed while its flag is on, even with every contract verified passing. Once the flag is off, it is healthy when every contract is verified passing, unhealthy when any is verified failing, and untested when any has no verified result or it has no contracts; reported passing alone reads untested.

5.7 · A verified entry can carry the kind of skip that left it not checked (owner, platform:<os> or other) and the earlier verdict it did not reproduce with that verdict's time; both read back from the contract's health and in the annotated tree, and an entry without them reads as before.
contracts.description: ADR-0825 D2: a skip is data, not silence. The recorder writes these; the library keeps them and derives the reason from them (5.8).

contracts.title: 5.8 · A capability that is not healthy carries one reason and who moves it: not built while proposed; otherwise, from its contracts' verified columns, failing, then not re-run, then no test names it, then out of CI's reach, then needs owner; with the contracts carrying it and the earliest time one was recorded so. Only needs owner is the owner's; a healthy capability carries none.
contracts.description: ADR-0825 D1: every card that is not healthy says why, and who moves it. The agent's work is ranked before the owner's, so the owner is asked only once nothing an agent can do remains.

contracts.title: 5.9 · The health worklist lists every capability that is not healthy with its reason, who moves it, the contracts carrying it and since when (the earliest time one was recorded so, or else when the capability was recorded), oldest first; one an open increment touches is routed and left off until that increment closes.

5.10 · In a project whose health nothing verifies (no verified entry anywhere), a built capability carries no reason and is marked as shown by the agent's report; its line says what the agent reports and that storytree does not check this project's tests yet, and it is off the health worklist
contracts.description: ADR-0630: a user's project shows what the agent reports, labelled as the agent's; nothing writes its verified column, so 'untested, no test names it, the agent's to move' is false there (increment_ef066f718a63).

contracts.title: 5.11 · A capability whose every contract carrying its reason has a pending mark from a run in progress, newer than its verified entry and younger than the run's time limit, stays on the health worklist saying the run it waits on; once that run records the contract, or its time is up, it is offered (or left off) by what is recorded. A pending mark is no verdict: the contract's health reads as before.
contracts.description: Keeps the health worklist from offering a capability whose numbered test landed on main while main's Own health run is still recording it (friction_87a4d32684e3).

contracts.title: 5.12 · A capability whose story's code changed on main after every contract carrying its reason was last verified, by a commit younger than the time a merge's own-health run takes, stays on the health worklist saying the commit it waits on; once its contracts are verified after that commit, or the time is up, it is offered by what is recorded. One with no contract carrying its reason is never held so.
contracts.description: friction_cf907de5ca3b: the worklist offered a just-merged package's capabilities as untested minutes before main's own-health run recorded them, and a lane was spent finding nothing wrong.

contracts.title: 5.13 · A capability not proven carries the arcs that park it in the annotated tree
contracts.description: annotate() marks a proposed or untested capability that is parked with the arcs that park it; a healthy or unhealthy one carries no mark, and its word is unchanged (ADR-0992 D2, D6).

contracts.title: 5.14 · A proposed capability with at least one contract and every contract verified passing is on the worklist still not built and the agent's, marked that its contracts already pass; one with no contract or any contract not passing is not so marked
contracts.description: Remedies friction_fd6154bff0be: the worklist said a built, merged capability whose proposed flag was left on was unbuilt work, and a landing parked a build increment for it. The reason set (ADR-0825 D1) does not grow; the item carries the fact as data.

contracts.title: 5.15 · A capability whose every contract carrying "no test names it" a test on main names stays on the health worklist held back, saying so with main's commit, until a run records it; one with any such contract unnamed on main is offered as before
contracts.description: friction_c7a7e6754c54: a merged but unrecorded test read as missing, so the health drain parked done work.

capabilities.title: 7 · Library API
capabilities.description: One small, fixed list of functions is the only way anything outside the library reads or writes it. The agent link, arc surface, forest and desktop app all call these, and `changesSince` lets them see what just changed without re-reading everything.

contracts.title: 7.2 · `changesSince(n)` returns only changes after `n`, in order, each carrying the new cursor to pass next time.

7.3 · The package's public entry exports exactly the documented API and nothing else, and its internals cannot be imported through the package. At runtime it exports `ConnectionError`, `DependencyLoopError`, `LifecycleError`, `LinkLoopError`, `MissingReferenceError`, `MissingUpgradeError`, `NOT_VERIFIED`, `NewerSchemaError`, `NumberTakenError`, `ProjectGoneError`, `ProjectNameError`, `RestoreRefusedError`, `RetireRefusedError`, `SEED_CONNECTION`, `SchemaError`, `SupersessionLoopError`, `UnknownTypeError`, `WaitLoopError`, `connect`, `wordAndWhy`. Everything else exported is a data type, including WriteOptions, HistoryEntry, HistoryFilter and the literal phrase query options and page. The connection offers exactly `openProject`, `listProjects`, `projectIdentities`, `snapshot`, `restore`, `dropProject`, `ownDatabase`, `close`. A project library offers exactly `name`, `identity`, `get`, `list`, `history`, `addStory`, `createArc`, `addCapability`, `editStory`, `editCapability`, `addContract`, `editContract`, `editArc`, `projectTree`, `arcsFor`, `addIncrement`, `advanceIncrement`, `closeIncrement`, `moveIncrement`, `editIncrement`, `parkArc`, `unparkArc`, `arcView`, `arcViews`, `addWait`, `removeWait`, `waitHolds`, `addWaitFor`, `removeWaitFor`, `waitsFor`, `holds`, `raiseQuestion`, `settleQuestion`, `questions`, `heldOnQuestion`, `checkQuestion`, `renewQuestion`, `editQuestion`, `lapsedQuestions`, `reportHealth`, `recordVerified`, `health`, `healthHistory`, `healthWorklist`, `recordDecision`, `numberDecision`, `numberDecisionsFromFullRecord`, `numberFoundingDecisions`, `setDecisionNumberFloor`, `setProposed`, `decisionNumberPlan`, `defineTerm`, `writeKnowledge`, `definitions`, `editNote`, `search`, `searchEach`, `rank`, `rankAll`, `findPhrase`, `relatedNotes`, `related`, `relatedEach`, `frontCovers`, `decision`, `decisions`, `composeStatement`, `retire`, `changesSince`, `close`. Project handles expose no pool, store or table; the connection's ownDatabase is the deliberate exception described by 7.7.

7.1 · An end-to-end "agent's day" against a real local Postgres: open a project, create an arc, add a story, a capability and a contract, report passing, record verified, record a decision as the capability's front cover and write a definition inside it, then read `projectTree()` and `changesSince(0)`. Every step is visible where the next step expects it.

7.4 · `editStory`, `editContract` and `editArc` change only the fields they name, merged onto what is stored now, and check a new reference as adding does (a contract's capability, an arc's stories). Each gives `null`, writing nothing, for an id that is not a live record of its type.

7.5 · `get`, `list` and `history` return whole records through the public API, agreeing with the in-memory twin. Live reads upgrade old records; history preserves original writes, including actors and retirement reasons, and can filter by id and sequence. Reads write nothing.
7.6 · Every public write carries its optional actor to history, as in 2.10. Health can name a writer separately from its reporter; omitting the writer preserves its existing `by` attribution.

7.7 · A connection hands its caller one named database of its own beside the projects, on the same server, local or Cloud SQL: created the first time (borrowing a granted creator role where the user may not create databases), never listed as a project, closed with the connection. Handed its table definitions, the library sets it up too (ADR-0973): only the statements the database has not yet applied, in one transaction under the database's own lock, so connections setting it up at once all succeed and one opening a database already set up runs no DDL a concurrent writer could block or deadlock; a caller that only reads may leave them out.
7.8 · `arcViews()` returns every live arc's view in a few reads, not one per arc
contracts.description: The same answer as calling arcView on each live arc, read from the library in a bounded number of record reads whatever the number of arcs, so a surface that needs every arc (the sessions list) costs a handful of queries per change instead of one batch per arc (ADR-0836 D3).

contracts.title: 7.10 · projectTree marks a parked capability with its arc
contracts.description: The plan the forest reads marks each capability not proven that a parked arc's open work names, and drops the mark once the arc is unparked (ADR-0992).

capabilities.title: 8 · Cloud connection (GCP)
capabilities.description: Instead of the local Postgres, a user can point storytree at a Postgres database in Google Cloud (Cloud SQL) and sign in with their Google account rather than a stored password. Everything above works the same, and each project still gets its own database, now on the cloud server.

contracts.title: 8.1 · Capability 2's behaviour suite, unchanged, passes against a real Cloud SQL instance reached with Google sign-in.

verified.note: 3 of 54 tests skipped (owner: live Cloud SQL proof needs STORYTREE_TEST_CLOUDSQL_INSTANCE/USER and a database user that may create databases, itself or through a granted role), at commit 394618153f72, run https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/actions/runs/38152269431

contracts.title: 8.2 · A missing or bad Google sign-in is refused with a message saying what to fix, never a hang.

8.3 · Two accounts sharing the role that creates project databases (a laptop owner and a machine's service account on one instance) both open, write and read one project and a connection's own database: each connection signs in as its account and acts as the database's owning role, so every table either makes is the role's and neither needs the other's ownership.

8.4 · An account granted exactly infra/ci-health/grants.sql or infra/library-host/grants.sql (CI's health account, ADR-0747) opens the project, records a contract's verified health, and is refused any other kind of record (a new one is refused by row-level security; one it may not change is not there for it to change) and any change to the tables; the owner's accounts are unaffected and read what it recorded. In storytree numbering mode, fresh-id health history cannot raise automatic decision numbers or reserve explicit numbers; owner decision writes, the stored floor and all non-health legacy reservations still work. Health history at the floor's own id, even written before the floor is set, neither sets nor blocks it.
8.5 · On a shared server, a library call waits for a free connection slot instead of failing, and each Cloud SQL pool holds at most three slots.
contracts.description: A server refusing a new connection for want of a slot (SQLSTATE 53300) is asked again with backoff for up to 30 s, so a read under a moment's slot pressure succeeds; each pool on a Cloud SQL instance opens at most three connections and queues busier work, so parallel sessions fit the instance (47 non-superuser slots when measured 2026-09-30). Tests: packages/library/src/project/shared-server.test.ts and cloud-connection.test.ts, "8.4".

contracts.title: 8.6 · On a shared server, each of a library's connections names the machine and process holding it (application_name), so a server whose slots run out shows who holds them
contracts.description: Every pool storytree opens names its connections storytree, the host, the process id and the script, in at most Postgres's 63 characters and with nothing secret; a name the caller gives (the seed's) is kept. Lets pg_stat_activity attribute slot demand during a recurrence (increment_254a6343d6f1).

contracts.title: 8.8 · A library call kept waiting, for a connection slot on a full server or for another session's write to the same project, says once what it waits for as the wait starts, goes on when it can, and past its wait bound (30 s unless the caller sets waitMs) fails with the server's reason, writing nothing
contracts.description: Friction friction_7c34d0e59065 and friction_a71746af7bed (2026-10-07): on a full storytree-pg, commands failed or sat 13+ minutes on one connection, silent. The slot wait is said through ConnectOptions.onWait; the write lock is tried first, and waited for under lock_timeout at the bound.

contracts.title: 8.7 · A caller that may be cut off bounds each statement (statementTimeoutMs), and the server ends one still running at the bound, so a cut-off process's slot comes free
contracts.description: Landed with commit 1cf74275 (Library 8.7, hooks' statement bounds, increment_f771883001d8) and tested as 8.7 in shared-server.test.ts, but never planned as a contract; recorded here so its test is named by one.

capabilities.title: 9 · Knowledge entrances
capabilities.description: Every story and capability has its own shelf of front-cover decisions, and a decision can be a front cover of one of them at most. Artifacts link only to other artifacts, so the only way from the work into the knowledge is through a front cover.

contracts.title: 9.1 · A decision can be the front cover of a story or a capability, and `frontCovers(nodeId)` returns that node's live covers, founding (oldest) first, and nothing else.
9.2 · A front cover that names anything but a live story or capability is refused, and nothing is written. Only a decision can be a front cover.
9.3 · An artifact that links to a story, capability, contract, arc or health entry is refused, and nothing is written. Artifacts link only to other artifacts.

9.4 · A link that would close a loop between artifacts, an artifact linking to itself included, is refused with the chain it would close named, and nothing is written. The knowledge is a DAG under its covers (ADR-0647 D2).

capabilities.title: 10 · Work in flight
capabilities.description: Each arc is whole: its intent, its end state and its increments. An increment moves from proposal to active to closed (ADR-0909 D4 retired the ready step; one stored as ready reads as a proposal). An arc reads closed when its last increment closes, and reopens when new work is parked on it, unless the owner has parked the arc. A closed increment stays, as the arc's log entry: its date, pull request, note, and whether it landed, failed or was withdrawn.

contracts.title: An increment moves forward: proposal, active, closed (ADR-0909 D4 retired the ready step, and asking for it is refused); its one step back is 10.9's, active work nobody holds returning to proposal. Closing records the date, pull request, note and outcome (landed, failed or withdrawn), and a close with no pull request needs a note. A dedicated correction replaces a closed outcome with a required nonblank reason kept in history, preserves its closure date unless supplied, and leaves it closed; an open increment or an invalid outcome is refused without a write.
10.1 · An increment belongs to one live arc. It is created as a proposal, stamped with the date it was parked, or born closed.

10.3 · An arc with increments reads closed exactly when none is open and none of its questions waits on the owner, and active otherwise; an arc with no increments yet reads active. A parked arc reads parked until it is unparked.
10.4 · An arc's intent and end state are required, and an arc written before they were is upgraded to carry them.

10.5 · An increment moves to another live arc keeping its id, lifecycle and waits, its history recording the move and why; closed history may move into a closed arc, while open work moving to a closed arc is refused and nothing is written.
10.6 · An arc parked until a day reads parked before that day (UTC midnight) and as if unparked from it on, worked out on read with no write in between
contracts.description: The owner's timed park (increment_6440942f1960): `arc park <arc> --until <YYYY-MM-DD>` holds an arc for a known date, and it comes back by itself, with no scheduler. A plain park still holds until unparked; unpark clears the date.

contracts.title: 10.7 · An increment stored as ready, a step ADR-0909 D4 retired, reads as a proposal keeping its parked date, and an edit stores it so.
contracts.description: The lifecycle is proposal, active, closed. Increments written while the ready step existed are upgraded on read by the library's upgrade path (increment schema version 2), so no one-off migration is needed, and claiming one still starts it.

contracts.title: 10.8 · Holds and wait checks read open work and named blockers, and one arc view reads only its own history: adding hundreds of long closed increments elsewhere adds at most 128 KiB per read.
contracts.description: arcView keeps its own full closed log, including outcome date, disposition, PR and note, but server-filters increments and questions by arc. arcViews still returns complete history: board lanes use closed increments, and existing consumers keep the ArcView contract. Snapshots select open work, named landed blockers, and at most one existence marker per named arc blocker with no open increments.

reported.note: 10.8 passes on counted Postgres: 700 closed increments and 100 settled questions leave holds and waitHolds at 2,117 bytes each and arcView at 1,660 bytes. All 43 work/wait/question tests pass.

contracts.title: 10.9 · An active increment returns to proposal, keeping its parked date, when nobody holds it; a proposal or closed one is refused with nothing written
contracts.description: The one backward step: work whose last claim is released without closing stops reading as in progress (friction_9ce4f31578b7).

contracts.title: 10.10 · An arc whose every open increment waits only on a dated event, or on its own work so held, reads parked until the earliest check-back day, worked out on read; free work, an owner wait or an open question keeps it active
contracts.description: The owner, 2026-10-09: an arc whose remaining work waits only on a date parks itself until that date, so the active board shows only what can move (increment_3529cf532f81). Nothing is stored and nothing is refused: raising a question or claiming reads only the owner's stored park. The arc view carries the wake day, said as 'parked until <day> (UTC)'.

contracts.title: 10.11 · An increment carries a capabilities list naming live capabilities only, parked empty and editable after parking, and cites anything else (its stories, notes, decisions) through links; one stored with the retired touches reads its capabilities in the list and the rest as links, and an edit stores it so (ADR-0949 D2)

10.12 · An active increment takes a pending change to a story, capability or contract it did not plan: the live record stays, the change keeps its base history entry and its before and after, a second change merges into it, and one another open increment already holds is refused naming it

10.14 · An increment's branch reads the plan with its pending changes laid over, every other reader the live plan; a pending change whose record has changed since it was read is named stale with the entry that moved it
contracts.description: ADR-0966 D3's overlay and D5's gate case, in the library: withPending lays an increment's pending edits (moves included) and retirements over the plan tree, projectTree({ pendingOf }) gives it, and stalePending names each pending change whose base is no longer its record's latest history entry.

contracts.title: 10.15 · An increment's pending changes apply through the plan's own editors when it lands, each history entry marked with its pull request; a stale or refused change is not applied and is parked as residue on its arc naming both history entries; applying again applies nothing twice
contracts.description: ADR-0966 D4 and D5's merge case: applyPending(increment, pr) and a landed closeIncrement.

contracts.title: 10.16 · An increment closed failed or withdrawn drops its pending changes, its history saying so, and the live plan is left as it was
10.17 · Settling closed increments' leftover pending changes applies those of each one that landed and drops those of each one that did not, and finds nothing left the second time
contracts.description: The one-off catch-up for increments closed between ADR-0966 D1 shipping and D4.

contracts.title: 10.18 · A capability is parked when every open increment naming it sits on a parked arc and asks nothing of the owner
contracts.description: parkedCapabilities() gives each capability that open increments name, where every one sits on an arc reading parked (owner-parked or asleep on a dated event) and none waits for the owner or is held on an open question, with the arcs that park it (ADR-0992 D2, D3).

contracts.title: 10.19 · An increment may name the one machine that can take it: parked with it, edited to another, and cleared by an edit to none, which removes the field
contracts.description: The increment's machine field (a machine's short name; absent means any machine) is kept by addIncrement and editIncrement on both backends; an empty name is refused as a schema error with nothing written. Which names exist is Machines' check, not the library's.

capabilities.title: 11 · Waits
capabilities.description: An arc waits on an arc, and an increment on an increment on any arc, each with a reason. A loop across both kinds is refused when it is written. The library alone answers whether a wait holds (`waitHolds`), naming its blockers and saying when one can never release.

contracts.title: 11.1 · An increment wait holds until the blocker closes as landed. A failed, withdrawn or missing blocker holds for good, and says it will never release.
11.3 · A wait that would close a loop across arcs and increments is refused, naming the loop, and nothing is written.
11.2 · An arc wait holds until that arc closes.
11.4 · `waitHolds(id)` returns the blockers still holding, each with its reason.

11.5 · holds() answers every live arc's and open increment's wait holds, and every open increment's owner holds, in one reading, each the same as waitHolds and heldOnQuestion give; closed increments have no holds and are omitted.
11.6 · An increment waits for the owner or an outside event with a note: an owner wait holds until cleared, an event wait until its check-back day, then reads passed
contracts.description: ADR-0938 D1. At most one note per releaser; an event wait needs a check-back day not before today, an owner wait takes none; a closed increment waits for nothing. holds() gives them as waitsFor, each with whether it still holds.

reported.note: waits.test.ts 11.6 passes on memory and Postgres.

contracts.title: 11.8 · A wait is cleared from the record that stores it as its blocker lands (an increment) or closes (an arc), with the reason in its history; a failed or withdrawn blocker's wait stays
contracts.description: No stored wait is ever stale, so no front door holds a stale-wait rule (owner, a question, option A). Cleared in the same step as the close, settle or retire that ends the blocker; the waiter's history keeps the wait.

capabilities.title: 12 · Owner questions
capabilities.description: A question is raised on an arc, with its stakes, statement, context and options, and settled with the owner's answer, which stays on the arc. An increment held on an open question reads as waiting on him (`heldOnQuestion`), and the library alone answers that.

contracts.title: 12.1 · A question is raised with its required fields, and is open.
12.2 · Settling needs an answer and keeps it, with the date and the decision that carried it. A settled question stays readable on its arc.

12.3 · An open increment held on an open question reads as waiting on the owner. Settling the question takes it off every increment's heldOn, keeping their other holds. A question that does not exist holds nothing.
12.4 · A question an increment is held on cannot be retired through retire; retireQuestion (12.9) is the step that releases its holders.

12.5 · An open question carries a review date and a lease, 7 days unless given. It checks fresh until the lease runs out and lapsed after, it is listed as lapsed until renewed, and renewing re-stamps it.
12.6 · Renewing a settled question is refused and nothing is written. A settled question checks settled and is never listed as lapsed.

12.7 · An open question's wording (title, stakes, statement, context, options, analogy, diagram, recommendation) can be corrected in place, changing only the named fields. Its arc, lifecycle, answer and lease are not edited this way, and editing a settled question is refused with nothing written: its answer stands.
12.8 · A question raised on a parked arc is refused, naming the arc, and nothing is written; once its wake day passes, it is raised
contracts.description: ADR-0835 D1: what a session would have asked goes into the arc's residue instead, to be raised when the arc is unparked.

contracts.title: 12.9 · Retiring a question with retireQuestion takes it off the heldOn of every increment held on it, open or closed (keeping their other holds), and retires it in one step, naming the increments released. A record that is not a live question is refused with nothing written.
12.10 · An open question carries the session putting it to the owner, set and cleared in place through editQuestion; settling clears it, and a settled question cannot carry one
contracts.description: So two sessions never put the same open question to the owner at once (friction_1e1a7ce50de1); whether the marking session is still live is the agent link's reading (its 5.36).

capabilities.title: 13 · Decision log
capabilities.description: Decision numbers do not collide, even across concurrent writers, and history reserves every number a decision has held. Other projects start at 1. In the project named exactly `storytree`, automatic numbers exceed the persisted floor and every number any non-health record has ever held; automatic numbering is refused if that setting is absent. An explicit free number remains accepted. The N1 move is complete: the 29 Full record decisions retain their 0.2 numbers, the floor is 662, and the 53 founding books are ADR-0663..0715. Ordinary edits cannot change or remove a decision's number. A decision's status is proposed or accepted, and it can be superseded: the superseded decision is kept, and reads as superseded. A decision carries the load-bearing mark, who decided it, in their own words, and one composed statement. Health events never reserve decision numbers, including in repair previews and writes; legacy non-health reservations remain.

contracts.title: 13.1 · In projects with automatic numbering, decisions recorded at once from separate connections get distinct numbers, each higher than any before. A number held by another decision is never reused, including retired decisions and old numbers kept in history. Ordinary edits cannot change or remove a decision's number and a refused edit writes nothing.
13.2 · A decision is superseded exactly when an accepted decision names it in `supersedes`. It stays readable, and a supersession loop is refused.
13.3 · Status and the load-bearing mark are stored and read back, and a decision written before status was is upgraded to carry one.
13.4 · A decision may carry one composed statement. A read returns it marked stale when the decision's text changed after it was written, and the full text is always readable.

13.5 · Only in the storytree project, numberDecision repairs a live decision once to the number in its own single Full record: ADR-NNNN line. Missing or ambiguous lines, mismatches, retired records, previous repairs, and numbers any non-health record has ever held are refused without writing. Concurrent repairs cannot share a number or repair a record twice. The old number stays in history; editNote still refuses number. decisionNumberPlan lists proposed old → new numbers and refusals, including duplicate targets, without writing. Decisions without a Full record line are untouched. Health events never reserve decision numbers, including in repair previews and writes; legacy non-health reservations remain.

13.6 · Only in storytree, setDecisionNumberFloor previews by default and apply: true stores 0.2's final number once as a positive safe integer project setting, retained in history and snapshots. Repeated or lower floor settings are refused, including concurrent attempts. Recording without an explicit number is refused while the floor is unset; afterwards, automatic numbers exceed the floor and every number any non-health record has ever held, with concurrent writers receiving distinct numbers. An explicit free number remains accepted; other projects still auto-number from 1. Health events never reserve decision numbers, including in repair previews and writes; legacy non-health reservations remain.

13.7 · numberDecisionsFromFullRecord previews by default; apply: true applies every eligible proposal through numberDecision and returns each refusal. Decisions already matching their Full record number are omitted. Duplicate targets are refused, the write checks history again under the project lock, and repeated bulk application writes nothing once all eligible repairs are complete.

13.8 · Only in storytree with its floor set, numberFoundingDecisions previews live decisions that existed at switch-on and have no Full record line, in first-creation history order. Targets exceed the floor and every number any non-health record has ever held. Preview writes and reserves nothing; apply: true rechecks every write and returns each refusal. The record keeps its identity, other fields and old number in history. Concurrent moves cannot share numbers or move a book twice. Completed moves, Full record decisions and decisions created after switch-on are omitted; a repeat can finish a partial run without renumbering completed books. Health events never reserve decision numbers, including in repair previews and writes; legacy non-health reservations remain.
13.9 · `decisions()` gives every live decision's view in one reading, oldest first, each the same as `decision(id)` gives.

capabilities.title: 14 · Ranked search
capabilities.description:
A library search ranks the live artifacts by how close their meaning is to the question, using an embedding model (bge-small) run on this computer, with no LLM, paid API or extra service, as the owner directed (0.2's ADR-0664). An artifact written or edited is embedded again before the next search ranks it, and with no model to hand the search falls back to word matches and says why.

As built: Windows delivery stages the locked Transformers Node distribution, ONNX Runtime CPU binding and DLL, and the Sharp runtime dependency beside the CLI and MCP entrypoints for x64 and arm64. No model weights ship. The existing lazy loader downloads bge-small on first use into <storytree home>/models. The installed-layout check imports Transformers and runs a weight-free ONNX Identity graph on the native CPU backend without a source checkout. Windows x64 execution is checked by installer CI; ARM64 PE headers are inspected, with ARM64 execution awaiting a native Windows acceptance run.

contracts.title: 14.1 · `rank(query)` orders the live artifacts by meaning, best first, with each one's score, and finds an artifact that shares no word with the question.
14.2 · An artifact scores by its best chunk (its rendered text packed into chunks of at most 3000 characters on paragraph boundaries), and at most `limit` artifacts come back, ten unless told.

14.3 · An edited artifact ranks by its new words at the next search; a chunk already embedded is not embedded again, and a library opened afresh on the same project reads the kept vectors, embedding only the question.
14.4 · With no embedding model to hand (switched off, or it cannot load), `rank` gives the word matches of `search` and says why, rather than failing.

14.5 · The installed Windows CLI and MCP tools resolve their bundled Transformers and native ONNX CPU runtime without a checkout or npm installation, on x64 and arm64. The installer ships runtime code and target binaries, never model weights; the embedding model remains a first-use download into <storytree home>/models.

14.7 · A ranked search puts first the records it names by title: one whose contract number (such as 7.17) is a word of the search, then one whose title (a definition's term) holds every word of it, ignoring case; each group, and the rest, keep their meaning order.

14.8 · rankAll ranks live stories, capabilities and contracts by their own wording alongside knowledge artifacts, labels each hit with its type, and finds a contract whose meaning matches even when it shares no query word.

14.9 · With no embedding model, rankAll returns word matches including a contract holding every query word, reports why it fell back, and never treats a plan record’s parent identifier as searchable words.

14.10 · Ranked searches reuse local vectors across processes only within the same server, project database identity and model. Only missing content keys come from Postgres, including after one note is added. Other servers, projects, recreated databases and old unscoped entries cannot alter ranks or scores. Writes reach Postgres and the scoped local copy; concurrent processes share it safely, and no identity or usable local storage falls back to Postgres.

14.11 · An explicit literal phrase lookup matches case-sensitive contiguous text within stored top-level string fields of selected artifact and plan kinds, returns full live records in id order with bounded pages and a continuation cursor, sees edits and retirement, and filters before records leave Postgres. Ranked search is unchanged.

capabilities.title: 15 · Connection by address
capabilities.description: Instead of the local app's Postgres or Cloud SQL with Google sign-in, storytree reaches any Postgres by its address (Neon, Supabase, RDS, self-hosted, Cloud SQL with an ordinary user), its password resolved as a key.

contracts.title: 15.1 · A library at a Postgres address, with its password saved as the `postgres` key, opens, writes and reads a project as a password-authenticated role.
contracts.description: Proven against the throwaway test server with a role that must give its password (scram-sha-256).

contracts.title: 15.2 · With no password saved for the library (no `postgres` key and no PGPASSWORD), connecting is refused saying so and how to save one, before anything reaches the server.
15.3 · A password the server refuses and a host that cannot be reached are each refused as their own problem, with what to fix, and never show the password.
15.4 · A remote address gets the password only after its certificate is checked
contracts.description: ADR-0943 D1, narrowed by ADR-0997 D1: a library at a non-local address connects only over TLS whose certificate chains to a trust anchor storytree was given (the address's sslrootcert when it names one, otherwise Node's authorities alone; no build trusts a certificate of storytree's own) and names the host it dialled; otherwise it is refused before any password is sent, on the admin pool and every project's. A plain-text password request is refused even over TLS, and no sslmode or connection-string override weakens it.

stories.title: Session management
stories.description: Session management keeps the record of who is doing what, so the user's own Claude Code or Codex can work on a storytree project and be seen doing it. A passive layer of hooks records what every agent does, so even an agent that ignores storytree shows up as unplanned activity; sessions, claims, the context reading and which project a folder belongs to are read from that record. Named Session management rather than Sessions, which is an overloaded term (ADR-0969 D4); until 2026-10-11 it was The agent link. The agent's tools are served by the MCP server story, whose wrapper calls what this story exports to name the caller, record the call and end merged claims (ADR-0969 D1). Registering the hooks, the setup check, making a folder a project and wiring the pipeline belong to The app setup (ADR-0969 D3). Red-green is a convention the habits card teaches, not a loop storytree runs.

capabilities.title: 1 · Project routing
capabilities.description: The first time an agent session starts in a folder that isn't a storytree project, storytree asks the user (through the agent) whether to set one up; if they say yes, this leaves a small marker in the folder naming the project, and from then on it routes everything an agent does anywhere in that folder to that project, whichever project the user happens to be looking at in the app. It never picks a project by itself: a folder the user hasn't said yes to is ignored, and when storytree isn't running it says so at once, so everything built on it quietly does nothing.

contracts.title: 1.1 · A folder whose marker names "site" gives "site" asked from the folder, from a sub-folder of it, and from a git worktree of it.
1.2 · A folder with no marker, in it or above it, gives "not a storytree project".
1.4 · With the app's database stopped, asking where to send activity answers "storytree isn't running" in well under a second.
1.5 · A leftover address from a crashed app counts as not running: it answers in well under a second and never hangs.

1.6 · With the library set to Cloud SQL, a project folder routes to that instance (its connection name and user) whether or not the app's local database is running, and no local address is tried; with it local, routing is exactly as in 1.1 to 1.5.

1.7 · Routing reads only the library setting: damage elsewhere in settings.json (an unusable context guidance, say) does not stop it, while a damaged library setting, or a file that is not a JSON object, refuses naming the file and is never read as local nor rewritten.

1.12 · A marker alone reaches no project (ADR-0942): a checkout whose marker names an existing project, with or without its identity, is refused until its trunk on this machine is approved, and a trunk recorded before approval counts as unapproved until it joins on purpose; an approved trunk and its git worktrees reach it.
contracts.description: Approval comes only from setting the folder up or joining on purpose (storytree doctor --join, set_up_project with join). A legacy marker no longer registers or routes itself.

contracts.title: 1.15 · Session management's routing entry alone (@storytree/session-management/routing) routes a folder: one that is no project gives "not a storytree project", and a project whose app is stopped gives "storytree isn't running", without the caller loading the package's root
contracts.description: So the command line can answer "not a project" / "not running" without loading the MCP server, zod, the library's driver and the rest of its root barrel (increment_89f2daefba21; the latency proof is CLI 1.3).

reported.note: package.json exports "./routing": "./src/routing/index.ts"; the test passes.

contracts.title: 1.16 · An authenticated local installation routes only through its private, matching versioned credential handoff; damaged or exposed material refuses without a passwordless fallback, while legacy discovery, app liveness and explicit remote routing remain usable
contracts.description: Prove authorized SQL access to a disposable SCRAM cluster through discovery; missing, unreadable, malformed, mismatched or insecure handoffs fail closed without revealing secrets. POSIX checks current-user ownership and private modes; Windows checks the current-user DACL. Windows privacy refusals carry a fixed non-secret reason distinguishing a process timeout, process failure, owner mismatch, inherited rules, exposed grant, missing owner grant or unexpected output; raw subprocess output, filesystem paths and credentials never cross discovery. The local-postgres producer and legacy server migration remain separate.

reported.note: Focused Linux run passed 20/20 tests: 4 new 1.16 tests plus all 16 existing project-routing tests. Synthetic SCRAM SELECT 42 succeeded through route(); absent/wrong passwords rejected; malformed/mismatched/exposed material refused; cluster stopped. Platform-specific ACL cases still require Windows/macOS CI.

contracts.title: 1.17 · Only a git worktree its trunk's repository registered inherits the trunk's project and approval; a copied or forged .git file pointing at a trunk makes no worktree of it
contracts.description: ADR-0942 D2: worktrees inherit approval, so the worktree link must be the repository's own record, not a file a downloaded folder can carry.

contracts.title: 1.18 · A forgotten trunk's remembered approval opens nothing: removing the project from this machine, or deleting it everywhere, drops this machine's remembered approval for it, so its folder is refused until approved again (ADR-0942)
contracts.description: The approval cache (approved-trunks.json in the storytree home) only spares hooks a trunk query; it must never outlive the trunk record that granted it.

contracts.title: 1.19 · An imported folder is recorded on its project beside the trunk, per machine, approved by the import; recording it again updates its repository and commit, and forgetting the trunk forgets its imports

capabilities.title: 2 · Agent activity log
capabilities.description: Session management's own logbook of what agents do, one per project and kept beside the library rather than inside it, with one line for each thing that happens: a session starts or ends, a file is edited, a command runs, an artifact is read, work is claimed, released or landed. Lines are only ever added, never changed, and can be read back in order as "everything since line N", including lines that other processes wrote.

contracts.title: 2.1 · Two separate processes write lines for two sessions, and reading from the start returns every line once, in the order written.
2.2 · Reading "since line N" returns only the lines after N, in order, each carrying the number to pass next time.
2.3 · Lines written for project "site" never appear when reading project "app".
2.4 · The log never shows up in the library's list of projects, and writing lines leaves the library's own records and change feed untouched.

2.5 · The log opens on whichever server the library resolved to, reached through the library's connection: lines two machines write for one project on one Cloud SQL instance are both read back from either, in order (live, opt-in).
