verified.note: 3 of 6 tests skipped (owner: live Cloud SQL proof needs STORYTREE_TEST_CLOUDSQL_INSTANCE/USER), at commit 4803657df400, run https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/actions/runs/38154140373

contracts.title: 2.6 · A line may name the earlier line of its own project's log that caused it (`causedBy`, ADR-0746 D2), and reads back naming it. A line naming a line its project's log does not hold (another project's, or none) is refused, whether appended alone or under the project's lock, and nothing is written.

2.7 · A bounded read sends only the lines it asks for, oldest first: by kind, session, cursor and time, by a field's value, values or absence, by a field carried, the latest for each key, the newest or oldest few, and inside folders whatever their case or slashes, with the fields it never reads left out.
contracts.description: Every reader asks the log for what it needs, narrowed on the server, never the whole log (#668). Proven by packages/agent-link/src/activity/activity-log.test.ts.

reported.note: Passes on main since #668 (gate and three-platform CI).

contracts.title: 2.8 · A read inside folders, latest line per session, on a log of many lines elsewhere is served by an index: it never scans the project's whole log
contracts.description: The worktree reaper's folder read ran as a scan of the project's whole activity table on storytree-pg (2026-10-07), and hooks cut off mid-scan left it running. The folder match is an index range on the line's normalised folder key (activity_project_folder_idx).

contracts.title: 2.9 · An activity line can be formatted with its complete recorded command, including quotes and line breaks, for both started and finished commands; its number, time, session, kind and recorded cause remain visible. Compact formatting still clips long commands to 60 characters.

2.10 · A claim-refused line's text names the part, the session holding it, the file whose edit asked for it and the refused session's reason; a claimed line's text names its file and the session it was taken over from
contracts.description: Claim failures can be read from the sanctioned front door (storytree noticeboard log) without a script: the stored fields of claim-refused and claimed lines appear in their text form (friction_0ea70e7bdaf8).

capabilities.title: 3 · Hooks
capabilities.description: Small commands that Claude Code and Codex run by themselves when a session starts, after every file edit, before and after every shell command, at the end of each turn, and when it ends, each adding one line about that session to the agent activity log, so an agent that never calls storytree still shows up. At each prompt, one more adds the project's definitions for the terms the prompt names, for the agent to read: every matching term not yet given this session, longest first, with no cap (3.7). The cap of five that 0.2's ADR-0201 set, never measured and never chosen by the owner, is removed by the owner's named choice ("turn the cap off.", 2026-09-28; ADR-0739 D3, ADR-0633); the once-per-session and harness-notice rules, which 0.2 did measure, stay. The same prompt hook carries capability 9's fresh-session nudge to a Claude Code session past its context guidance (9.9). At a session's start in a folder that isn't a storytree project yet, the harness waits for one more (Codex's own start hook, a second one for Claude Code), which has the agent ask the user whether to set storytree up there before the task it was given, and sets nothing up itself (8.12). Every hook also records the transcript path the harness named for its session, so capability 9 can work out any session's tokens used when asked, never from a transcript found by folder (ADR-0725, ADR-0728). They run in the background and always exit cleanly, so they can never slow down or break the agent, and when storytree isn't running they do nothing.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Real, recorded Claude Code hook inputs (a start, a file edit, a shell command, an end) are fed in, and four lines appear on that session, carrying the file path, the command and the machine's name.
3.2 · The same holds for real, recorded Codex hook inputs, where the edited files are read out of its patch text.
3.3 · With storytree stopped, with garbage input, or outside a storytree project, the command exits cleanly in under half a second and writes nothing.
3.4 · It runs on Windows without a Unix shell, and it never prints anything the agent would see.

3.5 · Real, recorded hook inputs for starting a subagent, for a storytree tool call made inside it, and for one made by the orchestrator make three lines: the subagent's id, type and task; the subagent asking, by its id and type, with the call's id; and the orchestrator asking, with its call's id. The same holds for Claude Code and for Codex.

3.6 · Real, recorded hook inputs from before a shell command, after one that failed, and at the end of a turn make three lines: the command started and the command finished, both under the call's id, and the turn ended. For Codex, whose hooks the agent waits for, the hook hands its line to one in the background and exits.

3.7 · At each prompt, the project's definitions for the terms it names are added for the agent: whole words in any case or plural, every one not yet given this session, longest first, with no cap (a prompt naming six gets all six), each once a session, each meaning's first line cut to 200 characters. A harness's own notice gets none, and with storytree stopped nothing is printed.

3.8 · The status line shows what this session holds, how many other agents are working, and a warning when another is editing a file it edited. With storytree stopped it says so, and outside a project it shows nothing.

3.12 · Real, recorded Claude Code and Codex hook inputs record on their session the transcript path the harness named (`transcript_path`), and a session's transcript reads as the latest one recorded for it. For a `claude -p` run whose transcript sits under a project directory unrelated to its `cwd`, and for a session whose `cwd` is now worktree B while its transcript sits under the project directory of folder A where it started, it is exactly the named path; no folder is searched.

3.13 · Each hook streams its session's new transcript records, and each subagent's (from <transcript>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl) under its parent session by the subagent's id, into the shared log, secrets scrubbed (9.12), from where the last hook left off (a cursor read from the store), only whole records, never twice, and at most 2 MB per hook (ADR-0749 D3, D4).

3.14 · Lines a hook writes while storytree cannot be reached (not running, or the store refusing) wait on this machine under the storytree home, each with the time and machine it was written at; the next hook that reaches the log uploads them before its own, oldest first, at their own times, and each line exactly once, however many hooks try (ADR-0749 consequences).

3.15 · Real, recorded prompt inputs make a prompt line on their session (without the prompt's words), for Claude Code and Codex alike, and a Claude Code Stop always makes a turn-ended line carrying how many background tasks are still running (ADR-0754 D5).
3.16 · Every line a hook writes records the git branch its folder is on (even one with no commit yet), beside the folder; a folder on no branch records none (ADR-0754 D4).

3.17 · When a turn ends with its session's work resolved and no standing close-out, the Stop hook's output reminds the agent to close out; a session that is idle or has exited is never prompted (ADR-0758 D4).

3.19 · A Claude Code session's end is recorded even though Claude Code stops its end hook after 1.5 s and the store takes longer than that to answer: run as setup registers it (with `--background`) and cut short at 1.5 s, the hook hands its line to a copy of itself that outlives it, and the session-ended line lands.

3.18 · A Codex hook that runs, in any folder, notes on this machine that Codex runs storytree's hooks; they read as waiting while registered and not yet run since, and a later registration reads as waiting again.
contracts.description: Codex runs a hook only once the user trusts it, which storytree cannot read (Codex keeps it as its own hashes), so a hook that has run is the proof the connect step, the setup check and the app show.

reported.note: codex-trust.test.ts: red first (expected running, got waiting: no hook noted it), green after runHook notes Codex hooks.

contracts.title: 3.21 · A hook's reads do not grow with the log's length: the same hooks (a command's finish, which also hands on the look around the machine, a prompt, and the status line) take about as much from the store in a project whose log holds weeks of history as in one whose log holds an hour's.
contracts.description: Measured through a byte-counting stand-in for the store, as Cloud SQL bills egress. Red on main before #668: 19.6 KB against an hour-old log, 66.6 MB against 22 MB of history. Proven by packages/agent-link/src/hooks/hooks.test.ts.

reported.note: Red first on main (19.6 KB vs 66.6 MB); passes on main since #668.

contracts.title: 3.22 · After a shell command, changed tracked and non-ignored files in its Git worktree are recorded as edits for that session, including repeated writes, additions, deletions and moves. Pre-existing dirt, read-only commands, staging, unchanged commits, and files left as a pull, merge, checkout, switch, reset or rebase wrote them invent no edits. Explicit edit hooks advance the baseline; failed commands and offline hooks retain their writes.
3.23 · A failing hook leaves a local trace
contracts.description: A hook whose writing throws, or that cannot reach storytree, appends one bounded line under the storytree home (time, harness, event, session, tool call, stage, error class and message; capped and set aside past 64 KiB), still exiting cleanly and silently; a healthy hook leaves none.

contracts.title: 3.24 · A hook cut off at its deadline while a statement of its waits on the server leaves no statement running there: the server ends it
contracts.description: Every connection a hook, its upkeep copy, the prompt's context and the status line open carries the library's statement bound (8.7) at the hook's deadline, so a statement a cut-off hook left behind does not hold a connection on the shared library.

contracts.title: 3.25 · A hook in a checkout not approved for the project its marker names writes nothing to that project's log, queues nothing for it, and lines waiting from such a folder are never uploaded
contracts.description: ADR-0942 D1: refusal comes before any activity is appended.

contracts.title: 3.26 · The hook before a file-edit tool, run as setup registers it, refuses a Claude Code edit and a Codex patch to a capability another live session holds, with the reason the agent reads, and says nothing for a file that declares no capability (ADR-0949 D3)
contracts.description: The foreground --edit-gate hook; fails open outside a project, unapproved, unreachable or late.

capabilities.title: 4 · Sessions
capabilities.description: Reads the agent activity log as a list of agent sessions, one per Claude Code or Codex window, each showing which of the two it is, which folder it works in, when it started and when it was last seen. A session is working from a prompt until its turn ends, or while a command it started runs, and waiting otherwise (ADR-0754 D5); ended once its end line arrives. A session whose hooks report no turns (no prompt line: hooks not running, or installed before D5) is working while its lines keep arriving and waiting after the quiet time, the user's `idle-after` setting (capability 10, 10.10; ADR-0739 D2), 30 minutes when unset. So it never reads as working just because nobody said otherwise.

contracts.title: 4.1 · A start line makes a working session labelled "Claude Code", with its folder, when it started and when it was last seen.
4.2 · A session whose hooks report no turns reads as waiting once no line has come for longer than the quiet time, and after its end line it reads as ended.
4.3 · A resumed window continues the same session instead of starting a second one.
4.4 · A Codex session whose hooks never ran, but which calls a storytree tool, still appears and is flagged "hooks not running", so a missing hook never looks like an agent doing nothing.

4.5 · A command that started 40 minutes ago and has not finished keeps its session working. Once it finishes, or its turn ends with no background task left running, it no longer counts, and one started longer ago than the longest a command may run no longer counts.

4.6 · A session is its harness session id, never a folder: one whose lines name two folders reads with both as its worktrees, in the order it first worked in each, while its folder stays the one it started in (ADR-0749 D2).

4.7 · A session with no line for longer than a command may run (12 hours) and no end line has stopped reporting: it reads as gone, never as ended, since nothing said it ended; up to that limit it reads as idle (ADR-0749 consequences).

4.8 · Working comes from turn state (ADR-0754 D5): a prompt makes its session working until its turn ends, however long the turn writes no line, and compacting mid-turn does not end it; its end makes it waiting at once; a turn that ends with background tasks still running leaves their command running, so the session stays working until it finishes.

4.9 · Who is listed (ADR-0754 D4): a session whose branches (every branch other than main its lines name, a merged line's excepted) still hold open work stays listed whatever its end line or silence says; once its work resolves (the latest branch-state line for each branch says resolved), a session leaves on its end line or after the leave-after quiet time, counted from its last line or the resolution, whichever is later; a session the Claude or Codex app keeps (a session-archived or session-unarchived line names it) shows done instead of leaving, is removed at once when archived, and comes back when un-archived.

4.10 · Each branch a session worked on is marked resolved once a pull request from it merged (asked of GitHub from any machine), or, on the machine it was worked on, once it has nothing ahead of the main line or is deleted (a branch with no commit yet is neither); one still ahead stays open, and one worked on again after it resolved is looked at again and reads open when it is ahead. A branch-state line is written only when the state changes, on the session that saw it (ADR-0754 D4). The hooks take this look once a minute through a copy of themselves that may run longer than a hook, so a merge is recorded though GitHub answers later than a hook may run. A claim's `merged` line resolves its branch as a branch-state line does, until a later look reads it open.

4.11 · Closing out records whether the session says it is safe to close and why, releases every capability and increment claim it still holds regardless of branch or whether a tool or edit hook took it, and returns the released ids. Other sessions keep their claims; repeating close-out releases nothing. Verification of safe still checks unfinished work and runs.

4.12 · A yes is checked, never trusted: it leaves the list at once when its branches are resolved and nothing of its own runs; otherwise it stays and needs you, naming the disagreement; a no stays with its why; a later prompt or new admitted claim voids it (ADR-0758 D3). Closing out first asks whether the project’s branches have merged, so a merge no hook recorded still bears a yes out.

4.25 · The sessions the Claude desktop app and Codex keep are read, read-only, from their own files on each machine (Claude's claude-code-sessions/<account>/<org>/local_*.json: cliSessionId and isArchived; Codex's state_5.sqlite threads: id and archived, headless runs and subagents excluded), and each session the project's log knows gets a session-archived or session-unarchived line when its state there changes, never otherwise. Absent files read as absent and damaged ones as unreadable, and neither writes anything (ADR-0754 D4).

4.13 · The sessions listing (`storytree session list`) first asks whether the project's branches have merged, so it never waits on a hook to have recorded a merge, then shows each session the list shows, one block each, with its state, listing, folder, open and resolved branches, its work on main as its flag or label (4.26), close-out and what needs you; a hidden one (a verified close-out) only with --all; --json gives the same sessions as data.

4.18 · The hooks reap a worktree once it can go (ADR-0790): a clean linked worktree whose head is in the main line, whose every session (at least one) has a verified close-out or is archived, which is not locked and holds neither the hook's folder nor a registered hook script, is removed and unregistered and its branch deleted; a dirty, unmerged, locked, unused, still-used, protected or hook-running one stays; its folder is moved to a trash folder first and the trash emptied out of the hook's way.

4.19 · How the app that keeps a session names and describes it reaches the log: for each session this project knows, the Claude desktop app's title and its post-turn summary's status, or Codex's thread name (else its title), are written as one `session-described` line (by whichever session read the records, never on the session it is about), scrubbed as transcripts are and held to 120 and 300 characters, and written again only when those words change. Each session read from the log carries the latest title and status.

4.20 · A line about other sessions (a claim's merge, a branch's state, what an app keeps or how it names a session) never makes its writer a session: a person, or the app, that only looked is not listed, and an agent's look does not count as its own work.

4.21 · The app looks at each project's branches itself, once a minute while it runs, asking from the latest folder this machine still has and writing under app:<machine>, so its sessions list never waits on a hook to have recorded a merge.

4.22 · A session reads, for each folder its lines name, the branches recorded there, in the order first recorded, with whether each still holds open work and, while open, its pull request as the latest look read it (4.24). The main line is no branch; a branch with no folder is placed in the folder the session last worked in.

4.23 · A session reads the commands it started and has not seen finish, each with its command text and start time, background ones a turn left running included: the same reading that keeps a session working (4.5, 4.8).

4.24 · The branch look reads every open pull request of the project's repository in one GitHub call, alongside its merged-pull-request call, under the same once-a-minute stamp and fail-soft rules: for each open branch, its number, whether it is a draft, its head commit's checks taken together (pending, passing or failing; none when it has none), and whether it waits in the merge queue. The branch-state line carries these and is written again only when one changes; GitHub not answering erases nothing; a pull request closed unmerged leaves the branch open with none. The Session reading carries them on each open branch in branchesByFolder.
contracts.description: Lets the sessions list label a worktree with where its pull request stands (ADR-0824 D2), from the same once-a-minute branch look that resolves merges.

contracts.title: 4.26 · Work on main is never silently dropped (ADR-0906): a session that edited files inside a folder on the main line while the latest look on its machine finds that folder's main uncommitted, or that holds an increment it claimed on main, stays listed whatever its end or silence, flagged "worked on main, outside a workspace"; while the repository has no commit yet it is labelled "setting up git, first commit pending" instead; a yes close-out is not verified while the flag stands; once the work is committed (and the claim gone) the flag goes and it leaves as 4.9 says. A file edited outside the folder, or a capability claimed on main, raises no flag.
contracts.description: Reproduces Conduit's GitHub adoption (app-setup evidence first-build/github.md 199-214): an ended Codex session that staged its first commit's files on main vanished from the default list. The flag is a field on the existing row, not a new lifecycle state.

contracts.title: 4.27 · The branch look (4.10) also looks, on this machine, at each folder a session edited files in, or claimed an increment in, while on the main line: it writes a main-state line saying whether that folder's main holds uncommitted changes and whether its repository has no commit yet, only when that changes, under the same once-a-minute stamp and fail-soft rules; a folder no longer on the main line reads as holding none.
contracts.description: How 4.26 learns its facts (ADR-0906's detection, the building session's call): git status and whether HEAD resolves, asked where the work was done.

contracts.title: 4.28 · The sessions read from the lines that decide them, and the claims read from those standing, are what a fold of the whole log gives at any time, from a share of its lines; the list's own read leaves out only sessions the list hides, and the status line's states agree.
contracts.description: The bounded readings (#668) are exact: checked against a fold of the whole log now, past the quiet time, past the leave-after time and past 12 hours. Proven by packages/agent-link/src/sessions/sessions.test.ts.

reported.note: Passes on main since #668.

contracts.title: 4.29 · A session last seen on its machine before that machine's recorded start reads gone, not working, to a reader on any machine, with no command running, and its claims read free; one seen since the start, or on another machine, reads as before
contracts.description: Headless lanes killed by their machine's restart write no end line, so they kept reading working for up to twelve hours on every list (the Mint box's reboots, 2026-10-06). The machine-started line (4.30) gives every reader the start to judge them by; contract 5.17's own-machine reading stands beside it unchanged.

contracts.title: 4.30 · The first hook on a machine to reach a project's log after the machine starts records that start there, once: a later hook reading the same start a moment apart writes nothing; the next start, or another project, is recorded again
contracts.description: The machine-started line, written by whichever session's hook reached the log first, carries the machine and its start by its own clock (from its uptime). The machine remembers under the storytree home which start it last recorded in each project.

contracts.title: 4.31 · A verb declared once reads a command's words and flags and a tool's arguments to the same input, refuses the same wrong input on both, and does the same work and answers in the same sentence for either door
4.32 · A session in a harness storytree has no hooks for reads as connected in the sessions list, never flagged hooks not running; a watched harness's session without hooks still is
contracts.description: Input: activity lines of a session whose harness is not Claude Code or Codex. Output: the session's tier is "connected" and its row says connected, not watched. A Claude Code or Codex session keeps tier "watched" and the hooks-not-running flag.

capabilities.title: 5 · Claims
capabilities.description: Before building a capability, the agent claims it with a one-line reason, so the user and the other agents can see who is on what, and every edit its session makes while holding the claim counts toward that capability. Only one live session can hold a capability: a second agent is refused with the holder's name and picks other work instead of queueing, and a claim ends when the agent lands or releases it, when its session ends, or when another agent takes it over after the holder has gone idle.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Session A claims "email form", and the claim shows A and the reason.

5.2 · A second live claimant is refused naming the holder and why it still binds, including any unverified close-out disagreement; a claim-refused line records the refusal. An idle holder, including one whose standing safe close-out is verified against its branches and running work, permits takeover even with stale command telemetry. A prompt, admitted claim or non-compaction restart voids that close-out.
5.3 · When A reports it landed, the claim ends and a "landed" line is written. A release, or A's session ending, also ends it.
5.4 · A claim on a capability the library doesn't have is refused, and when two agents claim at the same instant exactly one wins.
5.5 · An edit made while A holds "email form" counts toward it, and an edit from a session holding nothing counts as unplanned activity.
5.6 · While a command A started is still running, past the quiet time, B's claim on A's capability is refused, naming A.

reported.note: 37 existing claims/workspace/activity tests pass, including single-history-scan refusal, exclusivity, running-owner liveness, restart takeover, attribution, waits and cancellation. Red and green logs retained under /tmp/st03-claim-latency-evidence.

contracts.title: 5.7 · Session A claims a proposed increment, and the claim shows A and the reason while the library shows the increment active; B's claim on it is refused, naming A. An active one is not started again, and a closed one is refused.

5.8 · Claiming an increment whose own wait holds, or whose arc's wait holds, is refused, naming each blocker and its reason, and one held on an open question is refused as waiting on the owner. Nothing is written and the increment is not started. Once the wait releases, the claim succeeds.
5.9 · A capability claim is never refused because the open increments naming it in their touches wait: touches is a plan, never a lock (ADR-0944 D2). The waiting increment itself is still refused.

5.10 · A claim taken on branch `feature/signup` ends with a "merged" line once GitHub shows a pull request from that branch merged after the claim was taken, found at the next tool call or hook line; a pull request merged before the claim, or still open, ends nothing.

reported.note: 37 focused tests pass: no-merge board takes no project lock; observed merges still recheck current claims under lock and release them. Before/after benchmark includes both no-merge and actual-merge paths.

contracts.title: 5.11 · The public readings list current capability and increment claims and find the holder of one unit, with the same live or idle result on the terminal and the board. Released work and a unit in another project have no holder.

5.12 · Claude Code session A makes a workspace for a proposed increment: a new folder where its harness keeps worktrees, on a fresh branch cut from `origin`'s main as just fetched (a commit pushed after the clone is in it), and A holds the increment there, the claim naming that branch, and the increment is active. For Codex, preparation fetches main and returns its exact commit and a work-derived name for the app's `create_worktree`, without creating a folder, branch or claim. The agent then attaches the app's returned directory: Storytree verifies it is a linked worktree of this repository with HEAD at that exact commit, names a detached HEAD `codex/<name>` (keeps an existing named branch), and claims the work for that session on that branch. Moving `origin/main` after preparation does not change the expected commit.

5.13 · Making a workspace for work another live session holds, or for waiting work, is refused naming the holder or the blocker, and no folder, branch or claim is made, only a claim-refused line for held work (5.2); for work the session already holds it is refused naming the branch it holds it on. Codex checks before app creation and again when attaching; a claim lost to another session between the steps is refused naming that holder, leaving the app's worktree untouched.

5.14 · When main cannot be fetched fresh, as from a folder with no `origin`, it is refused saying why, and nothing is claimed or started. Attaching a directory from another repository, the main checkout, a subdirectory, or a worktree at the wrong commit is refused without claiming or changing it. If attaching fails after taking the claim (including naming a detached branch), that claim is released; the app's worktree is never removed (a started increment stays active).

5.15 · A claim cancelled while waiting for the activity lock or the increment activation write lock leaves no claimed line, activation or activation history. A capability or already-active increment claim checks cancellation before its claimed line too. Once admitted, a claim completes normally; a workspace claim creates or attaches its workspace only after admission.

5.16 · A claim's reason is its session's name in the running-sessions list, so it is held to 40 characters (measured from the list's label column at its default width): a claim, or a workspace, whose reason is longer is refused naming the limit and the reason's length, nothing is written and nothing is started; a reason of 40 characters or fewer is claimed as before (ADR-0737 D2).
5.17 · A holder last seen on this machine before it restarted is taken over at once
contracts.description: A session whose lines name this machine and were last written before this machine last started cannot still be running: its claim reads idle at once, so the lane resuming its work claims it (logged as taken over from the dead holder) instead of waiting out the idle-after window. A holder last seen after the restart, or on another machine, stays protected until idle-after, as before.

contracts.title: 5.19 · Making a workspace for a capability from inside a worktree whose branch this session already holds work on claims the capability there, on that branch, and makes no second worktree or branch. Asking for a workspace for an available increment from inside any linked worktree (named or detached, from any subfolder, either harness) is refused with the command that claims it there, and no worktree, branch, preparation, claim or activation is made
contracts.description: From friction_5ba71c4ec389: `storytree workspace capability_… --reason …` run inside an increment's worktree cut a second worktree and branch from origin/main; claiming each capability before touching it must not. From increment_a7e22ca60ad1: an increment asked for from a linked worktree went on to fetch and create (Claude Code) or prepare another folder (Codex); an explicit claim in place avoids silently adopting an old or queued branch. Held, waiting and already-yours refusals (5.13) still come first.

contracts.title: 5.23 · A claim takes from the library what deciding it needs and no more: one the session already holds takes almost nothing, and a capability claim takes about as much with five open increments naming it as with one.
contracts.description: Each claim, and each edit-claims look with new edits, read the plan tree, every arc view, and the whole work once per open increment naming the capability: ~5-10 MB of Cloud SQL egress per claim on 5 Oct 2026 (arc_0ab31fd59c88).

reported.note: a claim already held under 32 KiB (was ~3 MB); five naming increments within 128 KiB of one; the edit-claims look reads the plan once

contracts.title: 5.25 · Making a workspace for work that already has an open pull request (a head branch named for it, `*/increment-<id>-*`) is refused naming each pull request and its branch, before anything is claimed or made, unless the session says to build beside it; a GitHub that cannot be asked refuses nothing
contracts.description: So a successor session does not rebuild work already in flight (friction_4d14aad0e402: PR #713 rebuilt; friction_88b7ebf3f0bb: PR #718 duplicated #716). A refusal with an override, like a refused claim, binds by default.

contracts.title: 5.26 · The session manager ends a quiet session's claim with a release naming the holder and why; a live holder's claim is refused
contracts.description: ADR-0944 D7: after messaging a quiet holder, the session manager writes a released line naming the holder session and its reason, which ends that holder's claim in every reading (bounded and whole-log fold alike). The release is refused when the named session does not hold the work, or holds it and still reads live.

contracts.title: 5.27 · Closing or releasing an increment ends every capability claim taken while it was held, whoever closes it and whatever the disposition, in every reading; one claimed before it stands (ADR-0944 D5, ADR-0949 D4)
contracts.description: A capability claim's line names the increment its session held when it took it (`under`); that session's "closed" line for the increment ends the claim in the whole-log fold, the standing-claims reading and attribution, so a finished job leaves no stray capability lock.

contracts.title: 5.29 · Releasing an active increment without closing it, by the release tool, the session manager's release or close-out, returns it to proposal; a capability or a closed increment is untouched
contracts.description: Work nobody holds is nobody's work in progress: whichever front door ends a session's own claim on an unclosed increment, the library shows it proposal again, keeping the day it was parked (library 10.9), so it is never stranded active.

contracts.title: 5.31 · An edit tool aimed at a capability its session's claimed increment does not list, or that another live session holds by claim or on its increment's list, is refused before the edit, naming the way through or the holder; a file that declares no capability, or a session's own listed capability, is never refused (ADR-0949 D3)
contracts.description: The pre-edit half of ADR-0949 D3: refusal by the file's own declaration, recorded as a claim-refused line.

contracts.title: 5.33 · The session manager's worklist lists claimed increments whose holder is quiet, with no running command and no open pull request, routing a gone holder's to release and a quiet one's to ask; nothing is ended until the manager releases (ADR-0953 D4)
contracts.description: One stale-claim worklist replaces the hooks ending gone holders' claims themselves (endGoneClaims, ADR-0944 D6, retired). A GitHub that cannot be asked is said, never read as no pull request.

contracts.title: 5.34 · A takeover's claimed line names the holder, how long it was quiet and why
contracts.description: Every claim taken over from another session writes a claimed line naming the holder it took from, when that holder was last seen, and why it no longer bound (idle past the quiet time, gone past the longest command, its machine restarted, or a verified close-out); the activity log's text reads it as "taken over from A after N min quiet (why)" (ADR-0953 D2).

contracts.title: 5.35 · A refused claim names the increment its holder holds the work for
contracts.description: A claim refused as held answers with the increments its holder holds the work for (the one it was claimed under first, then every other increment the holder session holds), and the command line's refusal names them, so refused work can be chained after that increment closes (ADR-0955 D2).

contracts.title: 5.36 · A question one live session is putting to the owner is refused to another, naming it, and read as presented; it is free again once that session stops, ends or closes out, and a settled question is refused
contracts.description: presentQuestion, stopPresenting and presentersOf: the mark on the question (library 12.10) binds only while its session is live, as a claim's holder does, so the owner is never asked the same thing by two sessions at once.

contracts.title: 5.37 · When a claim on an increment ends because its branch's pull request merged, that increment's pending plan changes are applied first, marked with the pull request
contracts.description: ADR-0966 D4: endMergedClaims applies before it ends the claims.

contracts.title: 5.38 · A refused capability claim names the increment its session holds it under
contracts.description: A claim-refused line for a capability, from claim, claimRefusal or the edit gate, carries `under`: the increment the refused session holds, the latest it claimed; none when it holds no increment. The pool reads it to leave that increment out while the holder keeps the capability.

contracts.title: 5.39 · A claim's mark is one shape and one colour wherever it is drawn
contracts.description: Session management's browser-safe `claim-mark` entry gives every surface that draws a claim (the globe's flag, the arc surface's planted flag) the session's colour, the quiet rule (a third less saturated and four points darker, on a session's hsl() colour or on plain HSL numbers) and the pennant's outline at scale k, furled narrower and drooped when quiet (ADR-1003 D4).

capabilities.title: 9 · Context readings
capabilities.description:
How many tokens a session's own context window holds, worked out when it is asked for from what the hooks recorded (ADR-0725, ADR-0728; 0.2's `storytree context`, ADR-0716 O2). The hooks record each session's transcript path (capability 3). A reading is computed at ask time from that transcript as it stands, so it is fresh mid-turn, and in a `claude -p` run whose turn has not ended. On the session's own machine (the status line, `storytree context`) that means the transcript file itself. The app reads no transcript file: its readings and windows are parsed from the transcript records the hooks stream into the shared log (3.13; ADR-0749 D3), so an app on any machine reads every machine's sessions. Those records have obvious secrets scrubbed on the way in (9.12) and are kept 180 days, after which what was worked out from them is kept instead (9.13; ADR-0749 D4). A reading is a plain record: the session, its harness, tokens used, when it was read, and its source (the transcript it was read from). It carries no window size and no fraction (ADR-0728 D1). The guidance a session judges against is a token figure the user sets on the agent link settings surface (capability 10, `context-guidance`; ADR-0728 D2, D3). A reading states that guidance and whether tokens used are past it or under it (9.7); it is a soft line, never enforced. The same figure is the line past which a Claude Code session is nudged, through the prompt hook (capability 3), to hand off and start fresh (9.9; ADR-0739 D1): one setting, no second figure, and 0.2's separate 850,000 hard mark is not brought across. The nudge is advice; nothing stops the session. Codex sessions get no nudge until Codex matures (ADR-0739 D5). This capability owns the nudge because whether a session is past its guidance is this capability's reading (9.7); the prompt hook only carries the words. Built with advice once per session; later prompts in the same session do not repeat it.

For Claude Code, tokens used are the latest request of the session's own conversation: `input_tokens` + `cache_read_input_tokens` + `cache_creation_input_tokens`, counted once per `requestId`, with subagent (`isSidechain`) and `<synthetic>` lines left out. A transcript with nothing to count is an absence with its reason, never 0. For Codex, tokens used are the rollout's last token count. Any live session's reading can be worked out this way without that session asking, so the board can later show one per session; that display is not built here. It reads and never enforces: the session still decides whether to take on more work.

The transcript is always the one the hooks recorded as named by the harness (`transcript_path`, on every Claude Code and Codex hook input). Nothing ever looks for a session's transcript by folder. That is what fixes 0.2's two blind spots. 0.2 worked out who was asking from the `.claude/worktrees/<name>` folder the command ran in, then matched transcripts whose recorded `cwd` sat inside it. A batch (`claude -p`) session run from a main checkout or from outside that folder was refused or matched nothing (0.2 friction `storytree-context-cannot-read-a-batch-sessions-own-window`). A session that moved into a fresh worktree kept writing its transcript under the project directory of the folder it started in, so the new folder matched nothing. And because worktree folders are reused, the fallback could read another session's window (0.2 friction `context-verb-blinded-by-the-fresh-worktree-its-own-rule-mandates`: no reading from the new worktree, 506,097 tokens from the old one in the same minute).

As built (guidance-reading): `contextReading` and `readContext` add `guidance` without changing the existing session, harness, tokens, composition, at or transcript-source fields. Guidance is `{ value, source: "default" | "set", position: "under" | "at" | "past" }`, read afresh through capability 10's `readSettings`; its default is 600,000 tokens (ADR-0739 D1). An unusable settings file gives `{ absent: <the reader's reason> }` while retaining an available token count. No transcript remains an absence with no token count. `storytree context` and `read_context` state the guidance in their text and include it in their data; a count under, at or past guidance is never refused. Contract 9.7 is pinned in `packages/agent-link/src/context/context.test.ts`, and the existing 6.22 MCP test checks guidance output.

Remaining integration for 9.7: the current library-location routing reads the same settings file before it can open the activity log (ADR-0735). If that file is already unusable when `storytree context` or `read_context` starts routing, the call cannot reach the transcript record; the reader's token-preserving guidance error is therefore not reachable through those entry points in that case. This lane does not guess a local library or bypass the settings reader. Resolving that routing dependency is outside its context/tools-output file fence. Contract 9.7 must not be marked fully proved until that end-to-end case is resolved. `packages/agent-link/evidence/guidance-reading/captures.txt` records both the successful reader case and the route refusal.

As built (fresh-nudge): the Claude Code prompt hook calls the existing `readContext` for the session named by the recorded hook input. It adds advice to hand off and start a fresh session at the next safe boundary only when that reading is past its current guidance, naming both tokens used and the guidance. Definitions and context advice use separate per-session ledgers through the definitions hook's extracted `notYetGivenIds` helper; each nudge is given once per session across separate hook processes. Under or at guidance, absent readings, unreadable settings, and Codex inputs add no nudge. No threshold or switch is added: the existing reading supplies the sole setting, including the default change owned by capability 10. The built-hook contract 9.9 test covers boundaries, changed settings, repetition, definitions alongside advice, Codex, and absence/recovery; every prompt exits 0 with no blocking decision. The existing 9.7 routing qualification above remains.

contracts.title: 9.1 · A recorded Claude Code transcript whose last own request used 12,000 input, 300,000 cache-read and 5,000 cache-creation tokens reads 317,000 tokens used; a request repeated across lines with one `requestId` counts once, and a later subagent (`isSidechain`) or `<synthetic>` line does not change the figure.
9.2 · A transcript that is empty, unreadable, or holds only subagent or synthetic requests reads as an absence naming which, never as 0 tokens.
9.3 · A recorded Codex rollout reads its last token count as tokens used (ADR-0728: no window size).

9.5 · A session's reading is worked out when asked, from the transcript last recorded for it (3.12) read at that moment (9.1, 9.3), and carries the session, harness, tokens used, when it was read and its source, with no window size or fraction (ADR-0728). Any live session's reading can be worked out this way without that session asking. A session with no recorded transcript gives an absence, and another session's transcript is never read.

9.6 · `storytree context`, run with the harness's session id in its environment, prints that session's tokens used, worked out at that moment (9.5), even mid-turn with no turn ended since the transcript grew, and `--json` prints the record; it exits 0 whatever the figure, states no window size or fraction, states the guidance as 9.7 says, and with no reading it says so and prints no number.

9.7 · A reading states the context guidance in effect (capability 10: set, or its default) and whether tokens used are past it or under it; with 400,000 set, 317,000 reads under and 450,000 reads past, and the command still exits 0. With the settings file unusable (10.4), the reading gives tokens used and says the guidance could not be read, and why.

9.8 · A Claude Code or Codex reading carries its composition: estimated tokens in four groups, sorted from the labels the harness put on each record, never from a body's words. Injected: the system prompt and tool list (the tokens of the first request, or Codex's first token count, less what the transcript recorded before it), Codex's base instructions and developer messages, project guidance, catalogues, hook output, reminders, file-change notices and harness-authored messages (for Codex, a user message it never recorded as the user's own). Grounding: what reading calls returned (file reads, searches, web and library reads, subagent digests, a shell command that only reads, such as a grep; a Codex exec cell whose every tool call only reads). Implementation: what changing calls returned (edits, writes, any other shell command, such as a test run; a Codex exec cell with any changing call, and a wait on it) and every call the session authored. Other: its own prose and reasoning, the human's words, and any label nothing sorts, named. Subagent lines and harness bookkeeping are left out; sizes are bytes at 3.8 characters per token, except an image (a screenshot read, a pasted picture), which counts at its pixels ÷ 750 tokens, at most about 4,800, as the model pays for it, never at its base64 length.

9.9 · A recorded Claude Code prompt hook input, for a session whose reading (9.5) is past the context guidance (9.7), makes the prompt hook add for the agent advice once per session to hand off and start a fresh session, naming its tokens used and the guidance; under or at the guidance it adds none. Later prompts in that session add no more advice, even if its reading crosses the guidance again; a fresh session may receive its own. It is advice: the hook still exits cleanly and the prompt is never refused. The same input from a Codex session past the guidance adds no advice (ADR-0739 D5), and with the guidance unreadable (10.4) or no reading, none is added.

9.10 · A session's window is read from its transcript (ADR-0746 D1, ADR-0756): the tool results it holds now (after the last compaction, with the segment Claude Code says it kept; never a subagent's side chain), each joined to the call that brought it by the id the harness wrote; each note or file it opened (the MCP server's open, a shell's storytree library read, a file-read tool, a shell cat, head, tail or sed -n), in order, with whether that read is still in the window; and the notes it only glimpsed: named in a result it holds now but never opened, each once, in the order first named. Claude Code transcripts and Codex rollouts both read; nothing is inferred from timing or wording.

9.12 · Before a transcript record is stored, obvious secrets in it (API keys, bearer and OAuth tokens, private keys, connection-string passwords) are replaced by a marker naming what was removed ("[scrubbed: API key]", "[scrubbed: bearer token]", "[scrubbed: OAuth token]", "[scrubbed: private key]", "[scrubbed: password]"), and the record still parses; ordinary text passes untouched. The scrub is best-effort for obvious shapes, never a guarantee (ADR-0749 D4).

9.13 · The retention pass (the app runs it at each start) deletes raw transcript records older than 180 days; before they go, the session's context reading and window worked out from them are kept, and are what is read for that session from then on (ADR-0749 D4).

9.14 · A reading asked again over a session's stored transcript parses only the records stored since the last ask, and reads exactly as a reading of the whole transcript would (tokens, composition, guidance), for Claude Code transcripts and Codex rollouts alike, including a Codex user message whose UserMessage event arrives in a later ask; an ask with nothing new stored parses nothing. So the app's 10-second readings of long sessions cost what they gained, not their whole length (ADR-0836).

9.15 · storytree context reads the session STORYTREE_SESSION_ID names and refuses a shell naming none, saying how to name one; a transcript from a harness storytree does not know is never parsed as Claude Code's
contracts.description: Inputs: the shell's environment; a transcript and its harness. Output: the reading for the named session; an unknown harness's transcript gives no figure. Errors: a shell naming no session is told the three variables.

capabilities.title: 10 · Settings
capabilities.description: The user's own settings for Session management: read and written by this package, set from the command line and from the app's settings panel (ADR-0728 D2, D3; ADR-0729; ADR-0739; ADR-0649). Per user only: one file, `settings.json`, in the storytree home (`STORYTREE_HOME`, else `[home], capability 1) beside `project-choice.json`. Each setting has a name, a type, a default and a plain-language meaning. An unset setting reads as its default, marked as the default. A value of the wrong type, or a name that is not a setting, is refused with its reason and nothing is written. A settings file that cannot be read or is not valid is reported, naming the file and the problem; it is never silently replaced, and a set refuses to overwrite it.

contracts.title: 10.1 · In a throwaway storytree home with no settings file, `context-guidance` reads 600,000, marked as the default, with its type (tokens) and its meaning.

10.2 · `storytree settings set context-guidance 400000` writes it to `settings.json` in the storytree home, and `storytree settings show`, and a fresh read by Session management, give 400,000 marked as set.
10.3 · Setting a name that is not a setting, or `context-guidance` to a value that is not a positive whole number, is refused naming why, and the settings file is left as it was.

10.4 · A settings file that is not valid JSON, or holds `context-guidance` of the wrong type, is reported on read naming the file and the problem, never read as the default; a set refuses to overwrite it, and the file is left byte for byte.

10.5 · With no library setting, `storytree settings show` reads the library location as `local`, marked default; `storytree settings set library cloudsql <instance> <user>` saves the Cloud SQL instance's connection name and the Google account to sign in as, and reads back as set; `storytree settings set library local` returns to local.

10.6 · `settings set library` with anything but `local`, or `cloudsql` with an instance not written project:region:instance or a user that is not an email, is refused with the reason, and the settings file is left byte for byte.

10.7 · Settings in the app’s gear opens a panel headed Settings, with “Yours on this computer · all projects”. Every setting returned by the reader has its current value, meaning, and default or set-by-you source; values can be saved with capability 10’s writers. A newly listed numeric setting needs no panel change.

10.8 · A refused value shows the writer’s exact reason beside its row, leaves the settings file byte for byte, retains the saved source, and can be corrected and retried. A successful save reads back when the panel reopens. Library location uses the same local/Cloud SQL writer and reports that changes apply when the app next opens.

10.9 · A failed read of the Settings panel shows the failure's reason and Retry, never fabricated defaults in place of the rows, and Retry reads again; a save whose transport fails shows its reason and leaves Save available for retry. The overlay that holds the panel (its focus loop with the reachable gear, Close or Escape returning focus to the gear, and its fit at narrow window sizes) is the app frame's: The app 2.6 and 2.7.

10.10 · With no settings file, `idle-after` reads 30 minutes, marked as the default. With `storytree settings set idle-after 10m`, a claim whose holder was last seen 15 minutes ago, with no command running, reads idle and can be taken over, and a session whose hooks report no turns reads waiting, where unset the claim cannot be taken over and the session reads working; a session whose hooks report its turns is never judged by it (ADR-0754 D5). A value that is not a duration (such as `soon`, `0m` or `-5m`) is refused with its reason, and the settings file is left byte for byte.

10.11 · With no settings file, `leave-after` reads 1 hour, marked as the default; `storytree settings set leave-after 2h` sets it, and a value that is not a duration is refused with its reason and the settings file left byte for byte (ADR-0754 D4; default from ADR-0758 D5).
10.14 · The app shows who decides what, read-only, from the habits card's own lines
contracts.description: The owner sees, without asking an agent, the same split the habits card hands every agent (the kinds the agent decides, the kinds it asks about, that the user's instructions file overrides them, the promises no file moves), with nothing on it to edit, and the project's standing delegations when its library defines them (ADR-0842 D4).

contracts.title: 10.12 · `storytree settings set library postgres <address>` saves a postgres:// address (host, port, database, user, sslmode) and reads back as set; an address carrying a password is refused, saying to save it as the `postgres` key with `storytree auth set postgres`, and the settings file is left byte for byte (ADR-0846 D1).

10.13 · Routing reads a Postgres-address library as the library's connect options for that address, and the settings panel offers it as a third library location beside local and Cloud SQL, saved through the same writer.

capabilities.title: 11 · Machines
capabilities.description: The computers that work on a project, each with a short name its owner gives it, its hostname and its id, read from what the trunks and machine.json already hold; a way to give this computer its name and to ask which one it is; and the sessions list showing each session's machine by that name.

contracts.title: 11.1 · `storytree machine name <name>` gives this computer a short name, kept with its hostname and id; a name another machine has, or one that is not a short name, is refused
contracts.description: Inputs: a name. Output: this computer's record (its id from machine.json, its hostname, the name). Errors: a name another machine carries; a name that is not lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, at most 32 characters; the word none, which an increment's machine field reserves for clearing. Naming again replaces this computer's name.

contracts.title: 11.2 · `storytree machine list` shows the project's machines, each with its name, hostname and id, and marks this one; `storytree machine this` says which one this computer is
contracts.description: A project's machines: every machine with a trunk of the project, and every named machine. Each shows its short name (or that it has none), its hostname and its id; this computer is marked. `machine this` gives this computer's name when it has one, its hostname and its id.

contracts.title: 11.3 · The sessions list shows each session's machine by its short name, or by its hostname while it has none
contracts.description: Inputs: the sessions' lines, stamped with their machine's hostname, and the machines' names. Output: each session's block in `storytree session list` carries a `machine:` line, and its JSON a machine field holding the hostname.

contracts.title: 11.4 · An increment's machine is checked against Machines: a named machine is kept, "none" clears it, and any other name is refused naming the known ones
contracts.description: The one check both front doors call before they set an increment's machine field (arc increment edit/new --machine, edit_plan and park_increment's machine).

stories.title: The app
stories.description: The app is storytree 0.3's desktop window. It starts and stops the database that holds every project's library, lists the storytree projects on the computer and shows one at a time, and hosts the surfaces that show the project on show: the forest, with the arc surface as an overlay the forest hosts. The page inside it cannot reach the database, so the app carries everything a surface reads. It keeps itself up to date (capability 4, added 2026-09-27, ADR-0637).

capabilities.title: 1 · Lifecycle
capabilities.description: When the app opens it starts the database that holds every project's library, and it keeps it running until the app is quit: closing the window leaves both running in the background, with a tray icon whose Quit stops them, so agents' work is still recorded. The app can also be controlled from outside (ADR-0656 D0): asking it to quit from the command line stops it as the tray's Quit does. There is one owner at a time: opening the app again brings its window forward, another program holding the database is named, and while it runs the app leaves records saying where the database is and how to open the app, which is how an agent's session finds it or opens it.

contracts.title: 1.6 · With storytree closed, an agent's session start opens it.

1.7 · Closing the window leaves the app and its database running; the tray's Quit, or asking the app to quit from outside (`storytree app quit`), stops them: it stops the database once, and the app exits only after it has stopped. Quitting, including smoke teardown and restarting into an update, stops the page's polling before closing the library, without logging a closed-library error.

1.8 · Each project gets a snapshot in `[home]<project>/` once a day, keeping that project's newest 14 (ADR-0641 B1): when the app starts it takes one of each project whose newest successful snapshot is missing or a day old and reuses one under a day old, and while it runs it takes the next at each project's day mark; a failed or partial snapshot does not count. On POSIX, backup directories are private (0700) and partial and published snapshots are owner-readable and writable only (0600), independent of umask or an existing traversable application home. Startup and direct backups repair retained snapshot and partial permissions, including those of removed projects, before reuse; unrelated files keep their contents and modes. On Windows, backup directories and retained snapshots have protected DACLs granting only the current user access, and each partial is created exclusively with that DACL before snapshot bytes are written. Retained permissions are repaired before freshness reuse; a permission failure writes no new snapshot and prevents reuse. Unrelated home files and unrelated children keep their permissions and contents. Effective-access tests on Windows exclude an unrelated non-administrative identity even under permissive inherited and explicit ACLs; privileged administrator override is outside this promise.
1.9 · With the library set to Cloud SQL, the app starts no local Postgres and opens its projects, surfaces and snapshots on the instance; quitting leaves the instance alone.

1.10 · With the library set to Cloud SQL and the instance unreachable (no Google sign-in, a refused account, or no answer in time), the window says so in the refusal's own words and what to fix, and the app never falls back to the local library.

1.11 · With the library on Cloud SQL, where the app starts no local database, the running app is still found (its launch record carries its process id): storytree app quit quits it, a stopped app reads as not running, and a delivery waits for the app itself rather than for a database it never starts.

1.12 · The installed app opens at sign-in, straight to the tray with no window, unless the user has turned that off in the gear's Updates section; a development copy, a portable build or a runtime slot never registers itself
contracts.description: So its release updater runs all day and the hooks it installed follow each release (a question, option A). On by default for an installed app; a development copy, a portable build or a runtime slot never registers itself. The off switch sits in the gear's Updates section and is remembered across starts.
