1.2 · A part that is released, or whose window closes, without landing stays in progress, with nobody on it.
1.3 · A story is planned while every part is planned or it has no parts, landed once every part has landed, and in progress otherwise.

1.4 · A closed increment reads landed only when a landing was recorded or it carries a pull request. Every other close, whether failed, withdrawn or closed with nothing recorded, reads not completed (red), with the hover naming which. Nothing reads landed merely because it closed.

An open increment gets one reading, first match wins: waiting on you (held on a question you have not settled, or by a wait for an action of yours with its note; it drops back the moment you settle or clear it), then queued (its own wait, or its arc's, still holds, or a wait for an outside event before its check-back day), then held (an agent holds it, idle or not), then blocked (unclaimed, and its capabilities list names a capability another open increment holds through a live session; it names that increment and clears when it closes or releases, ADR-0949 D3), then open. An event wait past its check-back day holds nothing, and the reading says check-back passed (ADR-0938 D1). A proposal is never by itself waiting on you, but a question you have not settled holds it as it holds any open increment (ADR-0909 D2). An active increment whose agent released it reads open, still in progress, with nobody on it.

reported.note: Dropped the proposal exclusion in incrementState; the library's heldOn reading already carries proposals' holds (work-in-flight.ts:661).

contracts.title: An arc reads one state, first match wins: closed or parked, as recorded; then waiting (a question on it you have not settled); then blocked (its own wait still holds); then queued (every open increment is held, on a wait, on you or blocked by another increment, and it names what it waits on); then in progress (a live session holds one of its open increments, ADR-0949 D1); then ready · N to take (N open increments nobody holds and nothing holds up), even while an idle agent holds other work on it: an idle claim does not hide free work (ADR-0938 D3); then idle, shown "in progress · idle N min" (every agent on it is idle and nothing is free); then quiet (nothing open). Queued, ready and quiet are read from its increments on every live reading (ADR-0760 D1).

capabilities.title: 2 · Agents on the board
capabilities.description: Every increment and part an agent holds shows which agent: Claude Code or Codex, when its window opened, the reason it gave when it claimed, and whether it is live or idle, and for how long. It reads the agent link's own claim reading, so the overlay and the claim tool always agree, and an idle holder still holds its work.

contracts.title: 2.1 · An increment Claude Code holds shows "Claude Code", when that window opened, and its reason. Two Claude Code windows are told apart by when they opened.
2.2 · After 30 quiet minutes the holder reads "idle for N min" and still holds the increment. Once it releases or lands it, its window closes, or its pull request merges, nobody is on it.
2.3 · A Codex holder whose hooks never ran is flagged "hooks not running".

2.4 · An arc's holders come only from its open increments: the agent holding one of them, or a capability claimed under one of them (ADR-0949 D1). A capability claim counts toward the increment it was taken under, never an arc directly; a closed increment contributes nothing, so a capability held by another arc's session reads nothing on an arc whose landed increment lists it.

capabilities.title: 3 · Arc surface
capabilities.description: A full-width arcs-only bar sits below the app story's separate gear-only app bar and opens one read-only drawer over the forest. The bar carries no project name. Both bars reserve their space above the forest so its controls remain reachable, and the drawer opens below them. The drawer, half the window's height, leaves the forest usable below; it can be expanded to fill the window below the bars and restored (3.10). It lists root arcs as dense two-line lanes (state chip, title and small counted wait marks, then the bars alone, wrapping), with a bar for each increment, finished work first, each bar coloured by its work state, a count of what landed and what is open spoken on the bars' label but not shown (ADR-0980), and a chip with the lane's state and who is on it; Active, Parked and Closed each show their own arcs. It stays current while it is open: about every two seconds it asks for what changed in the library and the agent log, which the app carries to it, and it re-checks the clock once a minute, so an agent that goes quiet turns idle without any new record.

contracts.title: 3.1 · A full-width 48 px bar labeled Arcs sits directly below the app's separate 48 px gear-only bar, spans the whole window and carries no project name. Clicking either end opens or closes the drawer below both bars; the bar also works from the keyboard and Escape closes it, returning focus to the bar. The forest and its controls remain below both bars and receive input below the closed bar or the half-height open drawer while the app overlay is closed; an expanded drawer (3.10) covers them until it is restored or closed. The gear remains reachable above the arc bar and open drawer at wide and narrow window sizes. No action writes library data, and it carries no Library switch or artifact links. While its first read is on the way it says so, and a read that fails says so rather than drawing an empty board.

3.2 · Each root lane has its state chip, its title and its wait marks on line one, then its increments alone on line two: one fixed-size flat oval per increment in its state colour, finished ones first and then open ones, longest-waiting first, wrapping onto further lines when they do not fit; a claimed increment's oval carries its holder's flag (the globe's pennant in the session's colour, furled and greyed while the holder is idle), and the ovals sit close under the title, leaving only a flag's headroom (ADR-1003). The count ("3 landed · 1 not completed · 2 open", skipping zeros, never a percentage) is not shown; it is the ovals' accessible label (ADR-0980).

3.3 · Lanes sort by their arc's priority first, 1 first and unranked last, and a ranked lane shows it as "P1" beside its chip (ADR-0963). Within one priority they sort waiting, blocked, in progress, idle, ready, quiet, then the most recently active; a ready lane that also has idle claims sorts with the ready lanes. An arc tag never says claimed: a live holder reads "in progress" and an idle chip carries its age on its face ("in progress · idle 42 min", ADR-0949 D1), and its hover names who holds what; a ready lane that also has idle claims names them, with their age and the work held, in its chip's hover. At the right of its title a lane counts what its open increments wait on: an hourglass with the number of distinct other work and event note waits that still hold, and a question mark with the number of its open questions and owner note waits that still hold; a mark with nothing to count is not drawn, and each mark's hover and accessible label carry the full wording. Each bar's hover names its note waits (ADR-0938 D2, ADR-0980). Active shows on the first launch, then the saved scope is restored; Parked and Closed show only their own arcs, and there is no "All".
3.4 · In the app: a claim written while the overlay is open shows on it within about two seconds, without reopening.
3.5 · In the app: with no new line, a holder turns idle once the quiet time passes. The test uses a stand-in clock.

3.6 · In the app: the smoke check visits every scope and opens every root queue caret, then judges document.body.dataset.drew.arcSurface against the expected root lanes, expanded queue chips, root-lane increment bars and their agent marks. It does not count +N descendants or queued increments as drawn bars.

3.7 · Between launches, each project remembers drawer open/closed, scope and selected arc. A valid saved arc is restored; if it disappears the normal briefing fallback applies. Closing keeps scope and selection for the next open.
3.8 · The app's Surfaces menu lists the arc surface as Arcs, with no settings, on until the user switches it off; switched off, it is saved and reads off at the next launch (ADR-0750)
contracts.description: The arc surface's own declaration, read through the app's Surfaces menu: the user can turn the arcs bar off (the globe then gets the full height) and it stays off.

contracts.title: The open board re-reads the work only when its news holds an arc, increment or question change: news of lines alone, or of other records, redraws it from the work it already has, with the new lines; its first news always reads. Each reading carries the library's waits for the owner or an event (waitsFor) with the holds; an absent one reads as none.
contracts.description: The board re-read every arc view and hold (~4.7 MB of Cloud SQL egress on 5 Oct 2026) on any news, up to every 2 s while the drawer was open (arc_0ab31fd59c88).

contracts.title: 3.10 · The open drawer expands to fill the window below the two bars and restores to half height, the choice kept per project
contracts.description: The open drawer carries a control that reads Expand. Pressed, the drawer fills the window below the two bars, over the forest pane and everything in it (the Sessions strip included), and the control reads Restore; pressed again, the drawer returns to half the window's height. The control works from the keyboard and keeps the focus. The choice is kept per project in the page's storage beside the open choice (a missing or foreign value reads as not expanded), so a drawer closed and opened again, and a new launch, open at the kept size. At either size the bar opens and closes the drawer at both its ends, Escape closes it and returns focus to the bar, and the gear stays reachable, as 3.1 says (ADR-1002 D3).

capabilities.title: 4 · Waits
capabilities.description: Every arc or increment that waits on other work says so and names what it waits for: an arc queued behind another arc folds away under that arc’s lane, behind a ▸/▾ caret in a fixed gutter; expansion shows chips, and an increment waiting on another increment, on any arc, draws yellow and names its blocker and why. A blocker shows what it holds up, a wait that will never release by itself says so, and an arc with something waiting on you is never hidden under its blocker.

contracts.title: 4.1 · An arc waiting on an open arc, or whose every open increment waits on work in another open arc, appears only as a chip under that arc's initially collapsed caret, not also at the top; waiting on several, it sits under the first on the board. Selecting the chip opens the queued arc's briefing. Once the wait releases, or it has work nothing holds up, it returns to the top, with nothing written. Waits that form a loop are cut at the loop's first arc on the board, so no arc disappears (ADR-0760 D1).

4.2 · A one-behind-one queue draws as a chain (A → B → C). Two arcs behind one blocker draw as a set, with a · separator and no arrow between them. A queued arc that holds up others carries "+N", one also waiting on another arc says "+1 other wait", and one queued by its increments names the increment it waits on in the arc above it.
4.3 · An arc with a question waiting on you stays at the top while it waits on another arc, and its other open bars still read queued.

4.4 · An increment waiting on another names it, its arc and the reason, and the blocker names what it holds up. If the blocker closed without landing, or cannot be found, the wait says it will not release by itself.

capabilities.title: 5 · Briefing
capabilities.description: Picking a lane, or a queued arc, opens its briefing: rows you scan, each a door into its prose, and no prose until something is opened (ADR-0980 D5). The arc's intent is one folded line. Its questions are one table, open first, each row a title and a status (open or settled); opening a row replaces the table with the full reading, the answer on top when settled, and “← back to questions” restores it. The reading is statement first, with its stakes, diagram, options as for and against, a recommendation marked not binding, and the longer parts folded with their word counts. After the questions, every increment on the arc is a row: its colour, its title and one short cell of chips for what it is doing, landed ones folded behind one row; opening a row shows its objective, its waits by name, the questions it waits behind, what it holds up, who holds it and how it closed.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Picking an arc shows its title, its intent folded behind one closed line, then its questions as one table, open first, each row its title and its status (open or settled); an arc with no questions shows no questions section. The drawer restores a valid saved selection; otherwise it opens on the first arc with a question waiting on you (or the first lane).

5.2 · Opening a question row swaps the panel for one full reading; “← back to questions” restores it. The full reading is statement first, then stakes, the diagram or "no diagram stored", options split into for and against, the recommendation marked not binding, and analogy and context folded with their word counts. The row itself shows no word count, no diagram note and none of the question's prose.
5.3 · A settled question stays in the one table, below the open ones, with its status "settled"; it stops counting as waiting, and its answer shows only when it is opened, on top of its reading.

5.4 · A parked arc's briefing says once, on its questions, that the open ones are parked with the arc (they wait for it to be unparked), never "Waiting on you", and a parked arc's question does not pick the drawer's first briefing
contracts.description: ADR-0835 D2: parking an arc parks its questions too, off the owner's list until the arc is unparked.

contracts.title: 5.5 · After the questions, every increment on the arc is one row: its bar's colour, its title on one line and one short cell of chips, never a sentence: "you" when it waits on the owner (a held question, an owner note, or questions behind its waits), "N increment(s)" for waits on other work, "event", "check-back passed", "blocked" by another increment's claim, the holder's label with its quiet minutes, "to take", "not completed", or a landed one's pull request number. Open work comes first (waiting, in progress, to take), then not completed, then landed, folded behind one "N landed" row.

5.6 · Opening an increment row shows in place its objective, each wait by name with its reason, the owner's questions it waits behind, what it holds up, who holds it and how it closed (disposition, pull request, note), never its planning body; the intent fold, the landed fold and opened rows stay open across the live redraw.

stories.title: The command line
stories.description: `storytree` is the command a person types in a terminal to read and change their project's records. It is a front door and nothing more: each command is handed to the function its owning story already has (the library, Session management), so the command line and the agent's tools can never disagree.

capabilities.title: 1 · Front door
capabilities.description: `storytree <family> <verb>` works out which project the folder you are in belongs to, opens that project's library, and hands the command to the owning story's function, keeping no rule of its own. Every answer is a short plain sentence or listing; where it names records it may offer, under `next:`, the commands that open them, and nothing else (ADR-0786). A failure exits non-zero and says what to do; a command it does not have answers with the real one for that job.

contracts.title: 1.1 · In a project folder, `storytree library search <word>` finds an artifact written through the library.
1.2 · In a folder that is not a project, it exits non-zero with "not a storytree project".
1.3 · With storytree stopped, it says "storytree isn't running" within a second.
1.4 · A record the library refuses reaches you as the library's own message, and nothing is written.
1.5 · `storytree` alone lists the families.
1.6 · `storytree <family> <verb> --help` (or `-h`) prints that command's usage and summary and exits 0 without running it, even when the command needs arguments it was not given.

1.7 · A command or verb it does not have is refused (exit 2) naming the command for that job when agents are known to guess the word, else the nearest real one by spelling, and listing what the family has (ADR-0786 D3).
1.8 · An answer's `next:` offers only commands that open a record the answer just named or listed; no stock hints (ADR-0786 D2).

1.9 · `storytree --version` prints the 0.3.<n> of the build it comes from, the number the desktop app shows for that commit (ADR-0753 D2): from a source checkout, with its short commit; from an installed build, the release and commit stamped into it at packaging.

1.10 · Through `pnpm storytree` in a storytree checkout, a word arrives as written, holding double quotes, >, &, |, ^, %, backslashes or backticks, and nothing else runs or is written on its way (ADR-0851 D1).

reported.note: Commit 399163ab (.npmrc shell-emulator=true): the pnpm route prints exactly the door's own answer for the word, and no stray file is written. Windows, pnpm 9.15.0.

contracts.title: 1.11 · A word the script shell still changes on its way (a $, a line break) is refused before the command runs: nothing is done, and the refusal names the word and says to pass that text from a file (ADR-0851 D2).

reported.note: Commit 399163ab (packages/cli/src/handed.ts): refused before dispatch, naming word 1 and @<file>; by hand, a --answer holding $HOME was refused as word 5.

contracts.title: 1.12 · On Windows, a word given to the installed command whose double quotes the caller's own quoting changed, as Windows PowerShell 5.1 hands on a word holding a space and a double quote, is refused before the command acts, naming the word and saying to pass it from a file; a line quoted by Windows' standard rules (Git Bash, a program) is never refused (proven on Windows CI, skipped with a named reason elsewhere).
contracts.description: Windows PowerShell 5.1 wraps a word holding a space in double quotes without escaping the ones inside it, for every program it starts, so 'he said "x" ok' arrived as other words, in silence (increment_e95ceec15288, measured 2026-10-02). The installed command's launcher hands its line on, and the door refuses a line no standard quoter writes, as 1.11 does for pnpm's line.

reported.note: Green on the laptop and on CI's Windows runner for storytree-ai/storytree#492: from Windows PowerShell 5.1 the word is refused before the command acts, naming word 1 and @<file>; from Git Bash the same word reaches the command. Skipped on Linux and macOS with its reason.

contracts.title: 1.13 · A comma-separated id flag containing whitespace inside an id is refused before any write, naming likely PowerShell array conversion and showing a quoted retry example without guessing or splitting ids; valid comma-separated lists preserve their ids.

1.14 · A flag value opening with @ is read from the file it names; one holding whitespace that names no file is prose kept as written (so text opening with a scoped package such as @storytree/cli reaches the record); a one-word @ value naming no file is refused, naming the path.

reported.note: packages/cli/src/at-values.test.ts '1.14 …' passes on main (ran in this lane's gate, PR #788 branch); health read untested only because no report was filed

contracts.title: 1.15 · A command kept waiting on the library (a connection slot on a full server, or another session's write) goes on when it can, says what it waits for on stderr as the wait starts when stderr is a person's terminal, and says nothing of it while stderr is captured
contracts.description: The front door hands the library's onWait to stderr only when stderr is a terminal, so a person never waits in silence (friction_a71746af7bed). A captured stderr hears nothing of the wait: Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads any captured stderr as a failed command (exit 255), and a pipe cut short after that first line ended the command before it wrote (friction_ade225663411, 2026-10-08). A headless lane loses nothing it needs: every wait is bounded (30 s by default), and a wait that runs out fails with the reason.

contracts.title: 1.16 · In a folder whose marker names an existing project but is not approved as its checkout on this machine, a read and a write are refused before the project opens, naming `storytree doctor --join <project>`; after that join they work (ADR-0942 D1).
contracts.description: A downloaded folder's .storytree.json alone never reaches a project from the command line, as it reaches nothing through hooks and tools.

contracts.title: 1.17 · every answer is recorded on the calling session as a door-answered line: the command, how it went, and the next steps offered as commands; an unknown word with the command its refusal named
contracts.description: ADR-0983 D1 (in force through ADR-0998): the command line appends one door-answered line per answer, the verb walked over its own command table, so the front-door reading counts lines instead of parsing transcripts. Recording never changes the answer.

contracts.title: 1.18 · storytree doors prints the front-door reading for a window
contracts.description: `storytree doors [--days n] [--trend n] [--json]` reads the project's activity log and prints the reading, its declared commands walked from the door's own table and its declared tools as the tool server serves them.

contracts.title: 1.19 · storytree lag prints Lag in real use's report over the lag readings kept in the storytree home
contracts.description: A thin front door: `storytree lag` reads the readings file in STORYTREE_HOME (else [home]) through the lag-in-use story and prints its report; it needs no project and no library.

capabilities.title: 2 · Who wrote it
capabilities.description: Every write made through the command line is recorded as the person who ran it (their computer user name), so the library's history can tell a person's change from an agent's. When an agent runs the command from its own shell, the write is recorded as that agent's session instead (A1).

contracts.title: 2.1 · An edit through the command shows in the record's history as the person.
2.2 · The same edit, run with an agent session's id in the environment, shows as that session.
2.7 · A shell with STORYTREE_SESSION_ID acts as that session; with no session named, storytree processes refuses and says to set it
contracts.description: Inputs: the shell's environment. Output: commands write as session:<id> and processes acts for it when STORYTREE_SESSION_ID is set (after Claude Code's and Codex's own ids). Errors: no id at all, processes stop/clear refuse naming STORYTREE_SESSION_ID.

capabilities.title: 3 · Library
capabilities.description: Read any record whole, list a kind (optionally filtered by a field), search the artifacts, see what links to an artifact, and see a record's history of changes, all through the library's own reads. Write a new record of any kind, or edit named fields of one, with long text taken from a file, and a bad record is refused with the library's own message. Retire a record with a reason and its writer through the library's existing retire, preserving its refusals.

contracts.title: 3.1 · `read` returns the whole body.
3.2 · `edit` changes only the named fields.
3.3 · `new` without a required field is refused, naming it.

3.4 · `history` lists every write with its sequence, time, action, writer and reason; `--fields` also shows the stored fields after each write (the last state for retirement), so past values can be read after the fact.
3.5 · `list` shows only live records of the kind and filters by a field.
3.6 · `new memory` is refused with the reason that memories belong to the harness, and writes nothing (ADR-0650).
3.7 · `related <artifact> --unlinked` lists the artifacts most like it that no link reaches.
3.8 · `library retire <id> --reason <why>` retires any record the library permits, recording the reason and writer and returning the library's own refusals.
3.9 · `library search <words…> [--limit <n>]` shows the library's ranked answer (capability 14 of the library story), best first with scores, at most the limit; when it ranked by words it says why.
3.10 · `read <id> --field <name>` prints that one field exactly as stored and nothing else (a value that is not text, as JSON); a field the record does not have is refused, naming the fields it has.
3.11 · A list field given to `new` or `edit` as comma-separated ids is written as a list, from any shell; a shell-joined list is refused before writing, with the quoted retry.

reported.note: packages/cli/src/library.test.ts '3.11 …' (landed in PR #784) passes; ran in this lane's gate on PR #788's branch

contracts.title: 3.12 · library phrase returns a bounded JSON page of full records from the literal phrase API, accepts repeatable kind and field selections plus limit and after, preserves phrase whitespace, and gives a continuation cursor or a complete empty result.
3.13 · `library new check` writes a quality control check enforcing the principles or guardrails it names, and `library read` returns it whole.

3.14 · library edit and retire, run by a session holding an increment, hold a change to a story, capability or contract planned before it as a pending change on that increment, and library read of the increment lists each pending change as before and after, or its retirement
3.15 · `library new contract` numbers past the capability's contracts and the numbers its story package's numbered tests carry, as plan_contract does
3.16 · `new contract` with a title past 300 characters is written, and its answer adds an advisory quoting the library's definition of a contract; a shorter title gets none
3.17 · storytree import <folder> imports the folder into the project the command runs in, saying the mapped stories it added, retired and kept; a refused folder is said with its reason

3.18 · `library read <id> <id>…` prints every record named, whole, in one start; `--linked` adds each record their id lists name (a role's rules and context, a note's links) once; an id with no record refuses the read, naming each, and prints none
3.19 · `library list` refuses a flag it does not read, before reading the library, naming --where <field>=<value> as the way to filter, and lists nothing

capabilities.title: 4 · Arcs and increments
capabilities.description: See the arcs, and one arc whole: its intent, end state, increments and their states, the questions waiting on you, and what each waiting item waits for. Create, edit, park or unpark an arc; park an increment, record a landing that was never parked, close one with its outcome, and make an arc or increment wait on another with a reason, or clear the wait.

contracts.title: 4.1 · An arc with no intent is refused.

4.2 · A close with no pull request needs a note. The correct-closure verb replaces a closed increment outcome with a required reason kept in history; it refuses open work, missing reasons and invalid outcomes without a write.
4.3 · A wait that would close a loop is refused, naming the loop, and nothing is written.
`arc show` names what each waiting increment waits for: the work it waits on, and each wait for you or an outside event with its note, check-back day, and "check-back passed" once that day has come.
4.5 · `arc list` names each live arc with the library's state.
4.6 · Closing an increment ends its claim for any holder and outcome; a refused close leaves it held.

4.7 · `arc increment move <increment> --to <arc> --reason` re-homes an open or closed increment, keeping its id, lifecycle, outcome and any claim; without a reason, or for open work moving to a closed arc, it is refused.
4.8 · `arc show` reads the arc's view once and every hold in one ask, however many open increments the arc has: never a hold read per increment.
contracts.description: arc show was 12.7 MB of Cloud SQL egress per call on 5 Oct 2026, one whole-work read for the arc and each open increment (arc_0ab31fd59c88).

reported.note: arcView 1, holds 1, waitHolds 0, heldOnQuestion 0

contracts.title: 4.9 · `arc increment wait --for` makes an increment wait for you, or for an outside event until a check-back day, with a note, and `unwait --for` clears it; a wrong wait is refused readably, with nothing written
contracts.description: ADR-0938 D1 through the command line's front door, beside `--on`/`--reason`.

reported.note: arcs.test.ts 4.9, red then green, PR #818

contracts.title: 4.10 · `arc waits` lists every open increment's waits for you or an outside event across arcs, yours first, then events by check-back day with the overdue flagged, from one read of the holds and one of the arcs
contracts.description: ADR-0938 D4: the list grill-me's opening table reads.

reported.note: arcs.test.ts 4.10, red then green, PR #818

contracts.title: 4.11 · `arc show` says nothing of a wait whose blocker has landed: closing the blocker cleared it
contracts.description: The stale-wait line it once printed (friction_9ce4f31578b7) is gone with the concept: the library clears such a wait itself (11.7, a question).

contracts.title: 4.12 · `arc increment unstart` returns an active increment nobody holds to proposal; a held, proposed or closed one is refused, naming why, with nothing written
contracts.description: The verb that repairs work left active after its claim ended (friction_9ce4f31578b7).

contracts.title: 4.13 · `arc increment edit --remedies` adds live friction to an increment's remedies, keeping those it had, so `friction route --to tool` accepts it; friction that is not live is refused with nothing written
contracts.description: So a friction whose fix is already parked can be routed to that increment (friction_3ebd000166ed, increment_50bc4edb2dfc).

contracts.title: 4.14 · `arc increment wait --for owner` releases the waiting session's claims on the increment
contracts.description: An owner wait on an increment the calling session holds releases its claim and the capability claims taken under it, through agent-link's releaseAsked (ADR-0944 D4); a wait for an outside event releases nothing.

contracts.title: 4.15 · `arc increment new` and `edit` take --capabilities and --links, edit replacing each list; a story given as a capability is refused with nothing written, and the retired --touches is refused rather than ignored (ADR-0949 D2)

4.16 · `arc increment edit --capabilities` refuses a capability already on the list of another live session's claimed increment, naming that increment and its holder, with nothing written; the caller's own lists, and a released increment's, are not refused (ADR-0949 D2)
contracts.description: The command line's half of edit_plan's refusal (agent-link 6.48): two sessions never plan changes to the same capability.

contracts.title: 4.17 · `arc edit --priority` sets and clears an arc's priority, and `arc list` orders live arcs by it
contracts.description: An arc's priority is a whole number, 1 first, or `none` to clear it; anything else is refused with nothing written. `arc list` and `arc show` print it, and `arc list` lists ranked arcs first, by priority, unranked after, keeping today's order within one priority (ADR-0963).

contracts.title: 4.19 · arc show lists each open increment's pending plan changes under it, as before and after, or a retirement with its reason

4.20 · `arc increment settle-pending` applies the leftover pending plan changes of every closed increment that landed and drops those of every one that did not, naming each increment and what it did, and says so when none is left
contracts.description: The one-off catch-up for increments closed before ADR-0966 D4 shipped.

contracts.title: 4.21 · `arc increment new --waits-on a,b --wait-reason <why>` parks an increment born waiting on each named increment; one flag without the other, or a blocker that is not an increment, is refused with nothing written
contracts.description: A later step of a chain parked from the command line is never ready for a moment before its wait is set, so the pool cannot claim it early.

contracts.title: 4.22 · `arc increment edit --held-on none` clears an increment's hold, as an empty value does where the shell delivers one
contracts.description: Windows PowerShell 5.1 drops an empty-string argument to a native program, so the clear has a spelled-out value: `--held-on none` (or `--held-on ""` from a shell that passes it) leaves the increment held on nothing, as settling or retiring its last question does (friction_1007af65f199).

contracts.title: 4.23 · `arc increment edit --machine <name>` names the one machine that can take an increment, `--machine none` clears it, and a name Machines does not know is refused with nothing written
contracts.description: The command line's door to the increment's machine field: the name is checked by Session management's Machines before the library is written.

capabilities.title: 5 · Questions
capabilities.description: Raise a question for the owner on an arc (stakes, question, context, options, plus the analogy, diagram and recommendation 0.2 expected), optionally holding increments on it. Settle it with his answer in his words and the decision that carried it, retire one that was wrong, or list the open ones.

contracts.title: 5.2 · Settling needs an answer.
5.1 · A question with no stakes is refused.
5.3 · A held increment reads as waiting on you until its question is settled.

5.4 · `question retire` retires a question and releases every increment held on it in the same step, naming them; another record kind is refused without a write and points to `library retire`, which still refuses a question an increment is held on.
5.5 · `question list` lists open questions across arcs, or on one arc.
5.6 · `question check` says whether a question's review is fresh or lapsed; `question renew` re-stamps it, and renewing a settled question is refused.
5.7 · `library edit <question>` corrects an open question's wording in place; editing a settled question is refused, pointing at its standing answer.
5.8 · `question list` leaves out a parked arc's open questions, says how many wait there and on which arc, and that arc's own listing names them as parked with it
contracts.description: ADR-0835 D2: parking an arc parks its questions too, off the owner's list until the arc is unparked. A session can still see which they are: the cross-arc count names the parked arcs, and `question list --arc <parked arc>` lists them as parked with the arc (friction_19cf9102b69d).

contracts.title: 5.9 · `arc show` on a parked arc lists its open questions as parked with the arc, waiting for it to be unparked, not as waiting on you
contracts.description: ADR-0835 D2: parking an arc parks its questions too; the arc's own view says so.

contracts.title: 5.10 · Unsupported question new flags are refused before any write, with the supported --hold option in the correction.

reported.note: Focused built CLI run passes all 11 question tests. 5.10 refuses --holds and --unknown before any recorded library change; 5.3 reads back the persisted --hold link.

contracts.title: 5.11 · `question show <id>` reads one question whole: its arc and state, what it asks, its options, analogy, diagram, recommendation and answer when given, and the open increments held on it; another record kind or a missing id is refused.
5.12 · `question new --hold` releases the asking session's claims on the held increment
contracts.description: Raising a question that holds an increment the calling session holds releases its claim on that increment and the capability claims it took under it, through agent-link's releaseAsked (ADR-0944 D4); unrelated claims stand, and the reply names what was released.

contracts.title: 5.13 · `question present` marks a question as being put to the owner by the calling session; another live session is refused, naming it, `question list` flags it, and `--done` frees it
contracts.description: The command line's door to the agent link's 5.36, used by the grill-me round before it shows the owner a question.

capabilities.title: 6 · Decisions
capabilities.description: List decisions (current, by status, load-bearing) and record a new one with an explicit `--number <n>` or the next number, its status, who decided it in their own words, and what it supersedes. In storytree, automatic numbers exceed the persisted floor and every number any record has ever held; omitting a number is refused if the floor is absent. Other projects start at 1. All numbering rules belong to the library; the CLI parses and reports them. Pull a decision out as a markdown file, edit it, push it back, and write its composed statement (the owner's C2). The one-time number, renumber (both modes), and set-floor commands have been retired after the completed N1 move.

contracts.title: 6.1 · In projects with automatic numbering, two `adr new` run at once get different, increasing numbers.
6.2 · Pull then push with no edit changes nothing.
6.3 · A superseded decision drops out of `--current`.
6.4 · A composed statement reads stale after its decision's text changes.
6.5 · `adr pull` names a decision by id, number, or ADR number.

6.6 · `adr new --number <n>` preserves an explicit unused number and refuses a reused or invalid number. In storytree, omitting the number is refused while the persisted decision number floor is absent; when present, omitting the number allocates above that floor and every number any record has ever held. Other projects continue to auto-number from 1.

capabilities.title: 10 · Plan view
capabilities.description:
`storytree tree` prints the plan as an indented tree: stories, capabilities and contracts, each with the health its agent reported (labelled as the agent's) and any claim on it. Name a story to see only that story.
`storytree capability built <capability>` says a capability is built, so it is no longer proposed, and `storytree capability proposed <capability>` says it is proposed again (ADR-0744 D2); both call the library's `setProposed`.

contracts.title: 10.1 · A story with capabilities and a contract prints in order with "agent says passing"; each capability title is printed as stored, with no list position added to its number.
10.2 · An unknown story says so.
10.3 · `capability built` switches a capability's proposed flag off and `capability proposed` back on, each with its writer; an unknown capability says so.
10.4 · `storytree tree` prints each capability's word, and for one that is not healthy its reason, who moves it and the contracts carrying it.
contracts.description: ADR-0825 D1, at the command line.

contracts.title: 10.5 · `storytree health worklist` prints the oldest three capabilities on the health worklist, each with its word, reason, who moves it, the contracts carrying it and since when, and how many more wait; with none it says nothing waits. One a test run in progress will record is not offered: it is held back, counted, and the run named.

10.6 · In a project whose health nothing verifies, `storytree tree` gives each part the agent's report alone, and each built capability says storytree does not check this project's tests yet, never untested or a mover
contracts.description: ADR-0630 at the command line, for a user's project (increment_ef066f718a63).

contracts.title: 10.7 · `storytree health worklist` says on a proposed capability's line when its tests already pass and only its proposed flag is left, and then offers `storytree capability built <capability>` as the next step
contracts.description: Remedies friction_fd6154bff0be: for such an item the next line is switching the flag off (ADR-0744 D2), not parking a build increment.

capabilities.title: 7 · Board, read only
capabilities.description: Show who is on what right now: each claim on an increment or a capability, with its agent's harness, window and reason, and whether it is live or idle; or who holds one piece of work. Claiming and releasing stay with the agents' tools.

contracts.title: 7.1 · A claim made through the agent tool appears with its harness and reason.
7.2 · An idle claim reads idle.
7.3 · `noticeboard <id>` names the holder, or "nobody".

7.4 · `noticeboard log [--session <id>] [--limit <n>] [--full]` shows the activity log's latest lines (20 unless told), each with its number, time, harness, session and what happened. Each names the line that caused it ("caused by #n"), or says "cause not recorded", never "no cause" (ADR-0746 D2). Default output clips long commands to 60 characters; --full preserves the complete recorded started and completed commands, including quotes and line breaks. Both forms keep the requested session and latest-line limit, and say when no matching lines exist.

capabilities.title: 8 · Doctor
capabilities.description: Run storytree's setup check from a terminal, the same one every agent session start runs: is storytree running, are the hooks registered and last seen firing, is this folder a project, is `storytree` on the path, is `gh` signed in, is Claude Code or Codex installed and signed in, and are git and a Node of at least 24 there. It fixes what the check fixes by itself and names the fix for the rest, and it sets a folder up as a project only when you tell it to.

contracts.title: 8.1 · With storytree closed, it opens it.
8.2 · With `gh` signed out, it notes what gh is for and that storytree works without it, and names no fix (ADR-0751).
8.3 · In a folder that is not a project, it creates nothing unless told to.
8.4 · A second run changes nothing.
8.5 · Setup installs the full command beside its hooks; the launcher reads the library and runs `doctor`; `setup remove` through the bundled command removes it again.

8.6 · With Codex's hooks registered and none run yet, the doctor names the one step that lets Codex run them, and from an administrator terminal that Codex cannot run commands there (agent link 8.16, 8.17).
contracts.description: The doctor picks the setup check's lines one by one; the live laptop run on 0.3.358 showed it printing neither new Codex line.

reported.note: doctor.test.ts 8.5: red first (no Codex hooks line in the output), green once doctor prints the codex-hooks and elevated lines.

capabilities.title: 9 · Friction and re-steers
capabilities.description: File friction with concrete evidence, or a re-steer with your own quoted words, through the agent link's own capture functions, so vague evidence is refused from a person exactly as from an agent. Add a recurrence to a friction item when it happens again. List the friction due for a landing's pass and route it, through the librarian's own drain and route.

contracts.title: 9.1 · Friction with vague evidence is refused.
9.3 · `reinforce` adds a dated recurrence.
9.2 · A re-steer whose evidence is a paraphrase is refused.

9.5 · `friction route <friction> --to <route> --reason …` records the librarian's route and reason, with an optional --discharged-by stamp; the librarian's refusals (a tool route with no live remedy) reach the terminal unchanged and write nothing (ADR-0789 D2).
9.6 · `friction drain` lists the librarian's friction drain for the calling branch: up to three unrouted reports other branches filed, most recurrences first (ADR-0789 D2).

capabilities.title: 11 · Workspace
capabilities.description: `storytree workspace <increment> --reason <text>` makes a claimed Claude Code workspace, or prepares a Codex workspace by checking availability and fetching main. For Codex it prints the exact ref and name for the agent to pass to the app's `create_worktree`; the agent then runs `storytree workspace attach <increment> --folder <returned-directory> --ref <commit> --name <name> --reason <text>`. Storytree verifies the worktree and claims its branch; only the app creates the Codex folder. Both steps refuse held or waiting work, and only a running agent session may claim.

contracts.title: 11.1 · From a Claude Code agent's shell, `workspace <increment> --reason` makes a worktree on a fresh branch from `origin`'s main and claims the increment for that session on that branch, naming the folder to work in.
11.2 · Work another live session holds is refused naming its holder and the binding reason supplied by the agent link, and no worktree is made.
11.3 · From a shell no agent session runs, it is refused saying to run it from the agent, and nothing is claimed, for both preparation and attachment.

11.4 · From a Codex agent's shell, `workspace <increment> --reason` returns the exact freshly fetched commit and suggested name for the app's `create_worktree`, without creating a folder or claim. `workspace attach` with that ref, name and returned folder claims its verified branch for the same session and names the working directory. A bad directory is refused without a claim, explaining that the app's worktree is kept.
11.5 · `workspace release` ends the calling session's increment or capability claim without closing or landing the work.
11.6 · `workspace release` refuses another session's claim, an unheld target, and a shell without an agent session, without writing claim events.

11.7 · `session close-out --safe yes|no --why <text>` from an agent's shell records the calling session's close-out, which the sessions reading then carries, and lists every released claim id or explicitly says there were no claims to release; from a shell no agent session runs it is refused, and a --safe other than yes or no is refused as a usage error (ADR-0758 D2).
11.8 · Work with an open pull request is refused naming the --despite-open-pulls flag, and with that flag a workspace is made beside it
contracts.description: From an agent's shell, `workspace <increment>` for work that already has an open pull request is refused naming it and the `--despite-open-pulls` flag, with no worktree or claim; given the flag, the worktree is made and claimed as usual (agent-link 5.25).

contracts.title: 11.9 · `workspace claim <increment|capability> --reason` claims the work for the calling agent session without making a worktree or branch, and is refused as the claim tool refuses it, including the binding reason supplied for a held claim.

stories.title: The librarian
stories.description: The librarian keeps a project's library honest as a library: new artifacts are genuinely new, an artifact links to what it really rests on, every accepted decision stays true, durable lessons move to where agents read them, and the question and friction queues are drained. It is 0.2's `librarian-curator`, ported whole. In 0.3 storytree runs no agents of its own, so the librarian is a hat the user's own agent puts on for a few minutes at a landing, using storytree's tools.

capabilities.title: 1 · Links
capabilities.description: The librarian links one artifact to another only where the first really rests on the second. It finds neighbours no edge reaches with related-but-unlinked search, alongside plain search (ADR-0654). This is how the whole-project decisions come to sit behind the covers that rest on them.

contracts.title: 1.1 · `link(from, to)` makes artifact `from` rest on artifact `to`, keeping its other links. Linking it again writes nothing.
1.2 · A definition rests only on a decision, and a friction or re-steer rests on nothing: any other link is refused, naming the rule, and nothing is written.
1.3 · The worklist names each accepted decision on no shelf that no artifact rests on, and drops it once one does.

1.4 · For each live artifact written since the session's cursor, including edits, the worklist lists neighbours ranked by likeness that no link joins in either direction. It uses the library's related-but-unlinked search and writes no links; the agent decides which are real dependencies.

capabilities.title: 2 · Decision log
capabilities.description: Every accepted decision stays true in full. When a later landing overtakes something a decision says, the librarian corrects it in place if the decision did not change, and records a new decision that supersedes it if it did; finished business is retired or consolidated.

contracts.title: 2.1 · `supersede(olds, decision)` records a new accepted decision, or names an existing accepted successor by ID, adding the old ones to its `supersedes` without duplicating it or losing existing links, wording or authority. Each old one reads superseded and stays readable; the successor inherits the first old one's shelf only if it has none, and any old one's load-bearing mark. Missing, retired, proposed or already superseded successors, invalid predecessors and supersession loops are refused before anything is written.

2.2 · `correct(id, fields)` changes a decision in place (its text, title or load-bearing mark), and the old wording stays in its history. A correction that would turn an accepted decision back to proposed is refused, since only the owner does that, and nothing is written.

2.3 · `annotate(target, { by, note })` adds a dated annotation to the target decision's text, naming the decision that narrows it. A narrowing decision that is not a live decision is refused, and nothing is written.
2.4 · The worklist's health report names each link or supersession that points at a record no longer live, with both ends.

capabilities.title: 3 · Catalogue
capabilities.description: Every artifact that lands is either genuinely new or an edit to the artifact that already covers it, and never a near-copy. Guidance any capable agent would work out for itself is pruned.

contracts.title: 3.1 · `retire(id, reason)` retires an artifact nothing points at. An artifact that another live record points at (a link, a supersession, a process's hand-on, an agent role's reading, rules or anti-patterns, an increment's remedies, or a question it settled) is refused, naming what points at it, and nothing is written.
3.2 · The worklist lists each artifact written new since a cursor, with the live artifacts a plain search for any word of its title finds, so the agent can see what might already cover it.

capabilities.title: 4 · Graduation
capabilities.description: ADR-0650 keeps the built graduation functions, but graduation is not needed for the MVP. Harness memories remain outside the library; promotion writes a proper artifact kind.

contracts.title: 4.1 · The worklist lists each memory in the memory folders that is new, changed since it was parked, or parked more than 60 days ago. A memory parked unchanged within its 60 days is not listed.
4.2 · `park(memory, reason)` keeps the reason, the date and what the memory said when it was parked, beside the memory folder, never in the library.

4.3 · `graduate(memory, kind, fields)` writes the lesson as a principle, process or definition, and only then deletes the memory. A write the library refuses leaves the memory where it was, and any other kind is refused.
4.4 · The worklist lists each process that names none of the tools served, and each tool served that no process names.

capabilities.title: 5 · Queues
capabilities.description: Open questions whose review lease has lapsed and unrouted friction reports are looked at on the librarian's pass, and nothing is closed without a reason. The library owns the review date and lease; the librarian uses its lapsed-question drain (ADR-0654).

contracts.title: 5.1 · The worklist lists only open questions whose review lease has lapsed, across every arc, longest lapsed first. Fresh and settled questions are excluded; gathering the list neither settles nor renews a question.

5.2 · The worklist's friction drain holds at most three friction reports not yet routed that another session filed, never one filed from the session's own branch. Reports with the most recurrences come first, with oldest first on ties; no recurrences counts as zero, and missing provenance still counts as another session's report.

5.3 · route(friction, route, reason, options?) records the routing judgement with its reason and an optional dischargedBy reference to the remedy that landed. The reference is trimmed and must be non-empty when supplied; omitting it preserves an existing stamp. An already-routed report can receive its stamp later. A route with no reason or a blank delivery reference is refused without writing.

5.4 · A tool route requires a live, non-closed increment whose remedies names this friction, unless the report already carries a delivered-by stamp or receives one in this call. An unrelated or closed increment is insufficient; refusal writes nothing and explains the missing remedy or delivery reference.

5.5 · A report already routed is routed again only to the same route (a later delivery stamp or a clearer reason); routing it elsewhere is refused naming the earlier route and its reason, and nothing is written, so two librarian passes cannot silently replace each other's judgement.
contracts.description: Regression for two landing sessions that drained the same friction 23 s apart, the later route replacing the earlier with no warning (2026-10-01).

capabilities.title: 6 · Rounds
capabilities.description: When the librarian runs, and how an agent is told to put on its hat. At a landing where the session wrote to a curated kind of artifact, storytree asks for the librarian's pass before the landing is reported.

contracts.title: 6.1 · The trigger fires when the change feed since the session started holds a write to a curated kind, and when there is no start to read from; graduation is due at every landing either way.
6.2 · The worklist gathers each capability's list into one report: graduation's and the friction drain always (ADR-0789 D3), the rest only when the trigger fired.
6.3 · `land`'s answer ends with the "next" line "run the librarian's pass" when the trigger fired, and with none when it did not.
6.4 · A test client lists the librarian's tools on the agent link's one server, beside its own, and calls them.
6.5 · The librarian's subagent definition names every librarian tool the server serves.

6.6 · The worklist and `land`'s next-line check take about as much from a library whose history holds weeks of changes, with health entries piling up since the session started, as from one whose history holds an hour's: the session's start is found from the first change since it, the trigger asks only whether one curated change came after it, and the links and catalogue read only note changes since it.
contracts.description: The whole-history read behind every worklist and land was ~96 MB of Cloud SQL egress per call on 5 Oct 2026, growing ~12 MB a day (arc_0ab31fd59c88).

reported.note: long-history run within 128 KiB of the short one (was 75 MB vs 25 KB)

contracts.title: 6.7 · The worklist reads the live notes about once however many notes the session wrote, and with no recorded session start it gathers every list but the catalogue and related ones, which it leaves unread saying why, instead of reading every note's whole history.
contracts.description: A stalled worklist (friction_b0333dc7c3ff: 1800 s with no answer) traced to a full read of the library per title word of each note written, and to a cursor of 0 when no start was recorded. The answer stays bounded and says what it could not gather.

contracts.title: 6.8 · A worklist call names each phase through the call's progress before it answers (graduation, friction, trigger, links, related, health, catalogue, processes, questions), and stops at its next phase once progress rejects, reading nothing more.
contracts.description: A slow worklist call says where it is through the agent link's progress notifications (agent link 6.41), and a cancelled call starts no further phase's library read. Increment increment_3deaed5e6247.

contracts.title: 6.9 · The worklist tool answers in a size a session can read: the friction drain's due reports (three at most) named, with how many more wait, and each other list's first five notes named by ID, kind and title, with how many it holds; any one is read whole by its ID.
contracts.description: friction_48a05ed10d3e: the tool returned the whole Worklist, 15,314,288 characters, while `storytree friction drain` listed the same reports in a few lines. The full worklist() stays for callers that need it.

stories.title: The knowledge core
stories.description: The knowledge inside the planet. The project's artifacts hang below the front covers on the stories' and capabilities' shelves, deeper the longer the chain of references that reaches them; replaced decisions sit as see-through ghosts beside the decisions that replaced them; and the artifacts one recorded session reached light up in each of its agents' colours. The owner looks inside the globe on purpose, pins an artifact to read it, and replays a session.

capabilities.title: 2 · Earlier decisions beside their replacements
capabilities.description: A replaced decision appears as a see-through ghost beside the decision that replaced it, and lights when its recorded reader reaches it. Its card tells an explicit supersession from an earlier cover found in write history. Proposed decisions stay out of this first slice.

contracts.title: 2.1 · An accepted decision that explicitly supersedes an old one makes a ghost, even when the old front-cover mark was never cleared. A proposal naming an old decision does not supersede it.

2.2 · For older records, a new cover on the same shelf linking to the old one, followed by clearing the old cover's mark, makes an "earlier cover" ghost when the replacement is unique. Clearing a mark alone, editing the wording, or merely linking to an old decision does not.
2.3 · A unique chain of replacements ends beside its current successor. A missing or ambiguous successor gets an outer ghost labelled "replacement not placed", rather than a guessed home.

2.4 · Depth and incoming-link sizes use only artifacts that are neither ghosts nor proposed; replacement relations are not support links. A ghost never changes that layout, and its own visit count stays inspectable.

capabilities.title: 1 · Knowledge under its shelves
capabilities.description: The project's artifacts hang below the stories' and capabilities' front covers, with depth counting the longest chain of references from any shelf. A shared artifact appears once, a loop is drawn as a labelled error, and an artifact no shelf reaches has "no depth". On the globe, shelf-placed knowledge is drawn beneath its islands. Story-text definitions are excluded from the drawing; the remaining no-shelf artifacts fill a ball within 0.55 globe radii, separated from one another and shelf points by at least 0.035 radii (ADR-0661 D3). Forest shows the core beneath the story nodes; Library shows it alone on the same globe (ADR-0660 D4). The separate Look-inside view stays unmounted.

contracts.title: 1.1 · With a cover A, links A → B → C and a shortcut A → C, C stays at depth 3: the shelf-to-cover step counts as 1. Visits and incoming-link counts never change that depth.

1.2 · An artifact reached by two shelves appears once, at its greatest depth, and names both entrances. A front cover keeps its own shelf as its home, and another shared artifact hangs under the oldest reachable shelf, with a stable tie-break.

1.3 · With A → B → C → B and C → D, B and C share a loop marked as an error at group depth 2, and D is at 3. An unreachable loop, like any unreachable artifact, is classified as no shelf, with no depth.
1.4 · Forty covers on their shelves and five artifacts on none, with no links, give forty artifacts at depth 1 and five with no shelf route, with no invented links. An empty shelf says it is empty.
1.5 · The globe draws every shelf-placed artifact once beneath its home island at its computed longest-chain depth. Ghosts, proposals, retired artifacts and story-text definitions add no points.

1.6 · No-shelf artifacts that are not story text fill a deterministic ball within 0.55 globe radii. Their centres remain at least 0.035 radii apart and at least that far from drawn shelf points, above the 0.012-radii dot diameter; every dot is wholly inside the shell. They gain no depth or invented shelf, and an empty corpus draws no points.

1.7 · Forest and Library submit the same complete set of eligible artifact points at the same positions and computed depths, with the same separated no-shelf artifacts; hiding story nodes leaves the live core mounted.

1.8 · isStoryText(record) is true only for a definition whose term or title starts with "Story text: stories/". Those records are excluded from the globe points whether loose or shelf-placed, while ordinary definitions, principles and decisions remain eligible and no library record is removed.
1.9 · Replaying a growth, each note appears beneath its home once the replay reaches its recorded date, in recorded order
contracts.description: Given the globe's growth reader, the core hides each drawn note until the replay reaches the moment its creation date falls at, then fades it in over a beat where the finished core draws it (under its home, or loose); with no growth, or under reduced motion, every note shows at once.

reported.note: landed in PR #581

capabilities.title: 3 · Reads by session and agent
capabilities.description: Choose one recorded session and see which artifacts its orchestrator and named agents reached, each in its own colour, with visits counted across the project's captured sessions. A peek only lights its artifact, full reads advance as jumps, and an unknown agent stays pale with no path.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Repeated peeks and whole reads of one artifact by several agents in one session count as one visit; a second session makes two. The card gives peek and whole-read totals separately.

3.2 · Interleaved agents replay separately in recorded order, including equal timestamps resolved by log line number; no step crosses agents or sessions. A missing agent field behaves exactly like "unknown".
3.3 · A peek neither draws a step nor replaces the agent's previous full-read stop. A whole read found "through a link" stays a jump, because today's record names no source artifact.

3.4 · Receiving the same log lines twice does not count visits twice. Switching projects clears the old project's picture, and a read of an artifact no longer present is counted as a missing artifact, not dropped or reconstructed.
3.5 · With no captured reads the picture says "no recorded reads"; it never says the knowledge was unused.

capabilities.title: 4 · Look inside and inspect an artifact
capabilities.description: On the globe in Forest or Library mode, clicking an artifact dot pins it and opens its summary card in the right-hand slot used by the story panel (ADR-0661 D2). The card shows the artifact's kind, title and description or another summary field; when there is no summary it shows the whole text. It has no links list, read counts, depth figures or entrances. Close and Escape dismiss it. Opening a story replaces the card, and opening a card replaces the story panel. The separate look-inside view, with its replay and size controls, was removed after staying unmounted (increment_64a16707ff78); the notes are drawn under the islands, each dot sized by how many distinct sessions read its note in the last 90 days (ADR-0926), and lit only by a selected session's reads and traversal (ADR-0921), which never changes a dot's size.

contracts.title: 4.1 · Clicking an artifact dot in Forest or Library opens the existing pinned-artifact card in the right-hand story-panel slot. It shows kind, title and description or another summary field; with no summary it shows the whole text. It contains no links list, read counts, depth or entrances.

4.6 · Opening an artifact card closes an open story panel, and opening a story closes the card. Close and Escape dismiss the card. The shared core pin and summary renderer serve both globe modes without writing to the library.

4.7 · With no session selected, no session lights a note, though the listed sessions have read them: the knowledge dots stay unlit, with no shared marks and no lines; selecting a session lights exactly what it read (ADR-0921).

4.8 · Drilling into a listed session colours its orchestrator in the session's own colour and each subagent in a distinct shade of that hue; an unknown agent stays pale, and a session with no row keeps the fixed palette (ADR-0738).
4.9 · The globe's knowledge dots light exactly as the core does: nothing with none selected, or the selected session alone in its agents' colours (ADR-0738 D5, ADR-0921).

4.10 · A selected session's reading path draws as curved lines: from each full read to the same known agent's next, in recorded order, pointing to the later read, bowed away from the globe's centre, in its agents' colours, only when it has no window to read, a subagent's first read stepping from the session's latest full read before it (where it was spawned); otherwise its window's traversal draws instead (4.16, ADR-0756). With none selected no path draws (ADR-0921). A peek or an unknown agent draws none, and a curve never claims a followed link (ADR-0740).

4.12 · A new step's line grows from its earlier read to its later one (one agent's new steps one after another, different agents at once), and opening the view grows nothing. With a session selected one replay walks all its agents' steps in recorded order, growing each line and lighting each note as it is reached, holds the finished picture, then clears and replays (ADR-0797). No looping glow is drawn (ADR-0921). Reduced motion neither grows nor replays; paths carry no arrowheads and no wisp model (ADR-0742).

4.15 · A note lit by a new read stays unlit until the growing line into it arrives (including a line queued behind that agent's earlier steps), then lights in its session's colour; a note already lit, or reached only by steps read before the view opened, is never held (ADR-0742 D2).

4.16 · Selecting a session reads its window from the host and draws it on the knowledge dots (ADR-0756): one line per step from each note it opened in full to the next, in reading order (files between do not break the chain; a note gone from the library is stepped over; a step taken twice draws once), in the session's colour, solid where a stored link joins the two notes either way round and dotted where none does, growing toward the later note when new and then showing direction with a faint fill that runs from the earlier note to the later. A note whose read is in the window now has a ring; one compacted out since is lighter, and its lines fade with it; one only glimpsed is tinted faint with no line. An answer for a session no longer selected is dropped, and with none selected no window is drawn or asked for.

4.20 · A selected session's file opens join its traversal (ADR-0804 D5): each file whose path names a surveyed file (any path ending packages/<package>/src/…) is a stop on the code's surface, beside the notes it opened, in reading order; a step between two files is solid when one imports the other and dotted otherwise, a step between a file and a note dives into the core (or rises out of it), a compacted file's read fades with its steps, and a path that names no surveyed file is stepped over, never drawn. Opening a capability lights its territory; an arc, an increment or any other plan record is drawn nowhere and breaks nothing.

4.18 · With no session selected, the core asks the host for no session's window, whatever the running-sessions list holds; selecting one asks for that session's window alone, and never again while its last ask is out (ADR-0921).

4.21 · Each knowledge dot is sized by its note's reach: the distinct sessions that read it in the last 90 days, a whole read counting 1 and a peek 0.3, a session once at its strongest read. Its area grows linearly from a visible floor for a note no session read (or when no reads are recorded) to a ceiling for the most-read note on the globe. A note a selected session lights or holds in its window keeps its size: that read shows in colour, brightness and rings (ADR-0926).
4.22 · Clicking a Library note answers within 100 ms with no frame over 50 ms, and its card is open within 1 s or shows progress (verified by the Mint box's lag run)
contracts.description: The budget of the lag catalogue's open-library-note action (ADR-1001 D2, D5). No test in pnpm test names it: the Mint box's lag run writes its verdict, failing once a slowdown against the action's baseline reproduced.

stories.title: The app setup
stories.description: A new Windows user gets from one command in a project folder to a working storytree connection they can understand and ask for help with. This story owns registering storytree's hooks and command, the setup check that runs at every session start, making a folder a project, wiring a project's pipeline and building storytree's commands (ADR-0969 D3). The database, the yes-before-creating-a-project step, the record the hooks write, the project switcher and app updates belong to other stories; this story joins a fresh installation to them.

capabilities.title: 8 · Setup check
capabilities.description:
The only thing the user installs is the storytree tool server, once, with the one-line command Claude Code or Codex already uses for any MCP server, and after that every session start checks storytree's setup and fixes whatever is missing on the spot. It opens storytree if it is closed, registers the hooks if they are missing (walking Codex users through Codex's one-time approval), and in a folder that isn't a storytree project yet it asks the user, through the agent, whether to set one up. It also says whether Claude Code or Codex is signed in and whether git and a usable Node are there, naming the fix for each that is missing, and never waits on a tool that does not answer (ADR-0716). It registers hooks for each harness home it finds except a harness the user disconnected from storytree (the app setup's contract 2.5), which gets its hooks back only when it is connected again. It also puts the `storytree` command on the user's path (contract 8.9): a shell script, or on Windows a small program of its own that hands each word on as the caller's command line spelled it (ADR-0854).

As built (increment_e0065ed16d5a, PR #452, contract 8.20): check_setup asks the agent to write .storytree-check with its own file-editing tool. Once this session's edit hook has arrived, each check file it names is deleted at the recorded path, resolving relative paths against that hook line's folder, including a worktree different from the tool server's folder, even while other hooks are missing. A file the operating system refuses to remove stays for the agent. The repository deliberately does not ignore .storytree-check: a leftover remains visible as evidence that the edit never arrived or cleanup failed.

contracts.title: 8.1 · In a throwaway home with only the tool server installed, the first session start registers the hooks for Claude Code and for Codex without touching any other setting.
8.2 · A second start changes nothing, and removing storytree takes out exactly what it added.
8.3 · With storytree closed, a session start opens it.

8.4 · In a folder that is not a project, check_setup says the folder is not a storytree project and that the user can add it (Add project in the app, `storytree doctor --set-up <name>`, or asking their agent), without telling the agent to offer setup (ADR-0752 D3), and nothing is created until the user asks. A successful yes creates the project and folder marker, then durably records that project as the user's choice for the app. A refused or failed setup does not report success or change the remembered choice; if saving the choice fails, the folder marker is restored to its previous state so the explicit setup can be retried. An ordinary session start, an existing-project setup check, or a repeated setup tool call in an already configured folder records no choice. The setup tools' input and output shapes remain the same (ADR-0657 D3).

8.5 · The agent fires a test of each hook (a session start, a call to a storytree tool, a file edit, a command), and the connection shows as verified only when storytree has received every one. Until then it names the missing hook and the fix, such as Codex's one-time approval.

8.6 · Live check: a real Claude Code session and a real Codex session, each in a new empty folder set up as a project by the installer's folder step (or `storytree doctor --set-up`), with nothing else configured by hand, and told "add a sign-up form, with tests", show up live, plan, claim, report red then green and land, and the agent activity log and the library show all of it. A second session that ignores storytree and only edits a file shows up as unplanned activity. *Subscription-billed: run once, as the final proof.*

verified.note: 17/17 checks passed, Run on the Mint box (Linux) against this checkout's dev build, through app setup's dev-home: a throwaway home and database, the agents' own sign-ins., evidence packages/agent-link/evidence/live-check/2026-10-02, at commit 1173ce2dab64c5ac6f2ca3f32899858906c854dc

contracts.title: 8.7 · A status line of the user's own is kept: storytree's is installed only where there is none, and removing storytree leaves theirs.
8.8 · With `gh` missing, signed out or signed in, the check never asks the agent to install or sign in to it; a person running the check in a terminal sees a note of what gh is for (ADR-0751).

8.9 · In a throwaway home, the first start puts a `storytree` command on the path, a second changes nothing, and removing storytree takes it out. On Windows, where the command is a program of its own (ADR-0854), `storytree setup remove` run through it exits 0 with the command off the path when it returns, its file deleted once it has exited, and the user's own settings kept (regression: storytree-ai/storytree#83; proven on Windows CI, skipped with a named reason on other systems).

8.10 · A terminal runs the shared check without an agent session and gets diagnostic lines and fixes, including when the app is stopped. Checking creates no project; an explicit setup request creates it, and the next check reports it ready. Where hooks are present, a `transcripts` line says each session's transcript streams into the shared log, obvious secrets are scrubbed before they leave the machine, the scrub is best-effort, and raw records are kept 180 days (ADR-0749 D4).

8.11 · The check says whether Claude Code or Codex is installed and signed in, naming the fix when neither is ready; a missing or old git or Node is a note, never a fix (ADR-0751); a tool that does not answer is reported as not answering within seconds, never waited on.

8.12 · At the start of a session in a folder that isn't a storytree project, no hook adds anything to the agent's context, for Claude Code and for Codex, an older install's asking start hook included; nothing is set up (ADR-0752 D3).

8.13 · The setup check has an archives line: ok, naming how many sessions the Claude desktop app and Codex each keep, when either record can be read; otherwise a note (never a fix) that says why and that sessions on this machine leave the running-sessions list after the leave-after time instead of when archived (ADR-0754 D4).

8.15 · On a machine whose hooks no desktop app installed, a session whose tool server runs from a checkout at origin/main registers the hooks, and the storytree command, from a build of that commit kept in the storytree home; a checkout off main, or hooks the app installed, are left as they are.

8.16 · Until one of Codex's hooks has run, the check says Codex waits for the user to trust them, with the one step in plain words (type /hooks in Codex, or answer "Hooks need review"), also where it registers no hooks (the app's folder check); once one has run, it says they run.
contracts.description: So the trust step reaches the user through check_setup, doctor and the app's diagnostics alike, and an agent passes it on in words the user can act on.
