capabilities.title: 1 · Get storytree
capabilities.description:
One command gets the Windows app and the tools its agent needs onto the computer, ready to run without a storytree checkout. Running it again reuses a working installation or explains what failed and how to retry.

As built: the release publishes install-storytree.ps1, its PowerShell one-liner and a version-matched SHA-256 manifest alongside the existing combined Windows x64/arm64 NSIS installer. Desktop packaging ships a native pinned Node 24 runtime, the complete agent-link buildBins output including imported chunks, a delivery helper and Node's license in resources/agent-tools. Delivery verifies and reuses a working installation before contacting the feed, explicitly launches its executable to show a hidden window or establish the first app launch, and waits for the app-owned database. It records stable installed tool paths in the 0.3 home's delivery.json and puts its CLI wrapper on the per-user Windows PATH; unrelated storytree commands are preserved and named. Failed steps include a retry action, incomplete existing apps are retained with repair/update instructions, and delivery does not create projects, change harness settings, install a developer toolchain, or touch 0.2. Ordinary updates remain the app's existing NSIS update route and replace the tool payload at the same paths. setup install retains its existing hook/command meaning; capability 2 owns connection.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/deliver/README.md. Linux tests use temporary homes, fake app launch/readiness and real PowerShell orchestration with injected effects; the actual built CLI, hook, setup, delivery helper and MCP server run outside a checkout. Both Windows runtime downloads match pinned SHA-256 values and their PE architectures. Windows CI additionally checks the installed x64 tool payload from a path with spaces. These proofs do not attest real first-ever/hidden-window startup, fresh-terminal registry propagation, interrupted NSIS installation, native arm64 execution, a live release update with active agent processes, or the agent-link 8.6 two-harness walkthrough; those remain the laptop acceptance lane.

As built: after delivery is ready, the one-liner prompts for Claude Code, Codex, both, or skip and calls the delivered Node/CLI directly with setup connect and the selected switches. This connects capability 1's installed paths to capability 2's existing registration functions through delivery.json. A connection failure does not reinstall the app or discard a successful connection; the command reports per-agent recovery. Tools registration is never presented as hooks verified. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/join/README.md.

As built (ADR-0854): on Windows the installed command is `storytree.exe`, a 5 KB program of its own built with LLVM from the agent link's launcher source and shipped in the payload as `storytree-launcher.exe`, so no shell reads its words: from Git Bash, Windows PowerShell or a program that starts it, each word reaches the CLI as the caller's command line spelled it (contract 1.9). The batch file it was before, `storytree.cmd`, is replaced by it in its folder. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/native-launcher/README.md.

As built (groundwork for the macOS arc, arc_5b467265f126, contract 1.11): the delivery API also stages Apple Silicon's runtime. `macRuntime("arm64")` pins Node 24.21.0's darwin-arm64 archive and its bin/node hash, and `stageRuntime` extracts that executable with mode 755, refusing any checksum mismatch and keeping the previous runtime. `writePayloadManifest` takes the platform: a Mac payload needs `node` and no Windows launcher. `toolPaths`/`verifyPayload` read a .app bundle's Contents/Resources/agent-tools and Contents/MacOS/storytree-0.3. macOS packaging, the shell install and notarisation are the arc's later increments. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/deliver/README.md.

1.2 · The first-run journey displays the app and reaches its database both without a previous launch record and when the app is already running with its window hidden, without a separate manual "open once" step.

1.3 · Repeating the command in the same or a second folder reuses the installation without replacing user settings or touching 0.2's installation or data; run from a folder that is already a project, its folder step says so and creates nothing.
1.4 · An interrupted or refused installation reports the failed step and a retry action, without announcing a working connection or replacing the last usable installation.

capabilities.title: 2 · Connect an agent
capabilities.description:
The user chooses Claude Code, Codex or both, and storytree connects its installed tools to those agents. The next session uses the existing setup check to ask about the project and show whether the connection actually works.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/connect exports connectAgents and disconnectAgents for the chosen harnesses, with installedToolServerCommand(bundledNodePath, installedMcpScriptPath) as the delivery seam. Registration is per user, keeps unrelated settings and old entries, uses the existing storytree MCP name, and reports incompatible entries without overwriting. It captures no project or working directory. Repeating it leaves the compatible entry untouched. Missing harnesses, invalid settings, missing installed tools and failed writes produce separate recovery results for each harness.

As built: disconnect removes the selected registration and only hooks matching this installation, preserving other commands in mixed groups and any other installation's hooks. It keeps the shared command until no connection remains and removes only the matching launcher. A disconnected harness stays disconnected: disconnect records it in the storytree home (disconnected-harnesses.json), and the setup check, run from the other harness's sessions, registers no hooks for it until Connect connects it again. Installation results distinguish tools registration from hooks not verified; the existing setup check owns project consent and received-event verification. Connect also registers the chosen harness's hooks (and Claude Code's status line), never the unchosen one's, so the first session after installing already runs the start hook that asks the setup question; before this, hooks arrived only when that first session's tool server ran the setup check, too late for its own start. Registering is still not verifying: results keep saying "hooks not verified" until the setup check has received each event.

contracts.title: 2.1 · Choosing either harness or both registers the installed tool server per user for the chosen harnesses, preserving other servers, settings and any existing 0.2 entry.
2.2 · A new agent session in the invoking folder, and later in another folder, reaches that folder's existing setup check rather than a fixed installer directory or a hard-coded project.
2.3 · Repeating registration leaves one effective storytree entry per chosen harness; an incompatible existing entry is explained instead of silently overwritten.
2.4 · A missing harness or an invalid settings file gets a specific recovery action and no success claim for that harness; a successful registration for the other harness is reported separately.

2.5 · Disconnecting one harness keeps the other's connection and the shared command working; removing all connections cleans up only storytree-owned registrations, hooks and command, keeping project libraries and unrelated settings.

2.6 · The installation result tells "tools connected" apart from "hooks verified"; a missing hook stays named by the existing setup check until its event is received. For Codex it says whether its hooks run or wait for the user to trust them, naming the one step while they wait, and, from an administrator terminal, that Codex cannot run commands from one.

2.9 · Codex, which hides a tool server's instructions and tools until the agent searches for them, is told through the AGENTS.md in its home to call check_setup before its first change in a storytree project, and to ignore storytree in any other folder: one marked section, written again changes nothing, the user's own text kept, removed exactly.
contracts.description: Codex 0.158 always defers MCP tools and does not show a server's instructions, so the habits card never reaches a Codex session; its home's AGENTS.md does, trusted hooks or not. Measured on the owner's Windows laptop: 0 of 3 untrusted first sessions called check_setup without the section, 3 of 3 before their first change with it (packages/app-setup/evidence/codex-first-session).

capabilities.title: 3 · First-run guide
capabilities.description:
A short in-app guide tells the user what to do next, what storytree will ask, and what a working first project looks like. They can reopen it when adding another project or recovering from a connection problem.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/view mounts one Help entry outside the project surface, available with no project, either forest or a library error. First launch offers the guide; dismissal is remembered locally and Help reopens it. The guide covers the chosen agent, explicit project consent, harness approval, received-hook verification, first visible work, a second project, the unsigned Windows installer and feedback. Check a folder calls the agent link’s public runSetupCheck and displays its diagnostic lines and fixes. The adjacent copy action prepares a check_setup request for the agent; this folder check does not install hooks or the command and cannot verify hook receipt. The app’s existing projectSelection/followProjects refresh remains responsible for the project list.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Headless Chromium exercises the actual renderer and isolated library, including two setup fixtures and both selectable forests. Contract 3.3’s real two-empty-folder/two-yes harness walkthrough and the final installer handoff remain Windows acceptance work.

A folder already in a project is simply selected; cancelling the picker changes nothing (ADR-0752 D2).

3.5 · The first-run guide shows, each time it opens, that Codex waits for the user to trust storytree's hooks, with the one step, until one has run, then that it runs them; with no Codex hooks it says nothing of Codex.

contracts.title: 3.7 · Remove, in the app's Projects section or with `storytree project remove <name>`, takes a project added by mistake off this computer's list and frees its folder here (a marker git tracks is left and named); its records stay in the library, and a deliberate join brings it back. contracts.description: The non-destructive half of removing a project (increment_6bb0564567cb). Deleting its records waits on the owner's question on arc_cfc7db517fae; freeing the folder on this machine is increment_f600d1ee7b87.

contracts.title: 3.6 · Delete, in the app's Projects section or with `storytree project delete <name> --confirm <name>`, drops a project's records for every computer using the library once its name is typed, after saying where they live and who loses them; a snapshot into this computer's backups is taken first unless skipped, and restores it. On POSIX, that snapshot is private from its first write (0700 backup directories, including existing ones, and a new 0600 file), independent of the home permissions or umask. On Windows, owner-only ACLs protect both backup directories (including existing ones) and the exclusively created snapshot before any snapshot bytes, even under permissive inherited permissions; an unrelated non-administrative user cannot read it, and the same user can restore it. Failure to establish privacy or save it leaves the project intact. Its activity lines, transcripts and QA ledger rows go with it, and a computer that had hidden it forgets the name, so a later project of that name starts clean and is shown. Refused for a wrong name, the project in use (on show in the app here, or the one the command's folder belongs to), and while a live session holds a claim in it.

capabilities.description:
The license travels with the installed product and is available without visiting the source repository. The user can open it from the same help surface they use after installation.

The Windows installer check compares the NSIS-installed and arm64 unpacked resources with the repository license.

capabilities.title: 5 · Send feedback
capabilities.description:
A button in the app lets the user describe a problem or suggestion and opens it as a draft GitHub issue on storytree's repository. They see what they are sending and submit it themselves.

As built: Help → Send feedback provides editable title and message fields and an explicit Open GitHub draft action. The package constructs https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/issues/new with only those two user-authored fields; the desktop carries the OS external-browser action. It attaches no project contents, paths, transcripts or logs. A failed handoff preserves the message and offers retry or copy, with an explicit copy failure and selectable original text. Success says “Opened a draft”, leaving GitHub submission to the user. Closing help sends nothing.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Fake-opener tests and the actual desktop renderer cover no-project and both-forest access, cancellation, editing, retry, copy, exact payloads and honest success status. No issue was submitted by the checks.

2026-10-06 foundation: the view additionally accepts an optional feedbackIdentity bridge. Only entering Send feedback queries its status. Sign-in remains optional, and a separate Add account to message action inserts the verified email and portable Storytree ID into the editable message, which the user may remove before copy or browser handoff. No bridge is wired into the shipped desktop yet; that integration is parked on the identity arc. Local contract 5.5 and Chromium fixture captures: packages/app-setup/evidence/identity/README.md. These are not live provider or deployed desktop acceptance.

5.2 · Before submission the user can review and edit their message; the action sends no project contents, paths, transcripts or logs automatically.
5.3 · Failure to open the browser draft offers a retry or a copy of the prepared text.
5.4 · After opening the draft the app says it opened a draft, never that feedback was received.
5.5 · Feedback offers optional sign-in only when requested, adds the verified Storytree account only to the editable message on request, and remains usable signed out or after a sign-in failure.

Account attribution is visible, editable and removable before either copy or browser handoff. Identity tokens and provider subjects never enter the draft. The desktop bridge and live staging journey remain separate integration work.

contracts.title: 5.6 · The shipped desktop offers sign-in for feedback only when its build carries a public WorkOS client ID and an HTTPS identity endpoint; it signs in through the system browser and the storytree-auth callback, and no token reaches the page.
contracts.description: Without both public settings stamped into the build (STORYTREE_WORKOS_CLIENT_ID, STORYTREE_IDENTITY_URL), the page's bridge has no feedbackIdentity member and the Send feedback surface shows no sign-in. With them, the preload asks the main process once, before the page loads, and the bridge carries only status, sign-in and sign-out, each answered by the main process with createFeedbackIdentity's id and email; the main process composes WorkOS's official Electron SDK without the SDK's own page bridge, so no token reaches the page. Callbacks reach it through the app's own single-instance lock (second-instance, open-url, or a start's arguments); the packaged app declares the storytree-auth scheme (macOS and Linux packaging) and registers it at runtime when sign-in is offered (Windows NSIS does not declare schemes). No first-run prompt, no account gate. Session behaviour: identity 2.5.

capabilities.title: 11 · Pipeline wiring
capabilities.description: At setup, or when a project adopts a pipeline, the agent wires the project's tests and storytree check into the user's CI through `wire_pipeline`, and proposes branch protection for the user to approve.

contracts.title: 11.1 · In a GitHub project, `wire_pipeline` writes storytree's workflow: on every pull request and push to main it runs the project's install and test commands on each system the user chose, and storytree check from storytree's source pinned to the user's storytree release
11.2 · In a project not on GitHub, `wire_pipeline` writes nothing and answers with the commands to add to the pipeline the user has
11.3 · `wire_pipeline` proposes branch protection (merge only what CI verified) as a command for the user to approve, and never changes a repository setting itself
11.4 · The storytree check step installs only what the check runs on, and runs no install script, so a download it never uses cannot fail it
contracts.description: The workflow's check step installs Guardrails' runtime closure alone (pnpm --prod --ignore-scripts --filter-prod), never the library's embedding runtime (onnxruntime-node), whose postinstall download once timed out a user's run (shop3, increment_777594ede2fd).

contracts.title: 11.5 · When GitHub refuses protection on the repository's plan (a free private repository), wire_pipeline offers merging only after both checks pass instead of a command that would fail, and only reads the setting
contracts.description: Before proposing branch protection, wire_pipeline reads the main branch's protection (a GET through gh). A 403 naming GitHub Pro or a public repository means the plan refuses it: no PUT command is offered, the user is offered merging only after both checks pass, and a paid plan or a public repository is left as the user's call. A 404 "Branch not protected" still gets the proposal. Found by shop3 (increment_b705470df887).

capabilities.title: 6 · Make a folder a project
capabilities.description: After the user says yes, a folder becomes a storytree project: the one check that refuses a folder already part of a project or a second trunk, the project opened (and its library seeded with the starter pack the first time), the folder recorded and approved as this machine's trunk, the marker left, and the app's choice recorded. Joining an existing project from another machine's checkout is the same step on purpose. Reading which project a folder belongs to stays with the hooks, in project routing.

contracts.title: 6.1 · A project name the library would refuse is refused when setting a folder up, and nothing is written.

6.2 · A folder that is a project's trunk, is inside one, is a git worktree of one, or holds one is refused when set up as another project, even with its marker gone, and nothing is written (ADR-0757 D3).
6.3 · A second folder for a project that already has a trunk on this machine is refused, joining or not, saying to work in a git worktree of the trunk; the trunk keeps routing (ADR-0757 D1, D3).

6.4 · A new folder given an existing project's name is refused unless it joins on purpose, on any machine, and the refusal suggests the first name no project has (name-2, name-3…); a matching folder name never joins (ADR-0757 D3, D4).

6.5 · A machine with no trunk for an existing project adds its checkout only on purpose (join), after which a git worktree of that checkout routes to the project, one project shared by both machines; joining a project that does not exist is refused (ADR-0757 D2, D4).

6.6 · A trunk whose folder is gone from this machine (moved or deleted) is forgotten when the project is set up or joined; a moved folder is never adopted on sight and reaches its project only once joined on purpose (ADR-0942 D4). A folder still there keeps its trunk, marker or not (6.2).

6.7 · Setting a new project up seeds its library with the starter pack: every starter role (orchestrator, librarian, change-reviewer, explorer, story-author, frontend-builder, blind-reviewer, corpus-investigator), the six test-quality checks a review's brief lists, and the principles, guardrails, patterns and processes they stand on; joining it from another machine, or setting it up again after a failed try, adds no second copy
contracts.description: The starter pack (owner, a question; grown to the full system by ADR-0996): a new user's library starts with every role storytree's own sessions work with, adapted for a user's project (its own test command, storytree check and the pipeline wire_pipeline sets up, never storytree's own gate or machines), so a first build is guided rather than improvised; with the notes each role stands on, links as its required reading, rules and refusals; and with the quality control checks (tautological expected value, test title without a contract number, proxy assertion, wall-clock duration, module mock, hidden skip) that its change-reviewer answers for every green change before it lands. The pack's text lives in one versioned place in the app setup story's source (app-setup/src/project/starter-pack.ts, starter-notes.ts and starter-roles.ts), with where each piece came from in starter-pack-classification.md.

contracts.title: 6.8 · Setting a folder up as project "site" leaves a marker naming "site" and its database's identity, and the project's library exists
contracts.description: The making half of what was 1.1 (ADR-0969 D3): routing's 1.1 now reads a marker; this promises setting up writes it.

contracts.title: 6.9 · Taking a newer starter pack adds what the library lacks and replaces only the pack records its user has not edited; an edited one is left and named with the newer text beside it
contracts.description: In a project an earlier pack seeded, taking the current pack writes each record the library does not hold under its title, replaces a pack-written record whose fields differ from the newer pack's, and leaves a record whose newest change is the user's, naming it with the newer fields beside it. Taking it again writes nothing.

capabilities.title: 12 · Import an existing project
capabilities.description: A storytree project imports an existing JavaScript or TypeScript project's folder (ADR-0993 D1, D2, D6): the folder is recorded on the project beside its trunk, with its repository and commit when it is a git checkout with a remote, and each package the folder declares (pnpm-workspace.yaml, else package.json workspaces, else the folder itself) becomes a mapped story through the library's mapStories, the only way a story is made mapped. Importing again maps the folder afresh, keeping what stands. The founding choice: the import reads the folder and writes nothing into it; the deliberate act of importing is its approval (ADR-0942). Front doors: storytree import <folder> and the import_project tool.

contracts.title: 12.1 · Importing a folder records it beside the project's trunk, with its repository and commit when it is a git checkout with a remote, and maps one story per package it declares, named as the package names itself, with no capabilities; nothing is written into the folder
12.2 · Importing a folder again adds a story for each new package, retires the stories whose package is gone, and leaves every other mapped story as it stands
12.3 · A folder that does not exist, is inside the storytree project, or has no package.json at its top is refused, saying why, and nothing is written

stories.title: Process ledger
stories.description: A session can finish its work without leaving a process it started running unnoticed. It records who started each run, keeps sight of runs whose request ended or timed out, lists what remains on this computer, stops only the caller's own runs with their children checked, and tells an honest empty inventory apart from an incomplete one.

capabilities.title: 1 · Record who started each run
capabilities.description:
Every tracked run names the session that started it and the computer where it runs. Background shells and detached servers keep that owner after the request or launcher that started them has gone away.

As built (foundation): @storytree/processes supplies one launchOwned boundary for resolved Claude Code/Codex callers and explicitly session-bound manual callers, with ownerFromCall accepting the agent link's public caller and agent context. Each launch durably records its owner, machine, optional project, executable/arguments, folder, launch time, PID and native lifetime observation before reporting tracked. Explicit parentRun/parentSession/subagent links survive the launcher; no PID adoption or folder/time/command inference assigns ownership. Failed launches or registration return a named gap, including a surviving PID when known. Installed CLI/MCP inventory, stop and clear doors are wired through the own package. Existing command hooks alone still do not register runs; this landing does not add launch coverage.

contracts.title: 1.1 · A registered run keeps its resolved session, machine, project when known, process identity, command, folder and start time.
1.2 · Two sessions in the same checkout keep separate process ownership, including when their command text is identical.
1.3 · A detached child registered at launch remains attributed after its launcher exits.
1.4 · A background command launched through the supported Claude Code, Codex or manual launch path has a durable ownership record before its launch is reported as tracked.
1.5 · A launch without a usable owner or successful registration reports that gap instead of assigning an owner by folder, start time or command text.

capabilities.title: 2 · Keep sight of unfinished runs
capabilities.description:
A request ending or timing out does not mean its work has stopped. Each run stays visible until the computer confirms it has ended, with anything it cannot establish shown as uncertain.

As built (foundation): readLedger and observeRuns retain records independently of requests, turns, sessions, claims and age, without a library connection. Request outcomes stay unknown unless the caller records evidence; explicit timeout evidence never implies process death. Native probes distinguish live/gone/unknown and compare Linux boot/start ticks, macOS boot/native microsecond start time or Windows exact creation FILETIME before attributing the current PID to a recorded lifetime. Failed or partial reads stay visible alongside readable records. Only registered runs and explicit child links are covered; unregistered launch paths and descendants remain untracked. Stopping and closing consume these observations in later capabilities and must revalidate identity before any signal.

contracts.title: 2.1 · A surviving process or owned child remains visible after a request timeout, labelling the request as timed out only when the caller supplied that evidence; otherwise its request outcome is unknown.
2.2 · Ending a turn, restarting or ending a session, releasing a claim, or passing twelve hours does not erase a surviving process record.
2.3 · A probe reports live, gone or unknown; unknown is never treated as confirmed dead.
2.4 · If a recorded PID has been reused, the replacement process is neither attributed to the old run nor signalled under its authority.
2.5 · Unreadable records and failed inventory reads remain visible as observation gaps alongside the records that could be read.

capabilities.title: 3 · See what remains
capabilities.description:
The session can list its remaining work or inspect all recorded sessions' work on this computer with an owner beside each run. The answer identifies what is running, what ended without reporting back, and what the inventory could not observe.

As built (listing API): @storytree/processes/listing exports listRuns and renderInventory over the foundation's observeRuns. The self view requires an explicit resolved owner and includes explicitly delegated descendants; the all-session view needs no owner and grants no cross-session stop authority. Rows keep command/arguments, folder, age, owner, machine, run/PID/lifetime identity and independent process/request findings. Only the inspector's exact lifetime is excluded. Read gaps, uncertain readings, foreign-machine records and coverage remain visible offline. Optional shared lifecycle readings have no stop action. The API offers an action only when a surface supplies an installed stop entry point and the row has an owned local live identity; otherwise it explains the absence.

As built (scope alignment): inventory uses the same ownership and conflicting-registration checks as stopOwned. An explicitly unknown calling agent refuses self inventory with a pointer to all-session inspection rather than reporting an empty scope. A named subagent sees only its own runs in self scope; its siblings and parent have no stop offer. Session callers retain explicitly delegated descendants, including established multi-hop parentSession links. An unchanged ledger no longer offers an action that stopping refuses for scope or conflicting ownership. Stopping still revalidates at invocation, so changed ownership or lifetime can alter the outcome.

As built (installed doors): storytree processes / own --all and MCP list_own_runs / list_all_runs call the listing API outside a project and with the app/database absent. Each self view offers only its installed stop entry point (CLI command or MCP tool), retaining the API's scope checks and explicit coverage. Both doors include the public app/database lifecycle reading as shared work with unknown native identity and no stop action, pointing to storytree app status / storytree app quit. An unknown shared lifetime keeps the overall reading incomplete.

As built (caller identity, supervisor-directed): with the app/database down, a CLI caller's self is the harness session named by CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID or CODEX_THREAD_ID, using the workspace command's environment seam. Missing or competing harness signals refuse self inventory, stop and clear and point to read-only own --all. MCP uses Codex's per-call session/thread metadata offline. When the library is reachable, exact call-id hook records supply the corrected session and named subagent, limiting it to its own runs. Claude MCP's shared server environment cannot identify an offline calling agent, so unresolved self operations refuse and point to list_all_runs / own --all. No authority is inferred from folder, timing, commands or a synthetic MCP session.

As built (delivery): the shared agent-link builder bundles both installed doors and stages Koffi's physical loader plus the host native module in its supported build/koffi/<ABI> prebuild layout, accepted by the unchanged installer payload verifier; the standalone CLI uses the same staging function. Desktop packaging replaces the host native package with the exact win32-x64 or win32-arm64 target before hashing each payload. The desktop manifest explicitly copies the native dependency directory as an extra resource, because electron-builder excludes a root node_modules directory from its general resource copy. Missing native targets fail the build. The habits card teaches all four own tools. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/doors2/. Built CLI and stdio MCP tests execute native inventory/stop/clear on each CI host; Linux additionally assembled both Windows payloads and checked target PE architecture and manifest hashes. Real installed Windows x64/arm64 harness acceptance remains with the laptop supervisor.

contracts.title: 3.1 · The self inventory distinguishes live, unknown and gone runs with command, PID/run identity, age, owner and folder, excluding the inspecting command itself.
3.2 · The all-session view works without a current session identity and attributes every readable local run without granting cross-session stop authority.
3.3 · Self-scoped operations use the existing harness identity and refuse an unidentified caller rather than returning an apparently empty inventory.
3.4 · Inventory works while the app or database is unavailable and states its machine and launch coverage, including unsupported or unregistered paths.
3.5 · Live work is a normal inventory result, with a usable stop action for the caller's stoppable rows; shared or uncertain-identity rows explain why no such action is offered.
3.6 · The retained CLI forms and the MCP tools return the same ownership and process findings through the owning package's API.

capabilities.title: 4 · Stop the work I own
capabilities.description:
The session can stop the runs it names without stopping another session's work. It checks the run and its covered children after each attempt, and reports failure whenever their disappearance cannot be confirmed.

As built: `@storytree/processes/stopping` exports `stopOwned({ owner, targets, home?, graceMs?, forceMs? })`. Targets are registered run UUIDs. Parent sessions cover explicitly delegated sessions and registered `parentRun` descendants; a named subagent cannot stop its parent or siblings. Malformed/unregistered, foreign-machine and conflicting-owner targets are refused; uncertain or replaced lifetimes never authorize signalling.

Each result states its computer, registered membership, exclusions, gaps, attempts and final process readings. Ownership is reread before each delivery. Polite and forced phases each check the root and every covered child; survivors, unknown readings, ownership changes, late registrations and unreadable inventory make the result unsuccessful. All records remain for capability 5.

Coverage is explicitly `registered-runs-and-linked-descendants`, with `nativeTree: unconfirmed` and the foundation launch-coverage warning. A successful scoped stop is not proof that unregistered OS descendants or the whole computer are clear. Linux uses identity-checked pidfds; macOS uses combined birth/PID-version evidence and audit-token signals; Windows uses a FILETIME-checked handle, targeted WM_CLOSE when available, then bounded force. No process-group or PID-only fallback is used.

As built (installed stop doors): storytree processes stop <run…> and MCP stop_own_run call stopOwned directly. They preserve every per-target stopped, already-gone, refused or incomplete outcome, native-tree limits, exclusions and gaps; unsuccessful results exit nonzero / set MCP isError. Unknown callers receive no authority. CLI, bundled CLI, source MCP and bundled stdio MCP tests stop a real owned child while refusing another session or sibling. Online Claude hook attribution also retains the named subagent boundary after a session reset. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/stopping/ and packages/processes/evidence/doors2/.

contracts.title: 4.1 · A stop outside the caller's explicitly established ownership/delegation scope is refused with its owner, while an unregistered or malformed target is refused without receiving a signal.
4.2 · A target whose original process is confirmed gone receives no signal; a reused PID or uncertain target identity cannot authorise a stop.
4.3 · Stopping an owned tree/group never includes a process with conflicting or unestablished ownership, and the covered membership is stated.
4.4 · A bounded initial stop and, under C1, forced escalation are each followed by checks of the root and covered children; a surviving child prevents a stopped result.
4.5 · A live or unconfirmed survivor keeps its record and makes the stop unsuccessful, regardless of whether the operating system accepted the signal.
4.6 · Multiple named targets each receive an outcome, and any refusal or survivor makes the overall result unsuccessful.

capabilities.title: 5 · Finish with an honest inventory
capabilities.description:
The session can clear records of work confirmed gone without hiding work that may still be running. Its closing check distinguishes an empty observed inventory from an incomplete observation, so a tidy record cannot become a false claim that the computer is idle.

As built: `@storytree/processes/closing` and `@storytree/processes` export `clearOwned({ owner, home?, knownGaps? })`, `readClosing({ home?, owner?, knownGaps?, shared? })` and `renderClosing(reading)`. Clear removes only the caller session/harness's records, with named subagents limited to their own records; delegated sessions' records are untouched. Original lifetimes and all registered descendants must be confirmed gone. Live, unknown and foreign records remain; unreadable records and known gaps prevent unproved child clearance. Removal failures are reported separately from successful removals.

Clear rereads records and child membership after probing and before unlinking. Changed, disappearing, reparented or newly registered children retain the affected parent; only this call's confirmed removals may shrink its previously observed membership. It preserves request evidence and gap records, never signals processes, and changes neither claims, sessions nor increments.

The closing reading reuses the listing API in all-session scope, irrespective of the caller, session end or released claims. Its status is `empty`, `remaining` or `incomplete`. Live/unknown rows stay visible; persisted read/registration gaps and caller-carried gaps whose persistence failed make it incomplete and name missing evidence separately. An empty verdict says “no tracked session work remains on this machine”, with the launch coverage and an explicit remote-machine limit. Shared work remains separately visible and is never stopped automatically.

These are point-in-time observations, without a launch interlock. Only explicitly registered descendants are covered; neither whole-machine idleness nor remote clearance is claimed. Evidence: `packages/processes/evidence/closing/README.md`, `red.txt`, `red-membership.txt`, `green.txt`, `gate.txt`, and the PR's three native CI checks. As built (installed clear doors): storytree processes clear and MCP clear_own_runs call clearOwned without signalling, preserve removed, retained, failed and gaps as separate fields, then return an all-session readClosing. Read gaps from clear are carried as knownGaps into that closing reading. Failed removals or clear gaps exit nonzero / set MCP isError while retaining the full result. Remaining live work and unknown shared app identity remain visible in the closing verdict; clear success does not claim closure or whole-computer idleness. The current doors perform no launches and have no additional unpersisted launch-gap source. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/doors2/.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Clear removes only the caller's records whose original processes and covered children are confirmed gone, leaving every other session's records untouched.
5.2 · Clear retains live, unknown and unreadable records and reports failed removals rather than claiming they disappeared.
5.3 · The closing reading cannot say that no owned work remains while live or unknown work survives, even if the session has ended or its claims have been released.
5.4 · A known registration/read gap makes the closing reading incomplete under G1, with the missing evidence named separately from known live work.
5.5 · An empty closing reading says “no tracked session work remains on this machine” with its coverage, and never claims a whole-machine census or remote-machine clearance.

stories.title: The website
stories.description: A visitor can decide whether storytree fits their work from its public website. The journey lives in packages/website: a plain introduction, the invitation waitlist, the app engine drawing a saved public plan, license and contact, published as static files on here.now.

capabilities.title: 1 · Home page
capabilities.description: A visitor opens on chapter 1: one Run tap plays the agent swarm, with a silent default, exits to the globe, remembered return visits and static fallbacks. The static home page also explains storytree and provides its waitlist entry point, repository, license and LinkedIn contact without JavaScript, including a LinkedIn alternative for joining. It builds with esbuild into dist and leaves the globe to the forest capability; all website code stays in packages/website.

contracts.title: 1.1 · Building the website produces a static page with locally resolvable assets and a forest mount; the page can be served without an application server.
contracts.description: Serve the emitted dist folder from an ordinary static server. The home document contains the forest mount; home, waitlist and not-found documents reference their exact content-versioned assets so cached assets from a prior publication cannot replace the current build. Every local asset and the separate waitlist page resolve without an application server or live library connection; lazy scene activation belongs to the forest capability.

reported.note: Static output test passes; esbuild bundles the public forest-world renderer and every referenced local home asset resolves.

contracts.title: 1.3 · With JavaScript disabled, a visitor can read the page, follow its repository, license and LinkedIn contact links, and see how to join the waitlist by messaging Mick on LinkedIn.
contracts.description: With scripting disabled, the built home page offers a normal link to the separate waitlist page. There a visitor can read repository, license and LinkedIn contact links and a visible LinkedIn alternative for joining without JavaScript; no app or forest initialization is needed.

reported.note: Seven website tests pass. Headless browser checks also pass with JavaScript disabled, clipboard success/denial, unchanged exact command and 404 return home.

contracts.title: 1.4 · The emitted not-found page gives a visitor a working link back to the home page.
contracts.description: Serve 404.html as the static host error document and follow its home link. The retained 0.2 line is reviewed as copy, not pinned in a test.

reported.note: Seven website tests pass. Headless browser checks also pass with JavaScript disabled, clipboard success/denial, unchanged exact command and 404 return home.

contracts.title: 1.6 · At phone width, a visitor can operate home-page controls by keyboard or touch: focus stays visible without clipping, and standalone controls have tap targets at least 44 CSS px high.
contracts.description: At 320 px and 390 px viewport widths, tab through the command area, copy button, navigation and footer links in Chromium. Observe the focus indicator fully inside the visible page or control, distinguishable against its adjacent background (at least 3:1 contrast); capture the command-focus state for independent visual review. Measure rendered hit targets for standalone links and buttons, including padding, at least 44 CSS px high, and activate each by keyboard and touch without hitting a neighbor. Use browser geometry and interaction observations, not CSS source assertions. This contract excludes inline prose links and the forest scene. It pins the behavior behind the home-control polish increment; it does not choose CSS selectors, outline placement or layout structure.

reported.note: Real Chromium proof passes at1440/390/320: pending success/denial retain focus, duplicate activation causes one write, Tab-away focus is not stolen, touch activates. Nine targets>=44px high; command outlines3px,10.45:1,unclipped. Captures in evidence/controls reviewed against legibility/resting-view principles.

verified.note: 2/2 checks passed, visited the locally built site (packages/website/dist), with waitlist writes intercepted locally, evidence [home], at commit e17d6ce3c5e9c81fd121916b23a9a09cf89031fe

contracts.title: 1.7 · With text enlarged to 200% at 320 px and 390 px viewports, home and not-found headers stay readable without overlap, and home headings and waitlist controls remain visible and usable without clipping or horizontal page overflow.
contracts.description: In headless Chromium, double computed text sizes at 320 px and 390 px. Measure rendered text ranges to show wordmark and navigation do not intersect or clip on home and 404, and the home hero and waitlist headings remain within the viewport. Verify the email input, optional choices, disclosure and submit control fit within the waitlist section and viewport, with readable labels; reach and operate header links and waitlist controls by keyboard and pointer using intercepted submission transport. Capture headers, headings and waitlist controls for independent review. Preserve ordinary 320 px and enlarged-text 1280 px behavior. This uses injected text sizing, not native browser zoom, and claims no native-zoom coverage. It covers visible header, heading and form-control behaviour without prescribing CSS declarations or row counts.

reported.note: Chromium --verify-enlarged now passes home/404 at320/390 and1280 with injected200% text. Rendered ranges do not overlap/leave viewport; copy control/label fit panel; no horizontal overflow; keyboard header links and pointer/keyboard clipboard activation pass. Ordinary320/390/1440 controls proofs also pass. Nativebrowserzoom remains unverified; captures under evidence/enlarged.

verified.note: 1/1 checks passed, visited the locally built site (packages/website/dist), with waitlist writes intercepted locally, evidence [home], at commit e17d6ce3c5e9c81fd121916b23a9a09cf89031fe

contracts.title: 1.8 · Chapter 1 plays from one Run tap to twelve waiting agents and the finale; its exits reach the globe without navigation, its sound is opt-in, return visits skip it with Replay, and reduced-motion or no-script visits see the static peak.

verified.note: 1/1 checks passed, Locally built website served from packages/website/dist, evidence packages/website/evidence/allocation, at commit 88fc0e6c8ffb559aaeb050a79d442a7342310c88

contracts.title: 1.9 · Act 1's turn hands over to Act 2 in about the time it is drawn to take, drawing frames throughout: its grain stops as the turn starts

contracts.title: 1.10 · Every page's tab shows the mark: day colours on a light setting, night on a dark one, with .ico and Apple touch icon fallbacks
contracts.description: The built index, waitlist and not-found pages link /favicon.svg (whose colours switch on prefers-color-scheme between the mark's day and night colourways), /favicon.ico (the day colourway's .ico) and a 180 px /apple-touch-icon.png.

contracts.title: 1.11 · Wherever the site names itself, the mark sits beside the name, drawn in the page's own colours
contracts.description: Each wordmark and the home heading carry the inline mark, hidden from screen readers, whose four roles read --mark-* variables that the stylesheet maps to the site's existing colours; the inline mark carries no colour of its own.

contracts.title: 1.12 · The home and waitlist pages share as a 1200 x 630 picture of the mark and the name
contracts.description: Both pages carry Open Graph and Twitter card tags naming the absolute /share.png, and the built site serves that file at 1200 x 630.

capabilities.title: 3 · Saved snapshot
capabilities.description: A session refreshes a committed public snapshot of storytree 0.3 with one command. The website and CI read that file without connecting to the library; only the fields required to draw and explain the public plan are exported.

contracts.title: 3.1 · One refresh command saves the selected plan, surveyed land, knowledge and arc records with their capture time.
contracts.description: ADR-0852 D4 extends the public drawing with the records needed by the tour. Compare the refreshed plan, surveyed territories/files/imports, story places, selected knowledge fields, open arc views and complete question text; keep builds offline.

reported.note: Actual command ran against isolated Postgres and temp source fixture. Saved selected plan, surveyed line, knowledge, arc, requested recording window and capture time; refused invalid window and synthetic credential without replacing saved bytes. Green log: [home]

contracts.title: 3.2 · Building and rendering from the committed snapshot works with library access unavailable.
contracts.description: Refuse database/network library access in the build/render proof and observe the saved scene data still loads. A failed refresh must leave the last valid snapshot intact.

contracts.title: 3.3 · The saved recording keeps its requested dated window and project while private fields, home paths, cloud ids and credentials cannot be published.
contracts.description: Refresh from mixed activity kinds and boundary timestamps. Keep only tour activity kinds, preserve project, recursively drop folder/machine/transcript/branch/task, redact home paths and cloud project ids, and refuse credential-like content before replacing the last valid file.

contracts.title: A saved growth replays the project's own recorded history: each stage holds only the stories, capabilities, links, contracts, reported health and live claims recorded by its time, scrubbed as storytree's own reading is
contracts.description: ADR-0879 D7: concepts are introduced on Conduit's real library as it grew; nothing is invented, and its private fields never publish. The saved growth holds its full plan's places; the tour frames a round still small by that round's own plan (one place per layout, one eased move to the full plan's: a question), read from the saved stage's own scene.

reported.note: planAt replays stories, capabilities, links, contracts and reported health by time; refreshGrowthSnapshot saves stages with live claims, scrubbed, window-checked. Real conduit-codex read: 21 stages, no private fields.

contracts.title: 3.5 · A saved growth stage draws land only from the survey of the code as it stood at the stage's time: no land before the first landing, then each stage the files of the latest landing at or before it.
3.6 · A saved growth carries the project's knowledge notes as dated changes, with only their public fields, so its replay grows the knowledge core
contracts.description: The shop's time-lapse must show the knowledge graph growing (ADR-0889 2.2a); the notes are kept as storytree's own reading keeps them: title, number, status and anchors, scrubbed.

reported.note: conduit-growth.test.ts 3.6 passes; shop-snapshot.json re-exported with its notes, stages byte-identical.

contracts.title: 3.7 · The shop's saved growth colours each stage only by the CI results recorded by its time: each contract reads verified as the newest push run on main finished by then judged it (ADR-0902), and before any such run its land reads as the agent's report alone

reported.note: red on a stub, green; on branch claude/increment-a0e1efc68913-cf90f3

contracts.title: 3.8 · Storytree's own saved growth samples its dated history into stages: empty first, a stage as each story's island arrives, stages spaced by the knowledge notes recorded, and complete last, every stage a real recorded moment in order
contracts.description: ADR-0889 2.2b: Act 2's arrival replays storytree's own project growing. Its stages are drawn from the library's dated history so islands and notes appear in the order they were recorded, compressed to a bounded number of stages; nothing is invented.

stories.title: The world
stories.description: The drawing engine a project's world is drawn with: it lays a project's stories out as islands, builds their ground and coasts, and draws them on a globe the viewer can turn and point at. Its 3D flat canvas, which also dresses the islands with 0.2's pines and props, is mounted by no product surface since ADR-0804 D1. Its code lives in packages/forest-world (story id forest-world); the forest story draws with it.

capabilities.title: 1 · Scene layout
capabilities.description: Turns a project's stories and capabilities into a forest scene: islands and parcels on a hex lattice, trails between them and the props they carry, then maps that scene to 3D descriptors (src/core, src/scene.ts, src/world-to-3d.ts). *Noted in place, 2026-10-05 (ADR-0804 D1): the globe keeps only the scene's ground cells (each island's coast, parcels and reach); the trees, flora and props it still computes are drawn by nothing on a product surface.*

contracts.title: 1.2 · The same input always gives the same trail network, and no visible trail runs into an island that is not its own.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/forest-world/src/core/routing.test.ts.

contracts.description: Protected by packages/forest-world/src/forest-ground/forest-ground.test.ts. Rewritten 2026-10-05 for ADR-0920: the engine hands over ground cells alone, so 'each kind to its mesh family' has one kind left.

capabilities.title: 2 · Island ground
capabilities.description: Builds each island's ground for the globe: its relaxed parcel cells and the coast rims clipped from them, drawn in exact colour. *Noted in place, 2026-10-06: the stepped cliff edge and the banded ground shader with its grass, sand, wheat, rock, wear and shadow layers left with the flat canvas (ADR-0920); the shore band and the land's fall to its waterline left with the last road that stood on them (increment_1c39930c645a). Only the waterline's dip (SHORE_DIP) and the relief's height bound (landHeightRange) remain, sizing the plates' clearance above the shell.*

contracts.title: 2.3 · The ground is drawn in exact colour (no output transform, no tone curve, no input conversion), and a canvas with any one of the three wrong is not exact colour.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/forest-world/src/exact-colour.test.ts.

capabilities.title: 5 · The canvas
capabilities.description: The React-Three-Fiber canvas that hosts the globe: it says when it is ready, frames the camera, reuses prepared ground when the scene has not changed, and draws on demand, including under a camera another canvas drives. PlanetWorldCanvas is the live canvas; the flat ForestWorldCanvas and its evidence page were deleted under ADR-0920.

Pinned by planet.test.ts, island-surface.test.ts, planet-view.test.ts and knowledge-core's globe-points.test.ts; evidence in packages/forest/src/view/evidence/one-program-per-frame.

contracts.description: Roads keep their share of an island as the camera zooms, down to a floor that keeps them visible.

contracts.title: 6.6 · Globe framing sets the short-side span in radii, and a sideways CSS-pixel offset preserves the eye and any user zoom when only the offset changes.
contracts.description: A host frames the orthographic globe in radii and can move its projection sideways in CSS pixels to leave room for an adjacent card. Framing and offset follow viewport resize without turning or moving the camera. Changing only the offset does not reset wheel or pinch zoom.

contracts.title: 6.7 · The globe independently hides its sea, island grounds and roads while keeping its camera and mounted plate children; hiding the whole exterior still preserves its inside.
contracts.description: Sea, grounds and roads are separately visible by default. Grounds include their coast lines but exclude host-provided plate children. Changing visibility preserves mounted geometry, globe rotation and camera zoom. The existing surface=false gate hides every exterior surface and plate child together while continuing to draw the inside.

contracts.title: 6.8 · A lit link's lane is one unbroken strip from its capability's territory on the island built on, along its road between islands, to its capability's territory on the island building on it, following only lines drawn on each island; it fills its road with a soft glow in its colour beyond the road's edge, upstream blue and downstream violet, with a small mark in its colour at each end; where both colours share a road or an end, they remain distinguishable side by side
contracts.description: Each lit link keeps its identity and one continuous route. From each dock the lane runs on inland along the way the host gives (forest 3.7), the borders between the island's territories and the coast between two borders, to its capability's territory, a one-link road wide; where the dock is already on that territory, or the host gives no way, the lane ends at the dock (ADR-0991 D4, which re-decides ADR-0951 D1). A link within one island lights nothing. A lane fills its road's width, and a glow in its colour spreads beyond the road's edge (ADR-0951 D2). A mark in the lane's colour lies at each end, appearing when the lane's front leaves or reaches it. Opposite relation colours on shared stretches each take just under half the road, in separate lateral lanes parted by a hairline of road, meeting smoothly at their junctions, and their marks sit side by side at a shared end. Every road and lit lane is drawn solid, whatever its links: a type-only link (ADR-0991 D1) stays marked on its road and lane, but is drawn like any other, by the owner's direction of 2026-10-11 (resteer_354c8423f114). Nothing lights off the roads: the plain coast-to-coast lanes for row dependencies with no road were removed (ADR-0991 D5).

contracts.title: 6.9 · Every lane of a selection starts at once and grows from its start by physical distance at one steady pace in its animation clock, so the selection settles in its longest lane's time; one warm head shows per shared stretch of one colour, slow frames preserve visible growth, and reduced motion shows every lane whole immediately with no head
contracts.description: Every lane of a selection starts when the selection is made and its front moves at one steady ground speed (no per-lane ease), so fronts sharing a stretch travel as one; a lane's time is its length over that speed, and the selection settles in the time of its longest lane however many links light (ADR-1000 D1). The front sits at that cumulative route length, independent of mesh sampling. Each stretch of route (consecutive route points, compared by position) of one colour is led by the lane whose front reaches it first, ties going to a stable order; a lane's head shows only while its front is on a stretch it leads, growing in over a short distance, so links over one road show one head on it, a wave splits at a fork and merges at a join, and an added link adds no head on a trunk and no time to settle. An up and a down lane on one road keep their own halves and each its own head. The head is warm lamplight (ADR-1000 D2): near the front the lane is tinted towards cream and a little wider, fading behind it; the head fades out once the lane is whole. Each rendered frame advances the animation clock by at most 80 milliseconds, so slow rendering can extend completion beyond the nominal duration. Normal motion starts undrawn; unchanged selection and route geometry preserve progress across unrelated updates. Reduced motion shows every complete lane immediately, with no head (ADR-0951 D2).

contracts.title: 6.10 · The globe draws nothing while its canvas is off screen, and draws again as soon as any of it is back
contracts.description: While no part of the globe's canvas is in the viewport it asks WebGL for no frames, however busy its animations are, and keeps its scene and camera, preserving the running R3F clock without resetting it. Animations do not restart: recorded growth continues on that clock, while selection lanes retain their front and resume under contract 6.9's render-driven clock. As soon as any of it is back on screen it draws again. Where the browser cannot tell what is on screen (no IntersectionObserver) it draws as before. It lets a host mount the globe early, below the fold, without paying for frames nobody sees.

Restored while off screen it still draws nothing (6.10) and draws as soon as any of it is back. It does not cover a context the browser never restores.

contracts.title: 6.16 · Live roads grow by distance from dependency to dependent on first display and arrival; established shared roads stay drawn, unrelated updates preserve progress, and reduced motion shows the complete roads immediately
contracts.description: A host explicitly enables live road growth. Actual edge identities retain their arrival windows across rerouting; only newly arriving edges receive new windows. Shared segments keep the earliest established road, without disappearing or growing again when another link arrives. The physical front supports either segment orientation, and slow rendered frames preserve visible progress using the bounded animation clock. Recorded replay retains its existing schedule and clock. A road can reroute spatially when the real topology changes; staying drawn does not promise fixed geometry.

stories.title: The local database
stories.description: storytree runs its own Postgres on this machine from binaries it ships, so nothing needs installing: the app's library database and the throwaway database the tests run against both start and stop through it, and a data directory has one owner at a time, recorded beside it. Its code lives in packages/local-postgres (story id local-postgres).

capabilities.title: 1 · Postgres binaries
capabilities.description: Finds initdb, pg_ctl and postgres for this machine: from the @embedded-postgres package built for it (the x64 one on Windows arm64, run under emulation), or from the directory a packaged app ships them in.

contracts.title: 1.1 · The binaries come from this machine's @embedded-postgres package, and on Windows arm64 from the x64 one; with none installed, the error names every package it looked for.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/local-postgres/src/local-postgres.test.ts ("the binaries come from this machine's @embedded-postgres package...").

contracts.title: 1.2 · A directory handed over by a packaged app is used when it holds initdb, pg_ctl and postgres, and refused, naming it, when it does not.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/local-postgres/src/local-postgres.test.ts (same test as 1.1).

capabilities.title: 2 · A server on a data directory
capabilities.description: Makes a cluster in a data directory the first time, asking every connection for the installation's password (SCRAM; a legacy trust cluster is converted at start), starts a server on it listening on 127.0.0.1 only, makes sure clients' ordinary role (storytree: may create databases, owns every database, no superuser) exists and owns what the superuser made before, hands back its url signing in as that role, and publishes the private connection handoff (ADR-0941) while it runs; stops it; while it runs, an owner record beside the directory (`<dataDir>.owner.json`) names the process that holds it, which is how others learn whether storytree is running and where.

contracts.title: 2.1 · A cluster is made only where there is none, asking every connection for the installation's password and listening on 127.0.0.1 only; a directory holding anything else is refused and left untouched.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/local-postgres/src/local-postgres.test.ts ("2.1 ensureCluster makes a cluster only when there is none: asking every connection for the installation's password, and listening on 127.0.0.1 only"). Password-only since PR #941 (increment_428779c116fe, ADR-0941): there is no trust path.

contracts.title: 2.2 · A started server answers SELECT 1 at the url handed back; stop stops it, a second stop is harmless, and it can be started again, on a port asked for.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/local-postgres/src/local-postgres.test.ts ("start runs the server on the data directory...").

contracts.title: 2.3 · A start on a data directory a live process holds is refused with a DataDirInUseError naming that process and its owner, and the holder's server is left running.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/local-postgres/src/local-postgres.test.ts ("a second start on a data directory a live process holds is refused..."). The agent link reads the same owner record to find the running app.

contracts.title: 2.4 · A server left running by a process that died is stopped and replaced, and a dead owner's record alone is cleared, so the start goes ahead.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/local-postgres/src/local-postgres.test.ts ("a server left running by a process that died...").

contracts.title: 2.5 · A start can carry server settings for that run, as the throwaway test server runs with fsync, synchronous commit and full-page writes off; a start without them keeps the cluster's own, and a setting that is not one plain word is refused before anything starts.
contracts.description: The test runner's throwaway Postgres throws its data away, so it need not wait on a disk flush per commit or per project database (costly on Windows and macOS CI). The app's own server never gets these settings.

contracts.title: 2.6 · The server lets in only a client with the installation's password, which it hands over privately while it runs
contracts.description: No client without the password gets in, postgres included; a wrong password is refused. The secret lives in <dataDir>.auth (this OS user only), the owner record names the handoff without carrying it, and connection.json (ADR-0941 version 1) names this launch's token and port, is withdrawn at stop and the same secret serves the next start. Protected by local-postgres.test.ts 2.6.

contracts.title: 2.7 · A cluster made when local connections were trusted is given the password before its server starts again, keeping its data, and an interrupted start never reopens it
contracts.description: The password is set in single-user mode (no network), then pg_hba.conf replaced and a marker written last, so an interrupted migration is redone at the next start and no trust line survives a failed start; a trust line added later is removed at the next start. Protected by local-postgres.test.ts 2.7.

contracts.title: 2.8 · Clients sign in as an ordinary role that owns storytree's databases, never as the superuser
contracts.description: The url and the handoff sign in as the role storytree: it may create databases and owns every database in the cluster with what is in them, but is no superuser and makes no roles; the superuser's password stays with the launcher, and databases and tables a cluster's superuser made before are handed to it at the next start. Only a throwaway test server, asked to, hands out the superuser.

contracts.title: 2.9 · A throwaway test server can hand back the superuser's url beside its client's, for tests' setup, while its clients and handoff stay the ordinary role
contracts.description: Started with superuserUrl true, the handle carries superuserUrl (signing in as postgres, same port) besides url (the ordinary role storytree); the published handoff still names storytree; a start not asking hands back none. So pnpm test can run tests as the client role and keep the superuser for role-making setup only (increment_36281861bfe6).

contracts.title: 2.10 · On Windows the sign-in is kept private beside a data directory whose folder lets this user change files but not take ownership (a checkout under C:\code): the access list is set without asking to change an owner the user already is
2.11 · On Windows a sign-in folder a failed first run left behind is made private before any sign-in goes into it
contracts.description: A first run whose protection failed leaves <dataDir>.auth made but open to what its parent folder grants; the next run must protect it rather than trust it, so no sign-in is ever written into a folder others can read.

capabilities.title: 3 · Dropping a throwaway test database
capabilities.description: Every package's tests drop the databases they made through this one module, which rides out Postgres's known refusals, instead of each package keeping its own copy.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Only a database named with a test token is dropped; any other name is refused before anything is sent to the server
contracts.description: A mistake in a test can never drop somebody's real database on a shared server.

contracts.title: 3.2 · A drop ends the connections still open to the database, falls back to a plain DROP when Postgres refuses to end another backend, retries a bounded number of times while the database is still in use, and propagates every other error
contracts.description: The known teardown flakes are ridden out in one place, and a database that cannot be dropped is never left silently.

stories.title: The dev loop
stories.description: A session developing storytree gets from a change to a proven landing with one set of commands: its worktree is installed for it, the tests the change can reach run to an end that always says what passed, failed or never ran, the gate reports PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN, and the checks that keep the repo honest (package boundaries, agent guidance, the library's own health and backups) run the same way locally and in CI. Its code lives in packages/dev-loop (story id dev-loop), moved there from scripts/.

capabilities.title: 1 · Test scoping
capabilities.description: Decides from a branch's changes which packages `pnpm test` runs, the same way locally and in CI, and says so on its first line (`scope: ...`); flags force everything, name units, or rerun what failed (test-scope.mjs).

contracts.title: 1.3 · `--full` runs everything, `--only` runs the named units, and `--rerun-failed` reruns only what failed or never ran.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/dev-loop/src/test-scope.test.mjs.

contracts.title: 1.5 · A file named to run alone is a unit of its own whenever its package runs, and its package's unit runs every other file

contracts.title: 5.5 · An acceptance run's verdict on a contract is minted by its harness from the checks it observed: passing only when it ran checks for the contract and every one passed, failing when any failed, and nothing written when none ran or one was not observed. It is written to the verified column by "acceptance run", with the commit and the evidence path in its note.

contracts.description: ADR-0825 D2: a skip is data, not silence, and no verdict older than a skip stands unmarked. History keeps the old verdict.

The queue's run tested the very commit main fast-forwarded to, so it is that commit's CI evidence.

The marks hold its capability back on the health worklist until the run records it.

contracts.description: After a capability moves to another story, tests elsewhere still titled with the old story's package prefix keep passing but credit no contract. Own health says so for each such title instead of dropping it silently (friction_2f5f177c7e09).

capabilities.title: 6 · Running the tests
capabilities.description: `pnpm test` runs the scoped units against a throwaway local Postgres, each unit under a deadline, reporting which test is still running, and ends in a PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN table; a second heavy run on the machine queues behind the first, and a Node.js known to crash is refused at the start (test.mjs, unit-run.mjs, test-running-reporter.mjs, heavy-lock.mjs, node-runtime.mjs).

contracts.title: A unit past its deadline is killed with its whole process tree, naming the test still running; completed failures print their assertion details and location before the deadline can kill the unit; a test that fails while leaving a handle open ends its unit with that failure, not a hang. A run given a deadline (STORYTREE_TEST_DEADLINE) cuts the unit running at it the same way and leaves later units NOT RUN; stalled outside any unit past it, the run names where it stalled and exits non-zero.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/dev-loop/src/unit-run.test.mjs.

reported.note: The real deadline regression now retains a concurrent later file's completed assertion, actual/expected values, and source location before killing the hung unit and its descendant. Existing file stderr diagnostics still pass.

contracts.title: 6.2 · A second heavy run, including a browser evidence command, waits for the first and names who holds the lock; a gone holder blocks nothing, and interruption releases the command and its lock.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/dev-loop/src/heavy-lock.test.mjs: the command wrapper shares the gate/test lock, preserves arguments and exit status, inherits the hold into child work, and cancels waiting or running commands.

contracts.title: 6.3 · On Windows, a Node.js without libuv's fix is refused at the start, naming the crash and the release that fixes it; off Windows none is refused.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/dev-loop/src/node-runtime.test.mjs.

contracts.title: 6.4 · A run's start keeps the previous run's server log readable, one log deep, and says where it was kept.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/dev-loop/src/server-log.test.mjs.

contracts.title: 6.5 · The coverage run records, for each source file of a package, the passing numbered tests of each capability number whose test file executed its functions, times how many of its functions that file ran, in the test's own process or in any process it started, bundled code included through its source map. Story-owned browser proofs preserve their measured contribution across Node regeneration; failed or unexecuted proofs allocate nothing.
contracts.description: ADR-0838 D3: the writer of the coverage map the code survey reads (survey-coverage.json in each story's package). App's map stays in packages/app and also records App-owned apps/desktop/src from the same checkout, using package-relative paths and the same measured-function/source-map rules (Code survey 8.9). Node proofs under Desktop must explicitly name app N.M because Desktop also hosts other stories' mounted proofs; package-local numbered tests retain their existing own-story attribution. Browser proofs must name their own story and contract. Foreign-story source and other checkouts contribute nothing to App, and Node regeneration preserves passing measured browser contributions.

reported.note: Final full local gate passes all 17 units. Equivalent source-map cache URLs now preserve real captured functions after red; App/Desktop weights, foreign exclusions and repeated Node regeneration pass. Updated cross-platform CI required after initial Windows failure.

contracts.title: 6.6 · A test file whose process fails is named with its exit code or signal and the tail of its own stderr, apart from every other file's output
contracts.description: The test runner's reporter explains a file-process failure the spec reporter reduces to "test failed": which file, how its process ended, and what it wrote to stderr, even when files run concurrently.

contracts.title: 6.7 · The test ratio report gives test and implementation code lines per package and overall, counting no blank or comment line and no // inside a string, template or regular expression
contracts.description: `pnpm test-ratio`, the report a landing session reads at an increment boundary (never a gate): how many lines of test code there are for each line of implementation.

contracts.title: 6.8 · When CI requests test evidence, each unit keeps a separate result with its checkout commit, platform, run attempt and repository-relative test identities; later or nested runs cannot overwrite it.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/dev-loop/src/unit-run.test.mjs. The runner adds JUnit alongside the spec/watchdog reporters, creates a fresh directory per invocation, and strips the evidence destination from child environments. Existing Windows CI uploads one immutable artifact per attempt; no additional Windows job is needed.

reported.note: Real child test runs produced three separate immutable per-unit result directories across two units and a repeated run, each preserving actual checkout SHA, platform, run attempt and relative identities; evidence destination absent from child environment.

contracts.title: 6.9 · The tests are handed the superuser's url for their setup as STORYTREE_TEST_PG_ADMIN_URL, beside the url they connect with; a run given a server's url uses that one for both unless given an admin url too
contracts.description: The step that lets tests run as the ordinary role storytree while role-making setup keeps the superuser (increment_36281861bfe6). Until library, agent-link, cli and website setup read the admin url, the client url stays the superuser's.

contracts.title: 6.10 · A run tests several units at once (--jobs, else STORYTREE_TEST_JOBS, else 2 with a core left free, or the machine's own default under 6.13), slowest first; each unit's output prints whole under its name when it ends, and a unit's deadline is learned only from runs that tested as many at once
contracts.description: So a full run is paced by its slowest unit rather than the sum of all of them (increment_f465972caeaf), while the table, the record for --rerun-failed, the timing history and the deadlines keep their meaning.

contracts.title: 6.12 · A unit run alone starts only once every other unit has ended, and nothing starts beside it
contracts.description: So forest's software-GL browser proof does not share a 3-CPU macOS runner with other units' work (run 38038938459 stalled at load average 42; increment_ba747f54277d), without widening its 15 s no-new-frame wait.

contracts.title: 6.13 · Where the test Postgres runs under emulation (Windows arm64) the default is one unit at a time and the run says why, --jobs and STORYTREE_TEST_JOBS still deciding; and a unit with too few passes at this concurrency is never given a deadline under twice its slowest recent pass at any
contracts.description: So a full run passes at its defaults on a machine that cannot carry two units at once, and a unit slower than the default deadline is not killed again after every pass (increment_3f535ac2dc4e: on the Surface Pro two at once failed 6 of 26 units and took the same 16 minutes as one at a time).

capabilities.title: 7 · The gate
capabilities.description: `pnpm gate` runs the typecheck, the scoped tests and, when generated guidance may have changed, the guidance check, in one foreground run ending in a PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN table with a reason for every NOT RUN (gate.mjs).

contracts.title: 7.1 · The gate runs the typecheck and the scoped tests, and marks guidance NOT RUN with its reason, without failing, when no generated guidance changed.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/dev-loop/src/gate.test.mjs.

contracts.title: 7.2 · When the change scope cannot be read, the gate runs the guidance check rather than assuming nothing changed.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/dev-loop/src/gate.test.mjs.

contracts.title: 7.3 · An interrupted gate stops the running check and its children, marks it and the remaining checks NOT RUN, and exits nonzero.
contracts.description: Protected by packages/dev-loop/src/gate.test.mjs.

contracts.title: 7.4 · A branch that changes a capability its increment does not list fails the gate, naming the capability; a branch naming no increment is NOT RUN with its reason
contracts.description: ADR-0949 D3: check:capability-list maps the branch's changed files to capabilities by the edit claims' seam (a file's own declaration, else the code survey's inference) and fails, naming each capability and the files that changed it, when one is missing from the increment's capabilities list. Runnable alone for CI.

contracts.title: 7.5 · The gate installs an uninstalled worktree before its first check; one its install cannot fix leaves every check NOT RUN with the reason and exits nonzero
contracts.description: A pool lane makes its worktree with storytree workspace, so no session-start hook installs it; the gate must not report every unit failing on a missing module.

contracts.title: 7.6 · A branch's checks read the plan with its increment's pending changes laid over, and each pending change written against an older record fails the gate naming both entries
